ses•-•••-•••-. Ali OLD-TIME L Up the stair they merrily climb— Three little white gowns at sleepy-time. Big brother Benny and baby Grace, And funny Wee-boy with the happy face, And mamma sings, as they mount the stair, These cranky words to a queer old air— "Go to bed, sleepy-head, And sleep for money to buy a cow r' Said Benny, "Such a humlsug I never heard; And I don't believe it a single word. If I slept all night, and slept all day, Do you think I'd be any richer, say ?" The Wee-boy nodded his curly head, "Mamma, sing it aden !" the baby said, "Go to bed, sleepy-head. And sleep for money to buy a cow." Said Benny, "Who made such a silly song? It tells a story; #, must be wrong." • "I can't tell, Benny, I only know It was sung to me long years ago,' By your auld Scotch granny, sweet and dear, When I was as small as baby here. So go to bed, sleepy-head, And sleep for money to buy a cow." ' "If grandmamma said it, it must be true; But I don't believe it, now say, do you ? And tell me, mamma, I'd like to know, - When she sent you to bed, did you alwaysgo?" "Yes, I always went, just as you must now.', Said the funny Wee-boy, "Then where's your coiv?" "Oh, go to bed, sleepy-head, The cow jumped over the moon, they said." NANCY PATTON MCLEAN.

OUR MEADOW. Grasses whispering to the breeze, Stately overarching trees, And a fringe of wildwood, Live, untouched by blame or praise, In this haunt of olden days— Meadow of our childhood. Here, when storms are on the wing, Cheery robins come to sing, Taking crumbs for payment; Not afraid of frost or snow, For their households bravely go Clothed in scarlet raiment. Here, beneath the April skies, , Spotless violets arise, Each a timid vestal • . Bluebells follow them betimes, f • Ringing out their joyous chimes, On occasions festal. Wreaths of polished briony, Honeysuckles fair to see, Twine amid the hedges; Wee forget-me-nots below With the little speedwells grow— -1 7 Summer's blue-eyed pledges. ';.." But we love our meadow most When it holds a mighty host s. .;• Of another order; When the buttercups unfold All their shining cloth of gold ' To its utinost border; When the clover round about ' Flings a wealth of perfume out, Which the bee appraises; ' And the children hither stray, ° All the happy summer day, i Ankle-deep n daisies! Sweet it is 'when morning beams Wake the blossoma from their dreams, O'er them lightly bending; • Or when zephyrs from the west , On its bosom come to rest While the day is ending; ' Sweeter when the fragrant breath Of the grasses, low in death, For a while hath tarried, Ere from hence the loaded wains Rumble through the shady lanes, And the hay is carried. But the past andpresent meet, And all seasons seem complete • Mid its lights and shadows; • Fairest field 'neath sun or star, None i like it near or far,: Loveliest of meadows! —Sunday Magazine.
MARY ROWLES.

RAILWAY MA/ans.—Delays are dangerous. A train in time saves nine. There is no place like home; the diffi- culty is to get there.. Do not halloo till'you are safe. A railway train is the thief of time. The great charm of a railway accident is, no matter how many are killed and =angled, no one is to blame. A Loma WIFE.—" He married her for love." "And did beget it ?" "Oh, yes; he got it. His wife is chuck full of love." "Glad to hear it, for Bill's a good fellow." "Yes, she's full of love—she loves to dress finely, loves to show off on the street, loves to go to theatres, loves -other men's company, and, seemingly, loves to give her husband all the worriment possible." An old Methodist minister, on account of long acquaint- ance, was disposed to spend a groat deal of his time in the office of the publishing firm of the Harpers of New York. One day- he said—" Brother Harper, I never could under- stand what your duties are here. I know that brother John is the cashier, that brother Wesley is the oorrespon. dent, and brother Fletcher is the editor; but I never could learn what -were the duties of brother James." "My dirties," replied Mr. Harper, "Are the hardest of them all. My business is to entertain the bores." An Englishman had taken a shooting in Scotland, and, he being an unpractised sportsman, the situation was 'rather novel to him. After the first day's shooting, when, with the assistance of the keeper, a bag of about fifty' brace of grouse had been got, the Englishman was asked 'what he wished to be done with the birds. "What is usually done with them ?" he inquired; and it was ex- plained to him that, after enough had been laid aside for larder requirements, the remainder were generally distributed among friends. The custom was observed, the shooting tenant sending grouse to his various friends. At the close of the second day the keeper inquired what was to be done with the fresh supply of birds, when the innocent sportsman looked at the heavy bag of grouse. "Oh, bury them !" he exclaimed. "I'll be shot if I'll write out more addresses !" A BOVINE STEEPLECHASEIL—A bullock bred and raised in the Bush, though he may be as fat as a pig, is ajvery • different animal from ;the sleepy creatures that one meets on their way to an English market, driven by a Couple of small boys and a dog. Ille is as quick on his • legs as a rabbit, and for a few furlongs it takes a good horse to get away from him, and, moreover, as a rule, he can jump like a deer. One day my brother was drafting in the "lane," and I was working "the pound." ' I had just turned a beast back into the lane, and was going back through the. gate, when my brother sang out, " Stranger ! clear out, or he'll have you !" Looking round, I saw a great hard-skinned white bullock belong- ing to the next station, with horns about a yard long, just behind me. He was charging up the lane full gallop, and as I sprang through the gateway and turned aside, he made a sweep at me which just grazed my ribs, but, fortunately, did no damage beyond 'tearing my shirt. Without the least hesitation, the brute went straight at the opposite fence of the pound, six feet high, and got over without a fall, though he hit the top rail hard with every leg he had. The performance was the more astonishing as he had not a very long run, and what there was of it up the lane was slightly up-hill. • We ran him round again, and into the lane, as he had jumped into the wrong yard. The next time he came up we all let him alone to see what he would do. He came 'full tilt up the lane as usual, looking for someone to kill, and when he got into the pound, he turned sharp to the right, pulled himself together, and going straight for the gate at the far end of the pound, five feet six high, he cleared it without a mistake. After this performance wa concluded to leave him alone until we had finished drafting. In some yards it is the fashion to leave a big post, or the stump of a tree, about four feet high in the middle of the big yard, so as to afford a shelter for ' anyone who is charged .and has no time to get to the rails at the side. We had nothing of the kind at Mount Spencer; but I remember a most ludicrous scene at Gracemere, a station near Rockhampton, where there was one of those harbours of refuge in the middle of the yard. Seven or eight men Were yarding up a mob of cattle, when suddenly an old cow came out and charged in a most business-like manner. Five men all ran for their lives to the post. The first who got there, of course, was all right; but there was only room for one, so the next man had to hang on to the belt of the man in front, and so on, till the whole five were extended in a row. The cow charged, and, of course, no one could tell -which side of the post she would pass, so it was not until she was within a few feet that the human tail swung round out of her way, a yell of terror escaping from the last two men, as the brute's horns passed within an inch of them. Quick As lightningg the cow turned and charged again,7and again the end of the tail had a narrow escape. Four time thecow charged, four time the tail swept round, their howls of anguish ming- lingNvith shouts of laughter from the men on the rails who were looking on.—Hon. Question for Debating Clubs.—Can a man, while aslee in the daytime, have the nightmare? EVENING WEAL—We are constantly told that "the evening wore on "—but what the evening wore on such occasions we are not informed. lAs it the cloSe of 'a summer's day? A little girl, walking one day with :her mother in a graveyard, and reading one after another the praises of those who slept beneath the turf, said, "Mamma, I wonder where they bury all the sinners ?" Seven-year-old from the North, who is on a visit to friends in town, seeing the father of the family on the first morning of his visit brushing his teeth: 'Div ye aye shairp yer teeth afolt ye tak' yer braikfist?" Ponce in a Vile.—" Don't you dake a liddle sleep after dinner ?" asked Jake .Levy of Mose Schaumberg. "I dakes a liddle rest vonce in a vile, put not every day." " Vy, don't you take a rest every. day?" " Pecause my vife don't go to schleep every day. yen she goes to schleep, den I gets my rest, but not odervise." What soothes suffering, what sanctifies la,bour, what makes a man good, strong, wise, Patient, benevolent, just and at the same time humble and great, worthy of liberty; is to have before him the perpetuaPvision of a better world casting its rays through the darkness of this lift. -None are truly happy but those who are busy; for real happiness lies only, ia„ useful work of some kind, either of the hand 'of the head, so long-as, over-exertion of eithei. is avoided. It should be the aim of every one to be employed. If all men and , women were kept at some useful employment, there Would. be. less sorrow and wickedness in the world. , Life consists, not in the abundance of thing's that:we possess, but in the good and honest work thatwe do. Let us vow that we will live, not to lade our souls with the thick clay pf .earthly riches—not to daub our lives with the untempered mortar of human praise—not to waste our labours on those gains of the wilderness which can neither satisfy the soul's hunger nor quench its thirst, but for what is best and greatest, to do our duty to all the world. Don't be a grumbler. Some people contrive to get hold of the prickly side of everything, to run against all the sharp. corners and disagreeable things. Half the strength spent in growling would often set things right. You may as well make up your mind, to begin with, that no one ever found the world quite as he would like it; but you are to take your part of the trouble and bear it bravely. You will be sure to have burdens laid upon you that belong to other people, unless you are a shirker yourself; but don't grumble. If the work needs doing, and you can do it, never mind about ,that other who ought to have done it and didn't. Thor workers who fill up the gaps and smooth away the rough spots, and finish up the jobs that others leave undone—they are the true peacemakers, and worth a whole regiment of growlers. Dose vere his lasht words, Mr. Viggins, unt ven I dells you you can haf dot goat at ten toiler unt sixty-five cents you vill know, ,I am selling eet for affection unt' not for money valhe." Wiggins had to take the coat. THE CURRENCY OF THE UNITED STATES.—In truth, the United States is the dearest country in tie world to travel in. I have made a careful computation, and find that a dollar, nominally valued at four shillings, will buy of the necessaries and luxuries of life exactly as much as a shilling will in England. Money is easily made here, wages are high, profits are large, and the country is full of men grown suddenly rich. A dollar here or there is a matter not worth the, expenditure of time for its con- sideration. 'lt is a broad, significant fact that a five-cent piece, value twopence-halfpenny, is practically the low- est coin current in the States, and that it will sometimes buy for you what a penny would bring in a More effete country. There are, of course, cents; but eicept to buy stamps, and in New York an evening paper, you might as well be without them. Where the currency begins in everyday life is with the quarter, value one shilling. With these liberally dispensed on the slightest provoca- tion one can get along comfortably through the little needs and services of the day. Last night, strolling about the town, I stopped to hear a street hawker, who with leathern lungs and considerable humour was dis- posing of his wares. He was selling a parcel of plated Jewellery and a pack of cards, the price being half a dol- lar. During the time I stood by he found at least twenty 'customers. No hawker in his senses would get up in the streets of London, or any other large English town, and attempt to sell things which he valued at two shil- lings. Sixpence would be a pretty high figure for such an audience as he would gather, and a penny a still more popular sum. Yet here in this Californian crowd two shillings were handed up as rapidly as he could pocket them. This is all very well for the Californians, but for slowwitted Englishmen a too rapid succession of experiences is apt to stun. An English gentleman in the city took his wife for a walk in the Chinese quarter. In a Peat little café the lady drank a cup of tea, for which one dollar was 'demanded. After this the gentleman thought he would have his hair cut. On returning to his hotel he sent for the barber, who cut his hair, shaved, shampooed him, and charged him two dollars and a half! It is true that in this case the gentleman was 'what the late Mr. G. P. R. James vats want to call "a belted earl." 'But making due allowance for that fact, -ten and six- pence for cuttinc, and shaving seems dear.—Henry W. Lucy. A. STORY OF THE CIVIL WARS.—As we Cross the Severn by the steam ferry to Portskewet, in Monmouth- shire, the names of the shoals which occupy so much of the river bed, known as Welsh ground and Welsh banks, show that, in popular estimation, the county we are about to enter is really a part of Wales. Indeed, it was not until the reign of Henry the Eighth tat Mon- mouth became—so far as the King's council could make it so—an English county. The ferry is not withoirt historical interest. Here, no doubt, was the Trajectus of the Roman itinerary, and ferryboats passed to and fro, while the sunshine flashed on the helmets of. the Roman legionaries, and glittered on their bright accou- trements. Saxon chiefs, too, in their barbaric bravery, thronged across as they followed their Lord Harold to the wars against the Welsh. . Harold himself built a palace at Portskewet, and there entertained the Con- I tessor when he held his court at Gloucester. And yet, the ferry is called the New Passage! The New Passage, , in fact, owes its' name to a strange incident in the Civil' Wars. It was towards the close of the contest—Naseby had been fought and lost by the King, who, having discovered at the Nebireh Mound, which is now.estab- lished to be the site of the famous Greek city of Naucratis, and the cradle of Greek art. The thorough I exploration has resulted in laving bare what was the I earliest Greek settlement in Egypt, and in bringing to light arcliological treasures beyond price. Innumerable objects of purely Greek art, statuettes, terra-cotta figures, painted vases, votive offerings,. bronzes, sculp- tures have been found, together with an immense quan- tity of pottery in considerable variety. Naucratis was a city of potters, and Atheneus states that her ceramic productions were in great vogue around the shores of the Mediterranean. In the mound which covered the city potsherds were found in well-defined layers of- dif. ferent centuries, susceptible of exact classification, and as such forming an interesting chapter in the history of Greek art. The collection is particularly rich in the archaic variety of white faience pottery, of which, prior to Mr. Petne's labours, only three or four pieces were known to exist. He found bowls by the hundred. The connection of Greek pottery with that of Egypt is shown at every step, showing how the one descended by gradual Steps from the other. The scarabcei, amu- lets, pictorial ornaments, deities, tiles, and other articles found in early Greek tombs all around the Mediterranean have been found amid the ruins of Naucratis in the very workshops where they were produced. The sites of several factories were brought to light, each containing many samples of their products. One of these was a Greek manufactory of scarabs for exportation, full of such blunders as foreigners would male in the hiero- glyphs. In another part of the city, what had evidently been a flourishing iron manufactory was unearthed, where every stage of production was carried on by Greek workmen, for ore, slag, and finished tools have all been found. The tools are principally chisels for work- ing in wood; but there were also an axe, a hoe, a sickle, knives of various kinds, bodkins, and, what fs a novelty in archseological discoveries of this kind, fishhooki. There is satisfactory proof forthcoming that this,scene of early Greek iron-working ;was in full vigour in the sixth century before Christ.. ELECTRIC HOUSE BELLS.

_,_ , Writers"" The Way to Ichang," &a.- . N. XI.—TO THE SOUTH AFRICAN DIAMOND FIELDS. May all who are off, their luck to try, - Come back as merry as grigs, As they will, if their mottoes are "Never say die," And, "Better luck, 'plaze the pigs; " If diamonds are there, with all My heart,' I hope that they may find 'em; If not, like little 80-peep, let 'em start, - But leave their tales' behind 'era When Crcesus had wealth enough for gods, And Solon had not a rap, he .. Most calmly exclaimed, "Why, what's the folds As long as a fellow is happy ?" So, whatever occurs, it has been opined - By a gentleman merry and hearty, . That, alter all, "A contented mind , Is as good as a large tea party." 7 —F..M ROMANI,. ' • In-1889-70 exciting news was borne :across the seas from the shores of South Africa. Rumours that had long been in circulation of a rich dianiondiferous region in West Griqualand were confirmed-by subsequent dis- coveries, and it was freely reported that speedy fortunes were to be had for the seeking. Hearts throbbed with hope and expectancy; and in a verrshort time;from all parts of the world, adventurous spirits were directing their glance towards the Cape Colony. Sailing ships and steamers were chartered by enterprising merchants, and were at once crowded with passengers for the promised El Dorado, as in the old Australian days. Cape Town, Port Elizabeth, and Natal suddenly assumed unusual signs of activity; the inhabitants awoke to a new life; vessels crowded their harbours, each fresh arrival from the east and the west, the north and the south,- landing treasure-seekers on the African shore. The dream of wealth impressed thousands, affecting enthusiastic youths and greybeards alike; and the inmates of peace- ful houScholds in Europe and in America became dis- turbed by the hasty resolution and departure of some erratic member of the home flock. In the coast towns of South Africa, as well as places beyond the seas, the colonists were turning their faces towards the diamond fields; the infection entered the counting-house, the editorial sanctum, the college,, the barrack-room, the sailors' forecastle, and the slums; and ere long every grade of human life was represented in a fierce contest for the gems embedded in the soil of the Vaal valley. The newspapers of the day: published glowing accounts of the treasure-yielding region, and the tourney thither was viewed as one of romantic-interest and stirring ad- venture, a long march through a picturesque country, and plenty of excellent sport on the way; the dreary plodding across desert plains, through mountain ravines, and the passage over the turbid waters of treacherous rivers, thus far were left unrecorded, to become realities of the future. "Diamonds" was the mighty cry that raised the exodus; and, wrote one correspondent, "so many gems have been found over 20 carats in weight that it would be tiresome to chronicle their descriptions. The number of diggers is so fast increasing that it is quite impossible to estimate how many will be engaged in the course of a few months. Fortunately, the diamon- diferous regions are so extensive that there is ample room for all. They certainly include many thousand Square miles and extend between latittide 28 to 30 dogs. south, and longitude 24 to 27 degs. east. The climate is excel- lent, although during the summer months (from Novem- ber to February)., the heat is very great; but at night the temperature is not unpleasant. The fields themselves are situated in a pleasant country, where there is excel- lent sport. The Vaal river is skirted by trees, and there is fishing in it. Provisions of all descriptions are mode- rate in price. Meal and vegetables are sometimes scarce and dear, but the remarkably fertile region of the Trans- vaal Republic can guarantee ibuudant supplies; while the (Orange) Free State, which itself also forms a portion of the diamond regions, is a magnificent pastoral country, whose climate is as Salubrious as its soil is fertile. Great order and discipline has been preserved." Another cori respondent wrote—" Diamonds are coming in now much faster than before. Carts and horses are ready at a raiment's notice, and clerks travel about the country ;" and high officials of.the Cape Colony, too, sent letters of detail and encouragement to the home newspapers, giving graphic descriptions of the land where wealth was await- ing the ready and lucky toiler. " - Perhaps Algoa Bay was the favourite port of debarka- tion, certainly it was the one Most extensively advertised; and early in January, 1871, we landed there, en route for the diamond fields. Port Elizabeth, Algoa Bay, is the principal town and natural harbour of refuge. on the south-eastern coast of Africa. Low-lying off the harbour, about seven miles from shore, is a small group, of bare rocks called the Bird Islands, formerly valuable for their guano deposit. A lighthouse now stands on the-largest island, a warning to navigators venturing too near the land ; the ill-fated Doddington went to pieces on these rocks, and other vdsielsr have been wrecke.d on the same group since he; time. Algoa Bay was first des- ' covered by Bartolomeo Diaz in 1486. The Dutch took possession in 1785, yielding it to the English, who in 1798 built a stone defence, still existink on the ridge over- looking the Baaken valley, calling it Fort Frederick, after the Duke of York. The British settlers, to whom the present inhabitants really owe the foundation of the , town, arrived at Algoa Bay in 1820, under the leadership 1 of Sir Walter Scott's friend, Thomas Pringle, , the poet. t His residence there is tbe most interesting event in con- nection with the early history of Port Elizabeth, if we except the hardships endured by his devoted-band of ; emigrants, and their sturdy efforts to transform ,a sandy .! waste into a paradise of gardens and green pastures. 1 roor victims of Utopianism! In his graphic narrative, 1" Residence in South Africa," Pringle describes the sur- roundings as he saw them, and recited with fervid pathos the sorrowful experience of his fellow settlers-; many of his. poems and descriptions of African life and incidents were written during his stay at Port Elizabeth. At that time, General Sir Rufane Shaw Donkin, ALC.B., was acting governor of the colony, . and he several times visited the emigrants' encampment, showing them great 1 kindness. On the summit of the hill, overlooking the 1 town, stands a high stone pyramid erected .to the memory -of Sir Rufane's wife, after whom, the town , was named. On the north-west side is the following in- scription : - - ,

To THE MEMORY OF ONE OF THE MOST PERFECT OF HIIMAN:BBINGS WHO HAS GIVEN HER NAME To THE TOWN BELOW.: - The inscription on the landward side. of the monu- ment was almost obliterated, but we traced' it out as ftritows Elizabeth Francis, Lady!Donkin Eldest Daughter of D. George Markham, Dean oS York, Died at Morat in Upper Hindostan, of a Fever, after Seven days' illness, on the 21st August, 1818, Aged not quite 28 years. She left an infant in his Seventh month too Young to know the irreparable Loss he has sustained, and a Husband whose Heart is still 'Wrung, by Undiminished Grief. He erected this Pyramid, August, 1820. • The town of Port Elizabeth, built on the. level strand between the beach and the foot of the not a large place, but its one main street was full of bustle and ac- tivity. During our stay in the town the market square was constantly crowded with 'wool-laden wagons from all parts of the interior; and the scenes at the morning markets were deeply interesting to a stranger. The resi- dents claimed that the trade of their port, chiefly in wools and skins, was double that of Cape Town; and otherwise maintained the superiority of Port Elizabeth over any other South, African town. Certainly there was nothingwanting in the warm-hearted hospitality of many of its inhabitants. A sort of aristocratic retreat for merchants and officials was "the Hill," Where nume- rous villas stood within garden grounds; but all was destitute pf colouring, the everlasting sun-glare en sandy hills on the One hand, and stunted' bush and Cape aloes on the other. We found Port Elizabeth in the dream of a new life; the heat and the glare, the sand and the rocks, went for nothing; bullock waggons thronged the parched sandy streets; agents and transport riders were galloping about on fiery little steeds, or were gathered about the "steps" and verandahs of the hotels, soli- citing the patronage of the diggers bound for the fields; and to those who knew little or nothing of the mer- cantileolife of the place it seemed as if all business effort was concentrated in the transportation of pas- sengers to the, diamond regions in the valley of the Vaal. Ox waggons and mule carts, accompanied by bands of sturdy men, were- leaving Port Elizabeth almost daily; and within ten days after landing, fit- out with all the necessaries for a miner's life, our long and tedious journey for the banks of the Vaal river com- menced.

When we left Port Elizabeth, with the farewell cheers of friends ringing in our ears, it was fondly imagined that the time of travelling the 450 miles to the diamond region would prove season of romantic interest and stirring adventure. By no means was that dream realised; UN days were dreary and monotonous, plod- ding across stony plains unmarked by vegetation, over sandy deserts, through mountain gullies often swept by tWocis ; and excepting a far-away-heard-of springboks, setdom within rifle-range, the only signs of life encoun- tered were the flocks of sheep watched by some sour- tempered Boer or naked Kaffir. Thus onward, for forty- four days, without any charms of picturesque scenery attending the journey; our great dblight being the story- telling and impromptu concerts around the camp fire of a night. But a fire was not always to be depended upon: the nights were wet and cold, the rain and the dew .frequently soaking all our belongings, and it often occurred that wood was scarce. The most. varied ranges of temperature were experienced; the %night of chilly winds and heavy dew, the long hours of the day were passed without shelter, ezcpo6ed to the fierce glare of a burning sun; the poor oxen became so dreadfully emaciated by. want Of food and drink that some of them fell dead in their tracks; 4 club and whip, most cruelly plied by brutal Hottentots, failing to move. the living ones for several hours. Such were some of ' the incidents almost daily occurring, getting more common as we advanced on the journey, until we wondered again and again would our miseries In those sandy solitudes.

eveit terminate. Mir forty-third day out was a wet and miserable one in the extreme; blinding lightning and terrific thunder peals giving effect to the most fearful land storm we ever remember to have witnessed, the very earth trembling beneath our feet, ad the tempest howling for hours. -But the rough journey was drawing to a close; the low, flat-topped range of hills which marked Du Toits Pan, the great central camp, had been seen before the storm burst over us; and all going svell, the next day would land us on the scene of the grand lottery. So, while pinched by cold and without * dry stitch of any sort, we were suitterminating a doleful march through the most inhospitable' country in which a stranger ever cast his lot. _ The next afternoon, much to our relief, after' weary uphill travelling all the morning, and many stoppages and threatened breakdowns, our oxen were atlastinduced by some unaccountable circumstance to make a rush, and -the heavy Waggon was rolled into the great mining camp. At that time Du Toits Pan was the centre Of the busy life at the diamond-fields, and though men had been toiling there for many months before our arrival, we found the miner,worlidng mostly on the surface. At all events, excavations of any great depth were-few and far between. It was a sight tahrsoressanyone;, just one of those exciting scenes that stir the "pulse's- maddening play," and we felt like rushing at once into the'vortex of the restless anxious life which surrounded` us.. The diggers lived:principally under canvas in tbose'days, and -their white tents covered a great expanse of grat*id; the main street, se -called, was devoted to the interest of commerce, ranging over a wide field, being lined by odd wooden shops and stores, fitted up by enterprising merehants and others fronatthe coast towns,and certainly they were reaping their golden harvest. The business necessary for a new arrival to transact was to seek out and obtain froro the inspector a dig- ger's license, select \a• piece of ground about 30ft. square called a "claim," taking care that it had no other owner, and then start work: Many of the- diggers, those who had capital; employed native labourers, Zulus, Basuto4 and Hottentots, who had deserted their " kraala " its- large bodies for the mining camps; they were content ten labour for a small reward, and generally the Zulus were - honest and trustworthy fellows-. It was their work to use ' pick and shovel, break the earth, and pass it to the sieves. The gravel from the sieves was placed upon a temporary table, and the final sorting of the soil was done by the anxious owner of the claim. But the task of the miner was little varied; the incidents of one day were the fore- runner of the next. The actual work of diamond seek- ing, the labour to which the earnest man set himself and tenaciously followed in hopes of ultimate reward, was hard and irksome; and unless he mingled in the com- pany of the happy-go-lucky spirits of the- fields, there was really nothing to cheer his way. The-nsind was too excited in those days, and amidst such seenes, th regard men calmly; and only through the distance of years can we fully comprehend our companions • of that time. With some of them the purpose of their ' journey to the fields seemed altogether lost; a few shapedan indepen- dent course, and by their force of character achieved success; while the many held to the primary object of their visit, and they worked on without a% thought of anything beyond the gems for which they sinned and toiled. To some of the patient ones the good angel of success appeared; magnificent strokes of great luck" occurred to others; but the many were cast portionless about and in want, wrecked, as it were, in sight of a port where they saw, others- sailing gallantly in. So events sped on, with few variations, unless distiuted by whirlwinds or violent rain storms which were fre- quent in that exotic region. The flies and films -were miseries of hourly experience to the toiler, but' the dust storms were the most appalling visitors. The claim dust, rendered by the process of pick and shovel into a fine limey powder, would rise in clouds,; but fanned by the increasing wind, it swept over the fields like a scouring demon, impregnating food and clothing, blinding and choking any poor -wretch not having the sensioto cast himself face downward on the ground. The summer rain storms were equally violent, but certainly more en- durable than the sand hurricanes. The moan of the wind and a few ominous raindrops would startle the , digger; blinding lightning and terrific peals of thunder quickly followed, and before a shelter could be reached the rain descended in torrents, flooding excavations, and for a time leaving large tracts of claim land under water. .**** * * * * _

• -- Returning to Port Elizabeth, after our 'experience of the fields, we met old friends and made the acquaintance of new ones. There we met a son of the author of "Proverbial Philosophy," Henry de Beauvoir Tupper, a fine, bright young fellow, in the heyday of early man- hood and promise, who had just then landed in the colony. His happy sunshiny nature made him e most lovable companion, and his departure for the interior was greatly regretted; and later,- when his sad end was announced, a shudder went through the pulse of colonial life. Henry Tupper was killed' on the journey to the diAmond-fields ; he fell from the front of the bullock- waggon, and the heavy vehicle passed over his body; a few brave, hopeful words to his. comrades, and his young bright life was ended. His body was taken up and lovingly cared for by strangers; but "one touch of nature makes the whole world kin." They buried him by King William's Town, hundreds joining the funeral cortege, thereby evincing love for the dear ones in the far-off English home, The wind of the morning, as the ' heavy clouds roll up from the east, brings with it the faint sound of the bugles of the British soldiery ;and the fiery heat of the African sun scorches the tittle greenery laid tenderly by stranger hands about his grave. That is.where strangers laid the loved remains of a noble youth, and covered him with tears and bles- sings, and there left him.

.MILK-FEVER.—To prevent milk-fever, give 10 drops of tincture of aconite in a little cold water for a week before calving, once a day, and also a few times after calving. Let the cow have as much cold water as she requires; you will have no need to alter her food or . starve_ her down. , SHIRE HORSE BREEDINO.—A society has been estab- lished in Chatteris to encourage the breeding and im- prove the character .of Shire-bred fcols. The pree3ident of the society is Lord Ellesroere, and the vice-presidents are Messrs, Walter Gilbey, J. R. Bulwer, Q.C., M.P., E. Hicks, M.P., and A. J. Thornhill, M.P. s Crow LICENSE.—" A-0." asks if he requires to takeout a gun license for shooting rabbits on his own farm, where he has ground game? A tenant (or his son or servant) is allowed to carry a, gun for ,the purpose of "scaring" vermin, but killing them is another_matter, ' and it will be safer for you to take out the license. There appears to be a certain amount of vagueness in this matter since the passing of the Ground Game Actiwhich we would like to see cleared up. ADULTERATION or MANPRES.—There is often room to complain of the adulteration of manures in this country; but it is ' seldom done quite -so dutrageoTly as in the case of a potash manure, sold by an American firm, ac- cording to the Rural New Yorker, which says that while the selling price is 40 dollars a tofi, the Chethistof the New York Expeilment Station finds it to be worth only 1 dol. 52c. a ton. - Another analysis made by :Dr. P. A. Genth for the Pennsylvania Board of Apiculture flowed a commercial value of less than 6 dollars a ton.

ENSILING' or HEArn.—The yotzng shoots of the heaths which grow oirthe enclosed lands adjoining the; moors afford sustenance to bath grouse and sheep, and # is the practice to set fire to this ling, which, after being burnt, shoots up a crop of tender pasturage. In these IP and mountain sheep farms, winter keep is too frelluently most deficient, and now that many of our impiroving landlords are at the moors, may I venture to suggest that some simple trials may be made to ensile the grawing shoots of the heath? Where this has been a year or two previously burnt, a fine crop of tender flowering ling , will follow, and this might be mown, or better cut, and I collected by ,a lawn-mower. A wine-cask, a pine, or a butt, or smaller, forms a simple and most efficient silo, and its lid can be employed to place stones upon to give the necessary pressure to the silage. If our sportsmen who take an interest in the prosperity of pastural agri- culture would, now they are on the spot, initiate trials, no doubt considerable winter fodder could be stored for use at a season when the snow is feet in depth, and, therefore, when such a sheep food is too 'often greatly needed.—W. A. Woofer, Darlington. • THE WOBURN EKPERIMENTS.—AIthough the weather has been unusually dry and hot, the plots in Stockyard Field look remarkably well, with the exceptioir of the peas and tares, which are badly blighted. All the wheat plots dressed with ammonia salts are heavier than those dressed with nitrate of soda. This is also the case with the barley plots similarly treated, but the difference is not so noticeable as in the case of the wheat. For the last three years the plots of permanent wheat and barley which received annually the larger dressing of ammonia salts or nitrate of soda in conjuction with minerals have been divided. • The minerals are still applied to both halves, but the nitrogenous manures applied and omitted alternately. If We take the average of the yield over these three years, we find, speaking roughly, that where ammonia salts have been used or withheld the produce varies from 45 to 20 bushels, and in the case of, nitrate of soda from 43 to 17 bushels. The result of this experi- ment is most striking, and a very important lesson is to be learnt from it. The rotation barley stands up well, and is a splendid crop on the four acres. 'here is no difference between the plots dressed with cotton-cake, dung, maize meal dung, and artificfals equivalent to the maize meal dung but the plot which received 1841bs. of nitrate of soda is decidedly the best. The rotation wheat is excessively luxuriant on all four acres, there being no perceptible difference between them. The object of these rotation experiments was to test the relative ma- nurial value of cotton cake and maize meal. According to Sir J. B. Lawes' famous table of 1875, based upon chemical analysis, and calculated according to the market prices of the time, the marfurial residue from one ton of cotton cake was estimated at a 105.,\ and from one ton of maize meal at, £1 11s. Unfortunately the results obtained from these experiments have been- almost identical. Surma CHEESE-MAKING.—At Stranraer and Rhins of Galloway Agricultural Society's Show, Colonel M'Dowall, Logan, who acted as chairman at the dinner, took excep- tion to the system of cheese-making as now being taught in the district by Mr. J. B. Harris, of Canada. Ile—the Colonel—did not think if we were going to learn French we would go to Belgium for a teacher, and, for his part, he could not see the need of going to America for a cheese-maker. The Americans, he said, received their instruction from Somersetshire---lhe saine source as they in the Rhins had received it leng ago—and his ex- perience of the new system, with American modifica- tions, had been a step in the wrong direction. He main- tamed that if they made cheese acebrding to Mr; Harris' instruction, they had an article that would not keep, and, whatever the state of the markets might be, they were obliged to sell it. He theug,,,lit. the old system was much the best, and he advised them to stick to it. Mr. John M'llaster, Culhorn Mains, replied to the Colonel, and 'said that whatever might be wrong with the cheese. . .

they could not lay the blame on the s-ystem of making. He believed Mr. Harris' system to be a good one, and pointed out to the worthy chairman that the Americans had by their method beaten them on their own ground, as with the exception of a few prime Somerset-made cheese, the American products commanded the highest price in the London market. That was sufficient proof that they had still something to learn; and his experi- ence N Mr: Harris' method had been the opposite to Colonel M'Dowall's, as his Cheese had never kept better nor been of .a better quality. The farmers of Wigton- shire are unanimous with Mr. M'Master's views, and the prize-takers at the show that day, with one exception, had followed Mr. Harris' instructions in making their cheese.

SCALE OF FOINTS FOR AYRSHIRE CATTLE —The follow- ing scale of points for Ayrshire cattle has Toeon adopted by the Ayrshire Agricultural Association :-1. Head short, forehead wide, nose fine between the muzzle and eyes, muzzle large, eyes full and lively, horns wide set on, inclining upwards; 10 points. 2. Neck moderately long and straight from the head to the top of the shoulder, free from loose skin on the under side fine at its junction with the head, and enlarging symmhrically towards the shoulders; 5 points. 3. Fore-quarters-- shoulders sloping, withers fine, chest sufficiently broad and deep to.ensure constitution, briskekand whole fore- quarters light, the bow gradually increasing in depth and width backward; 5 points. 4. Back stiort and straight, spine well defined, especially at the shoulders; short ribs, arched; the body deep at the flanks; 10 points. 5. Hind-quarters long, broad, and straight, hook bones wide apart, and not overlaid with fat, thighs deep and broad, tail long, slender, and set on level with the back; 8 points. 6. 'Udder capacious and not fleshy, hinder part broad and firmly attached to the body, tlie 'sole nearly level, and extending well forward; milk veins about udder and abdomen well developed ; the, teats from 2in. to 2iin, in length, equal in thickness, the

thickness . being in proportion to the length, hanging perpendicularly; their distance apart at the sides should be equal to about one-third of the length of the vessel, and amiss to about 'one-half of the breadth; 33 points. 7. Legs short in proportion to size, the 'bones fine, the joints him; 3 points. .8. Skin soft and elastic. and covered with soft, close, woollyhaft ; 5 points. 9. Colour red, of any shade; brown or white, or a mixture of these, each colour being distinctly defined. Brindle or hlack-and=white is not in favour; 3 pints. 10. Average live weight in full milk, about .10icwts. ;8 points. 11. General appearance, including style and movement; 10 points. Total, 100 points. SELLING CATTLE BY WEIGHT.—The question of selling cattle by weight is one, which has come to the .front during the past year solely on account of the really prac- tical nature of the work, and from the fact that breeders and feeders have obtained much better results by it than by the old system of selling, in which they were generally bested by the butcher, usually a keener man in making a bargain over a live beast than they them- selves. A very ably-conducted American journal, the Breeders' Gazette, has recently' dealt with this question, finding, fault, and we think not unjustly, not with the proposed system of selling by weight, but of estimating for the purposes of -calculating the value, the dead 'or carcase weight of the' beast at so much per cent. 'An Irish writer lately quoted thti conclusions at which Six John Lawes had arrived in recommending selling by weight, inasintich as, he said, the value of a beast de- pended as much upon the quality of the meat as upon its weight. This is perfectly true, but, when selling by weight, it is quite as easy to fix the price per pound for 'meat, which varies in quality no more than any other article of food. It has been customary to assume that a moderately fat beast fit for slaughter weighs it the propor- tion of Bibs. dead weight to 141bs. of live weight, or, in other words, a beast weighing so many ordinary stones when living would scale so many Smithfield stones when dead. Consequently, a dead bullock which had weighed 1,4001b5. upon his legs would, when sold to the butcher, be calculated at so much per pound for 800113 s. This is what the Americans find fault with, and they assume that it would be just as easy and much mare profitable to fix the price according to the live weight, and calcu- late the value upon the actual weight of the beast. There is no reason why this should not be done, but at the same time it havizig been for so long the British cus- tom to sell by the carcase it is difficult 'to see how the change can ever be brought about. There will always be room for judgment, and the man who has the best will invariably make the most profit; but it is essen- tially to the grazier's interest to weigh his beast, as the plan will not only save him from continual loss, but will assist in improving a judgment which can never be too perfect. The Royal Irish Academy has organised a dredging expedition, which has left Queenstown for a region of the Atlantic about 120 miles west of Cape Clear:- A de- tailed report of, this, the first deep-sea expedition from Ireland, will be, of course, presented to the Royal Irish o fine Mosaic pavements of the Roman peniod have recently been discovered at Sainte-Colombe-les-Vienne, in the department of Isere. The pattern of one is n vase in the middle, with fishes t the corners; gif the other lan arrangement of birds in their na,tural colvrs, ex- tremely well preserved. . .

. The -deepest boring yet made is at the village of Schla- debach near,the line between Leipzig and Corbethis. It has bef:n made by, the Prussian Government to test for the presence of coal, and was bored with diamond grills. Its depth is 1,390 metres-4,560 feet--its breadth slt the bottom 21n., gild at the top llin. It has occupied three and a half years to bore, and cost aJile over £5,000. The temperature at the 'bottom is 118 deg. Fah. A well-preserved skeleton of an enoincionS aurechs has beet' found "at Aken, on the Elbe; by some workmen occupied in digging a canal ' The horns, from one ex- tremity to the other, measured over nine feet. The ver- ' tebrze and ribs resemble those -of - the antediluvian monsters. As the aurochs avoids the proximity of man, and as the district where the •skeleton has, been found was very populated at the time, Of Julius Czesar, it is believed that the skeleton is about 2,000 years old. , A large and interesting collection of letters and papers bearing upon the social and rural history of East Anglia during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, has turned up among the archives of the Marquis Townshend at Rainham Park. It was known that Sir Nathaniel Bacon, second son of Sir Nicholas Bacon the Lord ICeeper, had left a number of. MSS. behind hi;n, and that these had come into the possession of the Townshends at the death of Sir Nathaniel in 1622, but they had never been -examined or arranged. A piece of amber, weighing 81bs., is at present being exhibited in the Mark Museum at Dantzig, for which the owner has refused £1,500. It is probably the largest piece in the world' without blemish. Frqderick the Great, more than a century ago, paid the Same sum for a piece weighing 131b5., which is preserved lathe mine- ralogical museum at Berlin; but it has gaps" and cavi- ties. Two beautiful pieces of work in amber are also to be seen in Berlin. One is a flute, which also was an ac- quisition of Frederick the Great. The other is a com- plete tobacco pipe belonging to Frederick William the father of the present Emperor. It bears an admirably carved likeness of that monarch. ,

General Adam Bade= has among his possessions an old and worn memorandum book, tied round with a bit of string. Valueless as it looks, one of the most import- ant documents connected with American history is written in pencil across one of its pages. It is the origi- nal of General Grant's despatch to Secretary Stanton an- nouncing the surrender of General,Lee'e army at Appo- tomak. General Grant was riding to his headquarters from the farm-house where Lee hadt urrenderecl, when he suddenly remembered that he had mid° no official report of the surrender. He halted at once; and dis- mounting from 'his, horse, sat down on a wayside stone, and asked for a .bit of paper. General &dean, who was standing by, offered him his memorandum book. Grant took it, and laying it on his knee, wrote the memorable despatch, and handed it to General Badeaulto give to the telegraph operator. General Badeau asked, him if he might copy the despatch for the operator, atid'keß the original, and to this Grant assented. The memorandum book is now in the keeping of the Century. A NEW MicnosE.—According to the American papers, the researches which Professor S. A.,Forbes, of the Illinois State College, has instituted into the cause of the 'terrible mortality recently prevailing among fresh-water fish in someparts of the American continent have been rewarded with complete snecess. The retort he has just sub- mitted on the subject shows that the disease ls due to a 'minute spherical microbe or gerntvrhose:diameter is only about the 1-25,000 th part of, an inch. This germ he dis- covered in the liver and kidneys of , the diseased fish. There it forms abscesses, which ultimately destroy the cells of those organs, and therewith the life of the fish. Professor Forbes says that there are various species of this germ, the different varieties.of which cause specific diseases,such as fevers, and especially smallpox chicken- pox, hogcholera, and so forth: The case which more particularly prompted him to undertake this investiga- tion was the extraordinary mortality among the perch and other fish of Lake Mendota, Wisconsin, where the fish have for some time past been dying in enormous quantities. . GREtIC Arng,cmps.—On any Tuesday, Thursday; or Saturday until the end of September persons ef archteo- logical tastes may visit the rooms of the Royal Archteo- logical Institute, Oxford Mansions, near Regent Circus, to see the large and most interesting collection of an- tiquitiesewhich Mr. W. M. Flinders Petrie, working under the auspices of the Egypt Exploration -Fund, has found a precanous refuge at Raglan Castle, was moving hither and thither, closely pursued by his enemies— that one day the ferrymen were hailed by a horseman, accompanied by two or three attendants, whose horses showed by their condition that they had been ridden far and fast. The boatmen recognised the King, and hastened to get out the great horse-boat, and then ferried across the little oavalcade to the English shore. The tide was low and the channel narrow, the great sand- banks were high and dry; and, the boatmen pointed out that time would be saved by landing On the bank called the English stones, whence the King and his suite could 4 ride across to the shore without danger. The King I thanked the men rewarded them royally,„ and rode away. ,Hardly had the ferrymen returned to their station on the Portskewet side, when a troop of Parlia- ment horse, eighteen or so in number,rode up in hot_ pursuit, and shouted roughly to the men to get reacl".l their boats. The boatmen made difficulties and objec- tions, doing all they could to gain time; but the leader of the band drew his sword, and swore that he would cut them dowitif they hesitated or made the least delay. The boatmen sullenly drew up their boats, and took on board their unwelcome passengers—thus hot upon the King's trail. By this time the tide had turned and the fierce floodtide of the Severn sea was showing itself in whirls and' patches here and there; but the shoals were still high above the water, although the boatmen well knew that in a few minutes' time the tide would be running like a millstream between the shoals and the shore. But the ferrymen ran their boat on the ,English stone's, and mutely intimated that now the voyage was ended. There, indeed, on the margin of the now rush- ing waters *ere the fresh hoofmarks of the horses of the fugitives. The Roundheads hastily lauded, and rode off across the shoal, and the ferrymen pushed off and rowed away. There is no fiercer tide along all the English shore than that which rushes twice a day up the Severn sea. The wide mouth of the estuary, open- ing towards the great tidal wave that swirls across the broad Atlantic, gathers the rush of waters which dash up the narrower throat of the channel vr,ith the -Westerly gale, rising as they go in a bore or wall of waters seve- ral feet in height. And thus the fate of the unhappy troopers was quickly sealed—in front of them a swift channel now quite impassable, behind them the foaming. tide. There was a shout of rage and despair, a struggle in the foaming waves, and then all was silent, not a man, escaping to , bear witness to the treachery of the ferry,- theerear Round.

STRATTEERTNES.—If runners of these have been at- tended to as directed in this column on July 18th they ought to be good plants and fit:to plant out in the beds. The ground for their reception should be deeply dug, and if not in good heart, well manured. The rows should be no nearer than 21t., but the plants for the first year may be one foot in the row, and the following year after the fruit is gathered every alternate plant miv loe,cut Out or skimmed off with the spade. If the soil is not moderately moist at planting time the young plants should be well watered some hours before planting and again as soon as the operation is completed. Treated in this way the plants may be expected to produce as much fruit as two or three-year-old plants treated in the usual way of planting in the autumn, and frequently- with plants that had not undergone any previous prepara- tion. The result of this method is that no fruit is- pro- duced the first year, so that one year is a total blank, and the successive crops do net make up for it. The varie- ties of Strawberries are numerous, and a price list before us contains the names of 68 varieties, but only &very ' limited number will succeed in: the North. Baines' , prolific is extensively grown at Walton, because it is really what its name indicates, and the fruit being mode- rately firm it bears carriage well, an important charac- teristic in all fruit that has to be conveyed any distance to market. Mr. Came, gardener to G. Dewhurst, Esq., Clayton Green to whose hive of fruit-growing we have I had occasion to make previous reference—grows it in a collection of half-a-dozen more varieties' and speaks well of its prolificness. The appearance of the fruit itself is not, however, to be compared with Sir J. Paxton and President, which are earlier a little and good croppers. They produce large handsome fruit, the flesh solid and richly flavoured, even in the North. Unser Fritz is another large kind and vigorous grower. The fruit is a bright glossy crimson,, the flesh solid and sweet, and ripens about ten days later than the above, and where only two varieties are grown this should be.one where large fruit is desirable. Other useful sorts- that may be named are Viscomtesse Hericart Be Thury„. a medium- size fruit and a most abundant bearer, and one a the earliest. The plant possesses a vigorous constitution. Keen Seedling is another early, highly esteemed variety, and much grown-in many districts in the North. THE FRONT GannEs.—All flowers intended for exhi - bition purpose require constant attention and more liberal treatment-than those grown entirely for cutting or decorative purposes as numbers in the latter case are more acceptable than size and form of flowers. Exhibi- tion blooms, or those that should come to exhibition standard, are not grown haphazard without thought or care till a day or two before the show. No they are duly watered, and in dry weather they are mulched to prevent rapid evaporation from the surface of the soil. In seasons like the present we have witnessed four inches of half-decayed cow manure placed over the roots of Dahlias extending nearly 21t. from the stem. With a previously applied heavy watering the soil must remain moist for a length of time as the moisture cannot escape butie confined to be absorbed by the roots of the plant. Disbudding is another important operation of the exhi- bitors of cut bloom, when shown as single flowers, and Dahlias require severe handling in this way.- Asters and Zinnias require similar attention in addition to watering and mulching. If for two or three days previous to the show the flowers could be screened for a "few hours during the hottest part of the day with: some light tex- tile material, the colours of them would be preserved, and the flowers altogether would appear much fresher. In order to prevent the fabric resting on the flower a frame should be constructed to support it or a few pliable rods may be bent, and their ends thrust in the ground and so form an arc, Dahlia shades are usually made of tin, and iiire slipped up and down a rod as may be desired. Earwigs are very destructive to these flowers, and they should be trapped by laying pots containing dry moss or grass, which should be daily ex- amined.

THE WlNDOW.—aeraniunas and Pelargoniums are fre- quently spoken of by cottagers as if they were synony- mous, which they are not, though:all Pelargoniums are Geraniums, all Geraniums are not :Pelargoniums. The distinction is of not much importance except where cul- tural details appligable to one are applied to the other. We refer to the subject here because we wish to point out the Lieversity of treatment the cuttings require. Cut- tings of the various sections of Geraniums, :excepting the sweet scented ones, are best kept moderately dry for a week or ten days after they are put in, and fully ex- posed to the sun. Pelargoniums, on the other nand, should be watered as soon as they are inserted, and re- ceive a slight dewing once a day, and though they root fairly when exposed they do much better in the shade, and better still if in a moderately close frame, and shaded during the hettetit part of the clay for a.fertaight,

Be thought the proper coarse would have been to treat so cum- brous and untimely apiece of jocularity with the contempt It deserved. (Elea-, hear.) He did not know who the magis- trates were at Newton, but he could not but express his amazement that gentlemen who were sworn to administer the law should so ,flagrantly neglect to do their duty and to temporise with a question of the importance of that one by redacing the fines-they had previously, imposed, reducing them once and twice, and then to such a nemival sum as to be an absolute burlesque on the administration of justice. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. RATCLIFFE, referring to the anti-vacci- nators, said he'called those people respectable people for all that Mr. Harrison and Mr. Jolley had said, and as to what he had said ribout the magistrates at Newton it was only his own opinion. A NEW REFORMATORY SHIP FOR THE MIRSEY.—There has arrived in the Mersey the hull of an old wooden man- e-war, named the Royal William. The Royal William is to take the place of the Reformatory ship Clarence, which it will be remembered was set on fire several months ago, by some boys who were undergoing a term of discipline an board. Tne Royal William is an old three-decked vessel, and will carry about 80 gun!. It will be some considerable time before she will be ready to be pat on the station. Sin CELiRLES WARREN'S RECALL.—AI a meeting of the South African Committee and of the Committee of the Aborigines' Protection Society, held in London on Monday, a resolution was passed expressing deep regret at the stapercessien of Sir Charles Warren, and grave fears that his premature return to England would seriously jeopardise British authority in Basutoland and other native districts. Mr., W. E. Forster wrote that he greatly feared that the good which Sir C. Warren's mission heel effected would be undone. A FIENDISH PRiCTICAL JOlR.—From Goldshill, a few miles from Mallow, a fiendish practical joke is reported. Daring a wake which was being held on a woman a man named Horan fell asleep, and while unconscious a poker, which bad been heated, was put down his back, the flesh be- tween his shoulders being roasted. Horan sprang up, and in his frantic efforts to remove the poker burnt his body more and in his agony he rushed out and jumped into a pool of water. He is now in the hospital, and the matter is in the hands of the police. DEPARTURE OF MORMONS FROM LIVERPOOL.—On Satur- day, a party of Mormons left the Mersey in the Gaion Line steamer Wisimdain for New York, en route for Salt Lake City, Utah. the party numbers 329, and is in charge of 14 elders, at the bead of whom is Mr. John W. Thoralev. .The elders have been in Europe scime time conducting Mormon missions. This is the foutth party which has left Liver- pool during the present 'year, and makes up the total number to 1,331. The present contingent consists of 90 British, 125 Scandinavian, and 100 Swiss and German emi- grants. I ENORMOUS CATGEI OF HERRINGS AT WHITEL-011 Sat- urday about ens hundred boats arrived at Whitby, all of ;them heavily laden with herrings. Some of the boats bad over 70,000 fish each. A glut in the market occurred, and large quantities of fine herrings failed to realise more than 15s per last of 10,000. Many tons we carted away for manure, and large quantities, some 20,000 to 30,000 herrings, were piled up on the quay, and people were invited by the town crier to take them for nothing—an invitation which was taken advantage of by hundreds of people. FIORD WITH Somanens.—At Stalybridge, on Monday, John Flint, sergeant of the Sleuth Staffordshire Rigiment, ,was committed for trial for wounding a civilian named Stubbs. A number of men standing in the street used insult- ing expressions to soldiers who were passing. The result was a fight. The men rate,away, with, the soldiers fol- lowing. Some of the latter drew their bayonets in the pureutt. • Stobbit, who was said to have taken no part In the quarrel, was stabbed in the breast by a bayonet, which pierced the clothes and flesb, and punctured the rib bone. . .

Jimson and Co., Leicester, and stealing upwards of £l,OOO worth of bills, cheques, and postal orders. The prisoner was formerly in the employment of prosecutors as timekeeper, having the possession of a number of office keys. The ougietrAtes re- manded the prisoner. FURNITURE CATALOGI7E.—We have just received a Copy of the new Furniture Catalogue of Mr. T. Hall, 51, Bruns- wick-road, Liverpool. It is capitally illustrated, and the cover is quite a work of art. Mr. Hall's terms are "cash on or before delivery," and, as he is not troubled with bad debts he is in a position to give the most for the money. The illustrations rival the most elegant designs, and the prices are temptingly low. Goods are packed sod delivered free, and any article not approved is exchanged. It is hardly necessary to say that, doing business on this basis, Mr. Hall has a large number of very gratifying testimonials from customers of all classes. THE "PALL MALL GAZETTE" REVELATIONS.--IiXTRA- ORDINARY ABDUCTION.—At Bow-street Police Court, Lon- don, on Wednesday, a woman named Rebecca Jarrett was charged with abducting, in June last, Eliza Armstrong, a girl under 16 years of age, from the pess2ssion and against ihe will of her parents; with indecently assaulting the girl; with.adininistering or causing to be administered to her ' a certain noxious thing with intent to injure bar; and with conspiring with Mr. William Thomas Stead (editor of the Pall Nall Gazette) and other persons to commit these latter offences. Mr.,Polatid, who appeared for the prosecu- tion, stated that ha had been instructed to take charge of the case by the Home Secretary and the Attorney-General. The girl Armstrong was absent from home from the 3rd Jane to the 24th August, during which time she was taken to Paris. It was only through the intervention of the police that the girl was returned to her mother. Information had been ob- tained from Mr. Bramwell Booth, of the Salvation Army, that the re isonsr was in this country, and she surrendered herself at Scotland Yard on Tuesday'evcning. Mr. Poland then asked for a process against the persons who aided and abetted the prisoner, namely' Mr. Stead, Mr. W. Jacques (also employed on the Pall Mall Gazette), Mrs. Coombe, and Madame Elise Manley, at whose hones the girl was examined. It was stated that Mr. Stead was in Switzer- land. The prisoner was 'remanded, and summonses were I granted against the other persons named, returnable for 1 Monday next. The Pall Mall Gazette pzblisbes the fol- lowing telegram from Mr. Stead :—"Grindelwall, Wednesday night. The arrest of Rebecca Jarrett is of a piece with the City Solicitor's prosecution of the newsboys. I alone am responsible. Rebecca Jarrett was only my unwilling agent. I am returning by the first express to claim the sole respon- sibility for the alleged abduction, and to demand, if con- demned, the sole punishment. Meanwhile I am delighted at the opportunity thus afforded me of publicly vindicating the proceedings of the Secret Commission. MURDER BY AN INSANE FATllER.—Blachall, a village in County Wexford, has been the scene of a terrible murder. Owing to the violent conduct of a farmer named Hanley, who is believed to be insane, his wife fled from the house, leaving two little girls behind her. A snort time afterwards Hanley threw the eldest girl out of the window, fortunately without injuring her, and then murdered the other by forc- ing down her throat with a etick a band which the poor girl was wearing round her neck. He then hurled her life. less body through the window, and afterwards walked to a neighbour's house, where he commenced eating a picture. , The police subsequently arrested him, and lodged him in prison. Simons Accrparor To MR. Dir..awvle, M.P.—A very serious accident happened about seven o'clock on Monday evening, to Mr. L. L. Dillwyn, M.P. for Swansea. The 3rd Glamorgan Rifle Volunteer Corps' of which the Prince of Wales is honorary colonel and Mr. Dillwyn lieutenant- colonel, underwent its annual inspection on the sands during the afternoon' about 350'strong. Mr. Dillwyn was present on horseback. After the inspection had conzlnded, and while the corps was on its way to the drill hall to par- take of the annu4 dinner, the band struca up a merry tune, and the commandant's horse shied and threw its rider. The fall would have been a serious one for any one, but Mr. Dill vryn is well advanced in years, and when he was picked up and taken to the adjacent hospital, it was found that his collar bone was broken, and other injuries were sus- tained. . .

EXTRAORDINARY DEATH OF A CLERGYILLN.—An extraor- dinary fatality occurred on Saturday evening, near Malpas, Cheshire. A farmer named Griffiths was carting a load of corn from one of his fields to the stockyard, and a labourer carrying a pitchfork wag riding on the top of the load. The Rev. Mr. Vaughan. vicar of Tallarn Green, near Malpas, and Mrs. Vaughan were driving along the road, and on ap- proaching the waggon the rev. gentleman alighted from the carriage and walked by its side. Just as he was passing the waggon the labourer fell from the top of the load, and the pitchfork be was curving struck Mr. Vaughan, pene- trating his left side and causing instant death. The body WAS removed to a nelghb3nring farmhouse, where, upon medical examination. it was found that the pitchfork had touched the heart of the deceased. •Mrs. Vaughan, who was witness of her husband's death, lies very 111 at the

Mr. Healy spoke of the misery Inflicted upon the people by landlordism and other outcomes or tho present system of Government. After re- ferring to questions at issue between the landlords and tenants of the locality, he cautioned his bearers in dealing with the Purchase Act, which be styled the Land League Act, to combine and not to assist the landlords to make bard terms, as they had done previously. Lord Caruarvou ad- vised landlords to deal fairly, and the tenants should not help them to do otherwise. He (Mr. Healy) counselled them not to connive at outrages, and not to rely solely upon their Parliamentary representatives, who were only the van- guard of the army which carried the war into the enemy's 1 1 camp.—Mr. O'Brien said the people bad gained much which 1 would never be lost, whilst the landlords bad lost power which they would never recover. It was now a question of upon what terms they could be got rid of alto4ether. MR. Mr. Baows said that the inspector, Mr. Stephens. Ind recently visited the house and had left a memorandum to the effect that the punishment book of the Workhouse should be presented to the Guardians at their next meeting. He (Mr. Brown) was happy to say that the punishments in lthat house were of a very mild type.—The CLERK then read the list of the punishments recently inflicted on inmates, all of which were, as Mr. Brown said, of a mild type.

, SCHOOLS COMMMTEE. A meeting of the Schobta Committee was held OD the let September, the Rev. G. F. Roberts in the chair. Mr. W. Owen, architect, attended and received instructions to pre- pare a plan of the alteration intended at the hospital, and an estimate of the cost; and the clerk was instructed to convene the usual special Board meeting to approve same after approval by this Committee. With reference to the recommendations of the House Committee upon children at the echools visiting their parents at the Workhouse, when the parents were unable to visit the children, and with re- ference to the discharge of children and their clothing ; the Committee would consider at their next meeting what regu- lations on the subject were advisable. It was recommended th it tenders be gent to the Board at their next meeting for the laying of tiles or bricksiound the yard according to specifications prepared by Mr. Owen.—The SUPERINTEN- DENT reported that he had engaged a temporary nurse for the hospital, one being required for the daytime. The Committee approved of his doing su.—The CHAIRMAN. in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said that a fort- night ago a deputation from the Cemmittee went down to the hospital to see if they could suggest means of meeting , the difficulty there which arose through Mr. Henley, , G.vernment inspector, finding two adult beds in one of the wards, and which were need the women attending the sick children. Mr. Henley very properly pointed out that the wards were not the proper places for the nurses to sleep ' in and gaveinstructions that the matter should be attended to. When they came to examine how that could be done they foned that the room set apart for the woman to live, cook her food, and sleep in, measured 9 feet by 10 feet, and that was considerably rect.ced by the chimney and cupboards.-The CHAIRMAN explained the plans suggested to meet the difficulty, and stated that Mr. Owen had advised them to leave any structural alterations over until such times as Mr. Henley or other officers had been communicated with.—Mr. GREENING sconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. OWEN said be was surprised that the architect of the schools had not provided sufficient cubic feet in the room referred to, and also that the Local Gov- ernment Board had passed it —The minutes were adopted.

A REFRACTORY BOY. The Workhouse Master reported that tbe schoolmistress (Miss Gardner) complained that the boy George Warring- ton should have been put under her charge when he was found Unmanageable at Padgate Schools.—The CLERK told that the boy had previously been sent to the workhOute, and at a reasonable time after be was sent back to Padgate as cured, but unfortunately when he got there he was found to be worse thaa ever. As he had been reported .cured when he was in the workhouse they thought that the best place for him, and sent hint back again. It was a question, however, whether he should be in Miss Gard- net's charge at all, or whether it was better to put him to work under Greenway.—Mr. HARRISON asked what was the boy's peculiar idiosyncrasy.—The CLERK': Mischief of every sort. (Laughter.)—Mr. APPLETON said the boy was very industrious, and a good little tailor.—The Client:awe said it was au exceptional case. They had tried to send the boy to some other institution, but he was one of these ,anfertnnate cases which came under no head at all.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE mentioned that the lad was a 'foundling, flay- ing been found on a doorstep in the town, and had ,been trained in the workhouse ever since he was born almost. When sent to Padgate he bad wandered away to neighbour- ing houses, and once went away to Chorlton Union, and the Board had to pay the expense of bringing him back either once or twice.—Mr. BROWN said the boy would be educated in the workhouse until five years of age and no r longer, after which he would go to the school.—Aiter a little farther discussion the matter dropped.

Whitehead, D C.; Bro. R. W. Kirkus, D.S. ; Bro. E. J. Freeman, D.T. Bro. G. Lamb, D.Chap.; Bro. Walter Dunbabin, D.A.S. ; Sister Porter, D.D.M. ; Bro.. J. B. Col- lings, ; Bro. Crosthwaite, D.C.T., West Cheshire, dm.—Bro. Williams regretted that he could nottongratulate the order on an increased membership during the quarter. In many cases, however, the lodges were realty stronger, I though reporting a decrease. There were many persons who wolid like to be united with them, but who could not I possibly attend the lodge regularly, and he reeommended that they b 3 asked to become annual members by the pay- ment of a fee of 5s each. Since the last District Lodge meeting three of the subordinate lodges had ceased to meet, but he hoped to see two of them at work again very shortly. The Crosby Lodge had been re-opened, and in a few weeks bad admitted fifty members. (Applause.)—The W.D. secretary (Bro. Kirin's) said the number of members in ; good standing last quarter was 3,353, and that the number reported this quarter was 3.196, showing a decrease of 157 members.—The D. treasurer (Bro. Freeman) reported a small balance in hand. The District Lodge then proceeded to consider a code of bye-laws, eighteen in number, which had been drawn up by a committee for the management of its business; but after a long and rather warm discussion," the whole matter re- lating to the'hye-laws " was "referred back to the com- mittee," on the motion of Bro. Craig, seconded by Bro. Lamb. Ashton-in-Makerfield, Wigan, and Liverpool *ere submitted as suitable places from which to choose the next place of meeting, and the two former were withdrawn in fa- vour of the latter. District Lodge, is therefore, to be en- tertained on the last Monday in November next by the Hope of All Souls' Lodge, Liverpool. A vote of thanks was passed to the St. Helene friends for the manner in which they had entertained the District Lodge, and the compliment was acknowledged bp Bro. Brockbank. At the conclusion of the business the brethren and sisters formed in procession and, headed by the Lowton Temperance Brass Band, walked through several of the thoroughfares to the Methodist Free Church School, where tea was partaken of. Afterwards there was a pa'elic meeting in the open air, and a concert was given in the George-street Temperance Hall, at which there was a good attendance.

A DOG TARRED AT NEWTON. EXTRAORDINARY CASE. An extraordinary case of cruelty to a dog was heard at ' .the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, when the magis- trates on the Bench were Colonel McCorquodale and Mr. W. F. 4000 h, Ellen Pomfret, a married woman, residing in Rob's-lane, was summoned for cruelly ill-treating a collier dog on the 31st July, by tarring it. The prosecution was conducted by Inspector Lockwood, of the Royal Society for the Prevemtion of Cruelty to animals, and Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, represented the defendant.—The first witness called was John Ball, a young man, who said that on Thursday, the 31st July, he let his long-haired collie dog loose to exercise. When it returned about half-past six it was covered with tar from head to tall. It seemed to have been very much abased. It took them three hours to wash it off, and the dog was ill far three days afterwards. The hair bad been all clipped off from the head, along the back and fail, and down the legs, and with the sand and tar the dog seemed to be in great pain. In reply to the clerk, wit- ness said he could not tell whether the tar had been put on hot. The dog was unable to lift its tail, nor could it bend Its back for Some days. Along with P.C. Spencer he after- wards went to the defendant's house, and in the garden found a quantity of tar and a brush, and a bundle of hair like the hair on the dog. The defendant las sreeken to about the matter, and she at first denied having seen the dog, but when the was shown the hair they had found she admitted having taken the hair from the dog and then poured tar on the dog.—ln reply to Mr. Brown, witness sad he was not aware that the dog had done any damage in defendant's garden.—P.C. Spencer stated that the last wit- neat gave information of the occurrence, and he saw the dog, which was completely saturated all over the body with tar, after the hair had been cut off from all parts of the body, head, legs, and tail. The limbs were cone stiff, and the dog could scarcely move. It was in great pain, and was not able to walk, while it mild scarcely stand. He went to the defendant's house with the lest witaess, whose evidence he corroborated. He added that he asked the defendant why she cut off the dog's hair, and she replied that it had been in the habit of coming into her garden and doing damage to it. He asked her to show him any damage that it had done, but she could not show any damage. She then said the damage was done last winter.—lnspector Lock- wood, of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, said he had examined the dog, and found its eyes swollen and bloodshot. It was In the condition described by previone witness, and trembled and staggered when it tried to walk, as if it was suff .ring from paralysis. It was In acute pain. He spoke to the defendant about the matter, and she said ehi was sorry for what she bad done.—Mr. T. R. Stone, of Newton, veterinary surgeon, said he thought the dog had auffered great pain.—For the defence Mr. Browne said be would not deny that the woman had thrown, tar over the dog or cat off its hair. She had a gardea in which valuable flowers and vegetables had grown, and by which she made a little towards her living. She, however, had been dreadfully troubled by a dog, which bad caused darnaee amounting to about £5. She, had driven it away repeatedly, but it returned, and as she was unable to dis- cover its owner she cut off the dog's hair and then put the tar on an the hope that it woulil make the dog keep away. He urged that the woman bad not been guilty of inten- tional cruelty, and asked the Bench to deal leniently with her.—The ti.lairmart said the Bench considered it a case of great cruelty, and if she had not been in a lineable position of life they should have fined her very heavily indeed. As it was she would be tined 203 a`nd costs.
