The following opinion as to the right of officers, non-commissioned officers, and privates occupying rooms in barracks to be on the Parliamentary Regis- ter bee been obtained by the Liberal Central Associa- tion, London, from Dir. Alfred Lawrence, barrister- at-law :

I am of opinion that none of the occupiers of the barracks are entitled to be registered as voters, ex- cept, perhaps, he who is the officer " under whom" all the others "serve." They clearly were not so entitled before the Act of 1884, and their claim now depends primarily upon the true construction of sec- tion 3of that Act. Whether they are or are not en- titled under that section is, I admit, a very difficult question, and one upon which opinions may well differ. The words taken literally are in favour of the claim of those who occupy a room or rooms to them- selves. For the disqualifying provision, as to the ,1 presence of a person under , wham they 1" serve," contains the wards, " the dwelling- house," and if these words are to be read in the technical sense given to them by 40 and 41 Vic., c. 26,5. 5, it would seem that this disqualification does not attach, for the superior officer can scarcely be said to "inhabit" these rooms. It may well be that the words "the dtvelling-'aonse" have been in- cautiously introduced into this provision, and, that in it they should receive their more popular meaning, for otherwise this provision alone would not operate to disqualify a butler, or other domestic servant, to whose use a room or rooms were appropriated in his master's home. Howtover this may be, I am of Opinion that there is no such " separate occupation" in the case of these barrack quarters a 4 is essential to a right to the franchise under the Acs. I think It will be found that military di.ciplioe requires that the officer in command shall have the leeoll rialt to enter all quarters at any rwo An •and.ths.t ho rover seldom this right may in fact be exercised, it deludes the idea of separate occppation. The question is one upon which a case for the opinion of the High Court should certainly be obtained; in this case the facts as to the rights of the conimandings officer over all qu tr- ters should be clearly stated. (Signed)
A. T. LAWRENCE.
PUESCOT.

SHOP-DOOR Ronrigny.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs. Gibbons and Earle, James Hey. worth was charged with stealing a coat, value 4s 6d, from the door of the shop occupied by Wm. Jones, pawnbroker, Eccleston.street. An assistant named Heaton followed the prisoner, and found the trousers in his possessien —The prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was committed for seven days.

Sourauess ARABS.—A strange sight was presented on Tuesday evening by the appearance of ballet-dozen Arabs in their somewhat scanty costumes, showing their elaborately decorated and tattooed limbs. They had a woe-begotten appearance as evening approached, and the police book , them in hand and escorted them to the Workhouse for a night's lodgirg. When inside the gate they gave vent to wild ejaculations and cries, no douht thinking it was a prison instead of a hospice. Max Doo.—On Friday afternoon week considerable alarm was created throughout the town by the appearance of a dog afflicted with rabies. It was a strange dog, white and black spotted, and it attacked every dog it came across, large or small ; amongst others, a large retriever, belonging to Mr. Welsby, postmaster, which had to be destroyed. After traversing the streets it made off towards Whiston, attacking a child on the way. It re-entered Prescot by way of Kemble-street, and sought refuge from the crewa that WRS after it in the workshop of Mr. Yates, the Alley. It made a bite at the leg of Mr. Yates, senior, but was eventu- ally shot by Mr. Benjamin Heaps. In consequence of its ravages five or six valuable dogs had to be shot or poisoned. THE &MOW OF CHTLDREIL—Before Mr. E. Gibbons land Mr. F. W. Earle, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, William ILever, a baker, was charged under a warrant with failing to contribute to the support of his two illegitimate children, at present chargeable to the Pres- cot Union. Mr. C. M. Stuart, relieving officer, stated that orders of 4s and 25 61 per week had been made upon the defendant towards the support of his illegitimate children, at present in'the workhouse. Ile had paid nothing oe the orders, and the arrears amounted to £lO 12s. The Bench expressed the :minion that the prisoner was a good-for- nothing and heartless man, and his conduct had been die. graceful. He threw the children on the parish, and he ex- pected the parish to keep them, rather than allow them to Marve in the streets. He would be committed to prison for six weeks. OBTAINING BELIEF UNDER FALSE PRETENCES. A middle•aged man named Thomas Balmer was char,red, be- fore Messrs. F. W. Earle and Gibbons, at the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, with refusing to perform the work I allotted to him at Prescot Workhouse, and also with obtain- ' fug relief under false pretences. Evidence was given by IWm. Williams, porter at the Workhouse, and an assistant named King, to the effect that the prisoner was admitted to • Ithe Workhouse on the previous Wednesday. and on the fol- lowing day was given 41bs of oakum to pick. When the r time allowed for that purpose had elapsed he had only picked nibs. When the tramps were being discharged a tramp said the prisoner was hiding money in his shoe, and on the prisoner being searched, 35 was found In his posses- sion.—The prisoner was committed to gaol for seven days I in each case.

HIGHWAY &Num—The monthly meeting was held on Toesday forenoon. Present—Messrs. W. L. Evans, F. W. 'Earle. Tyler, Lowe, Cross (clerk), Goldsworth (surveyor), land W. Goldsworth (assistant surveyor).—The Surveyor re- ported that he and Mr. Leatherbarrow bad seen the surveyor of the Huyton-with-Roby Local Board with reference to the purchase by the latter of that Board's road sweeper and scraper. He (Mr. Goldsworth) had offered to pat the ' machines in a good state of repair and accept a discount of 125 per cent, on the original cost price. Ihat offer would be ! laid before the Huyton Local Board, and be had not since received a reply. The surveyor reported that at the lairt meeting the question of purchasing a steam roller Was die., i cussed. The cost of the roller which the Board intended purchasing was £4OO, and the idea was that it would be , paid for in three years, an arrangement which the makers I were prepared to accept. In order to see their position, he had prepared an estimate of the receipts and expenditure up to the 25th March next. The receipts were £2,701 35; ex- penditure and liabilities, salaries, the., £2,447 Is lOid ; leav- ing a balance of £254 Is li4.—After some discussion. Mt. Lowe said ha thought a steam roller would be a great advantage, and Mr. Eerie thought the roller would bring in a deal of money.—The Chairman expressed the opiniolar that their financial position was pretty safe, and on the ; suggestion of the Surveyor, the Chairman, Mr. Earle, Mr. I Tyrer, and the Surveyor were appointed a committee to - make arrangements for purchasing a roller.-The Surveyor's statement of expenditure for the four weeks ending Au.eust 27th n Las9l4e followsttd :—Bold, Id ; team labour, £54; Enewslev, X 5 14s 11d; Ise ; new materials, £56 35 lid; incidentals, £lB 03 5d ; total, £163 5s his was the only business. PHESCOT LOCAL BOARD —The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday night. Present: Messrs. T. S. Preston (in the chair), S. P. Hewitt, H. Whitfield, J. T. Hall, H. Makin, H. Cross (clerk), W. Goldsworth (surveyor), and Dickinson (inspector). At a meeting of the General Pur- poses Committee on the 31st ult., the assistant surveyor reported that the ruinous and dangerous buildings, 2 and 4, Store-street, Prescot, had been pulled down. After con- sideration it was decided that the clerk should be instructed to take the necessary steps to recover from the owner of a ruinous and dangerous building in Brewery-street, the ex- penses incurred in securing the same. The surveyor sub- mitted a plan of an improvement to the doorways of the King's Arms Hotel by Mr William Evans. The matter was left for the surveyor to arrange with the architect, and the proposed pilasters should not encroach on the foot- path. From the minutes of the Finance Committee it - appeared that the committee had resolved that Mr. Henry Fogg, registrar of births ad deaths, be appointed at a salary of £3 3s. to submit to each monthly meeting of the Board a detailed report of the births and deaths occurring in the Board's district simllar to that supplied by Mr. Peter Chorley, his predecessor in office, and to report to the medical officer of health any case of death caused by any iefectious disease as soon as such shall come under his notice. The collector was directed to announce that all persons who had not paid their ratea of the G:h May on the 2611 September be summoned. The clerk was instructed to advertise for tenders for borrowing £2,000 to enable the Board to repay the loan obtained from Messrs. Hesketb and Higson. Tbe minutes were con- firmed. This was the only business, the proceedings be!ng formal. BOARD OF GITARDIANS.--The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon, when Mr. J. Leatherbarrow presided. The Workhouse Master reported there were 393 inmates this week, against 411 last week, and 460 in the and Mr. corresponding week las; year. The number of vagrants relieved was 50, againsa 56 in the corresponding week Of last year.—The Clerk (Mr. S. H. div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 5, 188,5.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 5, 188,5.

„, de ruill was very severe last week in its con- Izaation of Warrington magistrates for the equality of their sentences. Two cases 44te cited. One was that of a poor woman WO, anxious to get home to her father in orcestershire, had in a moment of tempta- -7,?11 stolen twelve shillings from the till of a nrk butcher. The county magistrates who :tied the case sent the woman to prison for Lourteen days. The other case was heard the °dine day, but in the borough police court. A ttlan named BEDLY the throat and „ bnhaad seized his wife by ged her about the louse;” and it was added that "this was a frequent occurrence." lie, however, was not s.ent to prison—he was ordered to find sure- ies for his good behaviour. The inequality the sentences is of course glaring—the vornan seat to gaol for a first offence; the tiQau "let off" although, on the evidence, he ,ad beenUrequently guilty of the crime of heating his wife. The gentlemen who are Zlicm'a as "the great unpaid " do a vast ~1110unt of judicial work every week in the r, but, as much of it is so badly done that elstices' justice" has, in some places, become bYvford, the question arises whether it not be better to have it well done even 't has to be well paid for. We are not ollfg,gesting that there is worse administration %Justice in Warrington than other pa rtsof i the Country. What we gish to urge sthat st,,re should be an extension of the.syst ern of Pendiary magistrates which has worked so 17,e_11 wherever it has been adopted. Men who *.ve hot been trained to the law are too much iti`titilated by caprice and prejudice in passing th gfluent upon their fellow-men. It is true ere is a law clerk at hand to advise; but re are hard-headed and wrong-headed strates who seem to take a pleasure in Mv.,13,111.g. a paid official by disregarding his thro'—• When men of this stamp have over- -tell RIV„,11 a clerk, and crushed a prisoner—at one s h " -°ol3—they g o home beaming, as)Byron a it._

with such a face of satisfaction, trii,J,'3zon wear who've done a virtuous action. kir' late Mr. JOSEPH KAY, Q.C., in his ad- .---,‘4131e work on "Free Trade in Land "'says: CINN,:"11 some poaching offences, one land- iustice may sit alone, and, without irrlP,°r any check, try game offenders, and sentences which practically entail the offender's family and the destruc- 'hat his good name for ever." To show Of bie is not speaking unadvisedly, he tells tlhait'llg at dinner with a genial chairman of Det,:,er sessions who said it sometimes hap- 'ease'', that when he had remarked as to a %uffi ,uefore the Bench—" There is really not beebetent evidence against this man," he had tlff hanswered—" Oh, you must not let him ttairi,„ea's a d—d poacher I" A paid magistrate, evicie-: to sift evidence, and to decide on tose-,c,cet would not allow prejudice to inter- ," IC; tniS monstrous fashion. Nor should is_.etity" two such instances of judicial se- 'toti 11°t to say tyranny, as have been aht before the public during the past

week—instances which leave our local magis- trates altogether in the rear. The first is thus recorded ; Before Bailie Ilunter, at Dundee, on Saturday, Peter Lunan, labourer, was charged with stealing three apples from a garden. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and, in defence, said he was starving and took the apples to eat. The Bailie said he could have applied for relief to the proper quarter, and passed a sentence of imprisonment for forty days. Forty days' imprisonment for stealing and eating three apples 7. Bailie HUNTER M. St be one of those who regard the apple as sacred, and it would seem that he is de- desirous, in his little way, of emulating the terrible punishment which originally fell upon those who partook of the forbidden fruit. These are of the fantastic tricks which parody justice, and which make the angels weep. Bailie HUNTER is too big to be birched for his inhumanity, but the State can take from him the power which he has so grossly abused ; and if Scotchmen do their duty LUNAN, the labourer, will be released from gaol before the forty days have expired, and the Bailie will be Bailie no longer. The other case to which we would draw attention is that of a bricklayer of Dartford, named GEORGE FIELD, who was sentenced the other day to one month's imprisonment, ostensibly because he was twenty-two shil- lings in arrear with a rate of one shilling per month which had been levied upon him to- wards the maintenance of his father, an in- mate of the Dartford Union Workhouse. The real cause of his sentence would seem, how- ever, to be that he dared to speak out and speak the truth. His defence was that he had not paid because he could not pay. He had a wife and nine children to keep, and had met with an accident ten weeks ago, which had laid him up for seven weeks. He was starving, he said, with thousands of others; he had io to pay for back rent, and he thought he might just as well go to gaol. The chairman of the magistrates, a Conservative landowner, told this man he was a disgrace to his clas3, and committed him to prison for a month. FIELD ventured to ask why he was a disgrace —because he spoke the truth? And the Magistrate, with a simplicity which would be charming if it were not so utterly cruel, answered "Yes." It is added that "the court then rose, and the defendant• was removed in custody in the presence of his 1 wife and daughter, who were crying bitterly." We are glad to be ab!e to add that the un- fortunate bricklayer has, after all, escaped the clutches of the gaoler. His wife pawned his watch to pay the arrears; and, the case having been made public, subscriptions including £5 from Mr. Chamberlain—have been sent to Dartford to put FIELD on his legs again. It has been elicited that he is "a steady industrious man," and that he has got into debt—having nine children to provide for—" through ill health, and being occasionally out of work." With such facts before us we would ask—which of the two men is the disgrace to his class —the Tory squire or the bricklayer? The man who struggles manfully under a great burden ; or the magistrate who abuses the law and adds insult to injury ? There are terribly hard and terribly vindictive things done in the name of the law, and will be to the end of time ; but our point is that the hardship would be less and that vindictiveness would all but disappear if we had a stipendiary magistrate as chair- man of every Bench.

THE Conservatives of Warrington are not a little annoyed—and well they may be—that their candidate, Sir GILBERT GREENALL, should have been found guilty of complicity in the matter of the stoppage of the Morley Common footpath. It is in vain that the Tory agent protests that "Sir GILBERT had nothing to do with it." Bit by bit the truth has been got at, until now the denial pre- sents itself as an absurdity. What is the use of Mr. HAMPSON quibbling as to the exact form of the signature which Mr. T. SMITH BURGESS used when he wrote to the Railway Company as agent of Sir GILBERT; or as to whether the phrase " close the footpath" was part of the letter? Can his object be to convey the impression that n o letter of any kind was written on the subject? We, however, know better; Mr. BURGESS knows better, and what is more, he admits that such a letter has been written. We have the authority of Mr. GEORGE PLUMPTON, tool manufacturer, for saying that on Sunday, the 16th August, Mr. BURGESS explained to him and two other gentlemen, while they were in the neighbourhood of Morley Common, that he wrote a letter in February last to the Railway Company, after mentioning the matter to Sir Gilbert. His object, he said, was to call the attention of the Company to the fact that the footpath was being much used by the public, and that, if the Ship Canal scheme was proceeded with, it was likely to be much more used. He had no thought, not he, of Sir GILBERT GREENALL'S interests as a game preserving Squire in nam- ing this matter to his master, and in writing to the Railway authorities. It was out of pure affection for the Railway Company ; and it was the same benevolent motive, when the footpath was closed as a result of the letter, Stopping hinagctuited Sir GILBERT'S gamekeeper in op people from going that way under a threat of a prosecution. Of course, if there are people who can swallow such stuff .they are welcome to it ; but they are not, in our opinion, to be found out- side the narrow circle of the under- lings of Walton Hall and of the Warrington Conservative Association. With regard to the statement that the footpath was "made for Mr. CR. OsFIELD and that he paid them i to keep it n repair for his own con- venience," we are authorised to say that it is absolutely false. He found the foot- path in existence when he went to Walton over twenty years ago, and all he did was to ask one of the Company's servants to put i some cinders on it to keep t dry in winter. The path, being an ancient right of way, was open before he went to Walton, and it was toop e sn rw hGe hB Ee RlerftGWßaElEtoNn. ALL, Iti. n h caos nbj ue en nc t ft with with his agent, to take steps to get the path closed. He would deprive men of their rights in order to get a breeding ground for snipe; but he will find that the public are not to be defrauded without a struggle, and that as to the next election, so far from the Liberals being in any doubt as to their, candidate, there is a CRosrrELD ready to champion the people's cause, and give the final quietus to the reactionary obstructionist of Walton and Wilderspool.

THE Marquis of RIPON is a good sound Liberal, who, because he has an abiding faith in Liberal principles, earnestly desires that they shall triumph. When he was ap- pointed Viceroy of India by the Liberal Government, the Tories raised a cry against him on the ground that he was a Roman

Catholic; it was impossible, they said. that a Ruler wedded to the creed of Rome could do justice to people of another race and another creed. But events more than justi- fied Mr. GLADSTONE'S choice; and showed how much the Tories misjudged the man. There never was a more popular Viceroy than Lord RIpoN, and he was popular not because of smooth talk and big promises, but because he set to work to apply Liberal principles in India as he had been taught them in Eng- land. The natives saw that he had con- fidence in them, and they let it be seen by enthusiastic demonstrations that th-y had confidence in him. Lord RANDoLpH CHURCHILL blackened himself the other day by throwing mud at Lord RiPoN. In this way he unintentionally rendered a service to the Liberal party, for it enabled Lord RIPON last week to show how wise and statesmanlike had been his administration of affairs in our great Eastern Dependency. On Monday night the ex-Viceroy occupied the chair at a Liberal meeting at Ripon, and delivered an interesting address, in the course of which he said "he held more strongly than ever the same political principles which he had held from the commencement of his political life." He urged upon the electors to give a free, bold, and honest vote at the next election, re- minding them that, whatever might have been said in certain quarters, they might rely on the absolute secrecy of the ballot. With re- gard to Protection, his lordship made a few observations which farmers would do well to ponder. He said "he knew that the Conser- vative farmer was a most enduring person, a most long-suffering person, and that, politi- cally speaking, he could be fed upon the most empty promises and the smallest perform- ances ;" but he submitted that "the only result of putting a duty on agricultural pro- duce would be that the whole of it would go, into the pockets of the landowner to 1 increase or to maintain his rents." But the demand at present is to tax manufactured goods that are imported into this country. and if this were done the result would be that the farmer, without obtaining anything in the shape of relief, would find that he was saddled with an increase in the cost of clothing and of agricultural implements. The word has gone forth from the leaders of the Tory party that nothing is to be said about putting a tax upon corn ; they know that no Government that made such a proposal could exist for al week ; and as to a tax upon imported goods farmers must be easily deluded if they think they will profit by any such proceeding. The right course for them is to look to those who have helped them in the past, who have given them a Ground Game Act, a real Agricultural Holdings Act, and are prepared, if again returned to power, to remove other fetters which still shackle the oldest and greatest industry of the world.

A MARRIED woman named ELLEN POM- FRET was fined twenty shillings and costs, at Newton, on Saturday, for her extraordinary treatment of a dog. It seems that Mrs. Pohl- FRET has a garden in which she takes pride, and that a long-haired collie dog has been in the habit of visiting the garden and making itself too much at home. It is very irritat- ing, no doubt, when you have carefully reared a crocus or a cabbage, to find some morning that it has been trampled dowu by an unappreciative dog. But where there is a wrong the law provide's a remedy. That, at any rate, is the maxim of the law, though it is not the maxim of MTS. POMFRET, who, I the other day, took the law and the dog in her own hands. She meant her remedy to be thorough, for, with something like "malice aforethought," she had provided herself with a pair of scissors and brush, and with a plentiful supply of tar. With the scissors she cut off the long hair of that collie dog —it was a prepara- tory process ; and then she saturated the animal with tar by way of impressing on its mind the fact that there was something less agreeable than dog roses in Mrs. POMFRET'S garden. It is not known, except to the all- thoughtful Mrs. POMFRET, whether she let the dog "have it hot ;" but it is certain that the poor brute was sufficiently punished, for we learn that it was ill for three days, that it was in great pain, and that it trembled and staggered when it tried to walk. When questioned as to the damage said to have been done, the gentle dame replied that "the damage was done in the winter," from which it would seem that she had nursed her wrath for a long time in order to keep it warm. The magistrates, after being made familiar with the details, were in no wise enamoured of the new mode of training and trimming dogs. They did not, however, re- taliate with "tar and feathers ;" they were law-abiding and orthodox, and contented themselves with ordering Mrs. POMFRET to pay zos. and costs for her whistle; and little enough too—for such a whistle.

div.p: THE FXAMINEII. SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 5, 1885

WESTON CHURCH OF ENGLAND DAY SCHOOL—The chi'- den of this school had their annual treat on Wednesday to Overton fills, where they were conveyed by conveyances at the expense of Mr. and Mrs. E. Aaron. A very pleasant time was spent. SOOTHE ILLITSITIA.TED ALMANAC, 1836, AND DIREC- TORY OF RUNCORN, WESTON, AND HALTON —The atten- tion of the public is invited to this useful publication, which will be issued early in December next. It comprises the most extensive and complete local postal directory ever published. Early applications for advertisements to be made to the agent, Mr. W. Brookes, 7, Waterloo-road, Run- corn —Advt. _ _ _

SAMARETAN LODGE, LO G T., WIDNES. The usual weekly meeting was hel4 on Monday evening, when Bro. Machin, W.C.T., presented a report of the proceedings at the district lodge held on the previous Saturday. After the usual routine had been completed, the Brethren and ' Sisters of the Haste to the Rescue Lodge paid a fraternal visit, and entertained the large number present with the following programme :—Reading, "Butter Dick," Bro. Smith; song, " Polly Perkins," Bro. Andrews; song, "No one cares for me," Sister Smith ; song, " Safe within the veil," Sister Andrews; reading, "Sausage making," Bro. Kirkham ; recitation, "The Spanish Cham- pion." Bro. Galilee ; song, "The old arm chair," Bro. Griffiths.—The visiting lodge was heartily thanked for their entertainment, on the motion of Bro. Webb, seconded by Bro. Machin, and the vote was duly acknowledged. RUNCORN STARR BOWSETT BUILDING SOCIETIES.— The annual meeting of the First Society took place on Thursday evening, under the presidency of Mr. T. Booth. There was a capital attendance. The directors' fourth annual report, which was adopted, stated the subscriptions amounted to £1,235 108 6d, an increase of £l4O 2s over the previous year. The income from repayments had amounted to £176 16s, an increase of a f 4s. During the year eight appropriations had been made, and there had been advanced on mortgage of property £1,335, making a total advance of £3,165 since the formation of the aociety. The retiring directors—Messrs. T. Booth, 'l'. Hiley, J. Midwood, and J, D. Jones—were remleoted, as were also the auditors— Messrs. W. Brooks and J. Cunnah.— Mr. W. Handley was re-appointed secretary at a salary of £45, on the motion of Mr. S. C. Beckett, who said the society owed a great deal to the ability and energetic assiduity of Mr. Handley. A Ballot took place, and resulted in the success of Mr. Robert William Rushton, of Greenwaymoad, who is entitled to £2OO free of interest.—An appropriation meeting of the Second Societe was subsequently held. Mr. G. Moss pre- sided, and delivered an excellent address upon the principlee and advantages of Starr Bowkett Societies. An appropria- tion of £3OO was won by Mrs. Hester L. Davies, wife of Mr John Davies, of Penketh-street. ELECTION OF RUNCORN COMMISSION/MS.—The annual election of members to the Board of Improvement Commis- sioners took place on Thursday. For the six vacancies there were no less than eleven candidates, but the contest nevertheless passed off with very little excitement, and the mural literature was very scanty. Mr. W. Farrell, builder, came forward as an independent character, and opened the campaign with a trenchant address in which he dealt with what he regarded the deficiencies of the present rulers of the town. The Ratepayers Association issued a list of six candidates, and argued that an infusion of "new bloo4 " amonest the Commissioners would be the beet remedy for the bad humoure that had recently made their appearance in the Beard-room. The gentlemen in question were Mes.rs. J. N. Lello, E. lmison' W. Mellor, W. H. Rogerson, James Dobson, and J. W. Lightburn. Mr. Lightburn, however, promptly issued a handbill repudiating any connection with the association, and later his name appeared along with the other retiring members upon a list signed "A Ratepayer." This signature has always been adopted by the works, and was the means cn the present occasion of leading peonle to believe that the names published were the " black list," but it is an undeniable fact that this year the works have refrained from taking any active part in the contest. The following gentlemen had therefore only the influence of their names and character and their canvassers to rely upon for the issue :—Messrs. T. Norman, J. Prit- chard, J. Dobson, J. W. Lightburn, Joseph Williams, and G. J. Knight. The poll opened at nine o'clock, at the Market Hall. Mr. Robert Shaw was the returning officer, and he was assisted in his duties by Messrs. E. Marshall, W. Sutton, and J. D. Jones. Cabs were freely used for conveying the voters, and the committee-rooms engaged by the candidates were scenes of bustle and animation until the close of the poll at four o'clock. The result was declared as follows at a qua,ter to five:—

- - T. Norman J. Pritchard 677 J.N.tello 374 J. W. Lightburn ... 535 W. H. Rogerson J. Dobson • 503 J. Williams W. Farrell 499 G. J. Knight l5l E. Imison 474 The name of Mr. Farrell was greeted with cheers for the gallant and successful tight he had made. The first six gentlemen named are elected, and include four retiring members and one nominee of the Ratapayers' Association. The numbers polled are much below those of last year, when Mr. Like headed the poll with upwards of 900 votes.

THE INTERNATIONAL INVENTIONS EXHIBITION. —The Executive Council of this Exhibition have completed arrangements with the whole of the Railway Companies of the United Kingdom whereby parties numbering 25 and upwards can from the present time and until the close of the Exhibition, obtain at greatly reduced rates through tickets, combining the journey to London, carriage over the Underground Railways, passage through the South Kensington Sub-way, and admission to the Exhi- bition and back. Application for these facilities should be made to any Station Master in the coun- try.—Advt. RR. CHAMBERLAIN AND TORY SPEAXERS.—The following letter from Mr. Chamberlain is a reply to Mr. Spiers Turnbull, of Manchester, who called the attention of the right honourable gentleman to a statement by Mr. Barrington Balfour, Conservative candidate for Roxburglishire, charging him with jobbery in connection with gas and water under- takings at Birmingham at the tine he was in office as Mayor of that town :—" Birmingham, August 20, 1885.—Sir,—The statement made by Mr. Balfour, at Ancrum, respecting my connection with the gas and water undertakings at Birmingham, is an absolute and stupid falsehood. No lie, however malignant and improbable, appears to be too gross for a Tory speaker when he has occasion to refer to a political opponent.—l am, yours, &c., J. CHAMBER-.

DR. MACKIE AND THE MONTROSE BUTtGIIS.—Dr. Mackie, of Warrington, has become a Tory candi- date for the Montrose Burghs, solely in the hope that a split among the Liberals will enable him to wriggle in for this safe Liberal seat. It would be highly discreditable both to the candidates and to their leading supporters if there were to be any such disastrous issue of the election, as so great is the Liberal majority that it would be necessary for three of their candidates to go to the poll before the Tory could get in. No doubt wise counsels will prevail during the next two months and the most acceptable of the Liberals will be returned. There are so many hopeful seats in England which are still without Tory candidates that it amazes one to find Dr. Mackie or any other rational being seriously coming forward for so decidedly Radical a constitu- ency as Montrose.—Truth.

MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL ACT.—A demonstra- tion in honour of the passing of the Ship Canal Act and in recognition of the labours of Mr. Daniel Adamson and his colleagues on the Provisional Committee was held on Monday at Eccles and Patricroft. The festival commenced at Eccles by the public roasting of an ox, which was placed over the fire at half-past six in the presence of a large number of villagers, who gathered round the immo- lating fireplace as early as five o'clock. Many thousands of people attended, and the district was gay with bunting. A procession of public bodies passed through the densely-crowded thoroughfares, and everywhere Mr. Adamson and his coadjutors were greeted with the utmost cardiality. In the evening public meetings in furtherance of the Ship Canal scheme were held at Eccles and Patricroft. At the meeting in the:former place an address was presented to Mr. Adamson, who, in his reply, em- phasised his well-known arguments as to the under- taking proving not only of immense benefit to the trade of Lancashire, but of pecuniary advantage to the shareholders. Mrs. Adamson was presented with the photographs of the leading men of the local committee. DEFENCE OF THE POOR MAN'S PLATFORM.—The Daily News has published the following letter from the Rev. G. S. Reaney, formerly of Warrington "Last Sunday I bailed out two men, Socialists, who had been arrested for 'preaching Socialism in the streets.' The plea in one case was obstruction of the streets, and in the other drunkenness. Both pleas were false; there had been no obstruction, and there was no justification for the charge of drunk- enness. Now, I am not a member of the Democratic League, but I am jealous, in the interests of the poor, for the right to speak in the streets, under proper regulations. Some of us have done so for years, and do so still, but the Socialists have of late become objects of police raids. It was a sorry sight last Monday to see Mrs. Hicks, an intelligent and good woman, put into the dock where the refuse of the East-end so often appear, called the prisoner,, and having to defend herself from a charge for which there was not the slightest foundation. In Stepney, Limehouse, and Poplar we have no open spaces, but the streets. Surely some little license ought to be given to all creeds and all sorts of poli- ticians, under these circumstances, to make use of the poor man's only platform—the street—for the discussion of social questions in which all classes are interested. Who has set the police on to make this raid upon present-day Chartism? Pray give us the help of your influence in defending ourselves from the latest development of police authority,"

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

FRODSHAM MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—On Friday evening a meeting of the members of the Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, was held in the schoolroom, and it was decided to form a class to be called the Frodsharn Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Class. The following officers were appointed, viz.:—President, Rev E Mosscrop ; vice-presidents, Rev F F Edmonds, Rey R F Borwick, Mr Thomas Sant; secretary, Mr James Kent; treasurer, Mr. Boden. A committee was also appointed to draw up a code of roles. WESTON WESLEYAN DAY SCHOOL—The annual excur- sion of the scholars attending these schools took place on Friday, the 28th inst. It was of a most interesting and en- joyable kind. The children and friends were conveyed from Weston to Mersey View, Overton, by Messrs. Wm. Griffiths, Thomas Griffiths, James Ford, and James Dunbabin. The manner in which the children and adults enjoyed themselves showed how much these days of relaxation are appreciated. The arrangements for tea were excellently carried out by Mrs. Parker. Before leaving sweetmeats were distributed by Mr. A. Dunbabin. A FATAL Dxxxx AT WIDNES.— Mr. Brizhouse on Wednesday held an inquest at the Norton Arms. Widnes, touching the death of Patrick Drury, 4fr years of age, son of James Drury, of 70, Oxford-street. On Saturday night Drury made some tea for his wife, who was ill, and placed the teapot upon the table. During his ab- sence in another room the decease] took hold of the teapot and drank from the spout, very seriously scalding his mouth and throat. Dri3O'Keeffe was called in, but his kill was of no 'avail, an the child died on Monday. A ' verdict of "Accidental death" was recorded. The jury, of which Mr. Thomas Gerrard was foreman, discussed the dangerous character of the place where the accident occurred. Mr. Ferrand, of the selicitors' department, Lime-street Station, said people had no right to cross the line at that point.— The Coroner asked how the people were to get across the canal then.—Mr. Ferrand replied that they must walk along side the railway.—The Coroner : It is a strange tieing that there is a Commercial Hotel on one side the line and inhabted houses on the other and no means of protecting the people from the danger which they incur from passing ti air's. After some consideration the jury said i they con- sidered that the lighting of the place was totally insufficient and made a presentment to the effect that the company should provide more lights in order to protect the lives of , the people who found it necessary to cross the lines. A , verdict of accidental death was recorded

THEFT FROM A WIDNES REFRESHMENT HOUSE.—Patrick Cain was brought up at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wed- nesday, charged with stealing a knife and fork from the re- freshment rooms of Mrs. Unsworth, Victoria-road. The articles were missed on Saturday night, and afterwards found upou the prisoner, who had been in the house.—He was sent to gaol for 14 days. CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT WIDNES.—Wm. Townsend, carter for Mr. Percy, contractor, was brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Wednesday, charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse whilst in an unfit state.—lnspector Greenwell, S.P.C.A., ;roved that the animal driven by the defendant on the 20th ult bad a wound upon its back and another on its shoulders, and was suffering great pain.—A fine of Ll and costs 13s was imposed. FAILURE AT WIDNES —AA the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, on Thursday, before Mr. Registrar Cooper, the case of Joseph Pollitt came on for bearing. It was an examina- tion of the bankrupt, a provision dealer, having several shops at Widnes and St. Helens. The liabilities were stated to be £1,369, the deficiency shown being .£1,086. The debtor was examined by Mr. Ring as to his trading and the disappearance of some important books in regard to his transactions. The case was adjourned. PRIMITIVE METHODISM AT WIDNES.—The annual ser- mons were preached at Simm's Cross Chapel, on Sunday, by the Rev. W. Barrett, of Chorley, and the collections amounted to £3 2s 91-011 Monclty evening a tea party and meeting took place. There was a numerous attendance. Mr.F. Lawrinson presided, and delivered an address. Mr. Drought, the secretary, presented a report which showed that the receipts during the past year amounted to £162 28 10d, and the expenditure £lOl Sc Id, leaving a balance of 14s 9d.

ACCIDENT ON rue RAILWAY AT WIDNE.S.--,-00 Tuesday night Patrick Hanlon, of Dolman's-lane, Warrington, and employed at the Widnes Metal Company's works, was seri- ously injured. He Was crossing the Marsh near Messrs. Golding, Davis and Company's works, when he was knocked down by an engine and several wagons that were being shunted. He was dragged a considerable distance by the fire box, and his left leg was broken in two places and his body is very badly bruised. He now lies at the hospital in a dangerous condition.

ATTEMPT TO THROW A CONSTABLE INTO A WIDNES QUARRY.-At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday Thos. Cruise, a heavy strong-built man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting and resist- iog P.C. Almond. About a quarter-past six on Saturday evening the prisener was drunk in Appleton village, and P.C. Almond £I49F him throw stines at a woman, who would most certainly have been killed hid one chanced to strike her. The constable took the prisoner into custody, where- upon he threw him to the ground, kicked him several tim-a on the head, and attempted to throw him into the Appleton Quarry. The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour without the option of a fine.

ACTION AGAINST CAPTAIN LE COUTEUR AT RUNCORN.— At Runcorn County Court, en Saturday, before his Honour Judge W.Wynne Ffoulkes, Frederick J. Abbott, shipbuilder, Runcorn, sued Captain J. Le Couteur, of Weston point, for LI Sc, being the cost of repairing a narrow boat ',ay the order of the defendant.—Mr. J. Burton represented the plaintiff. In January last a narrow boat belonging to Mr. Wm. Tur- key came in collision with a boat which was being towed by a tug of the Weston Point Steam Towing Company. It was alleged that the defendant, who is agent to the com- pany, sent the boat and stated how it should be repaired. The boat was made all right, and the bill was forwarded to the Company, who, however, repudiated the transaction.— The defendant informed his Honour that he merely inspec- ted the boat in his capacity as Marine Surveyor, and sug- gested how it should be repaired. If he had to pay for jj2e repairs of all the boats he surveyed he would require floe purse of a Rothschild.—His Honour said he was of opinion when he heard the evidence of the first witness that the de- fendant's observations did not constitute an order to do the work. He gave judgment for the defendant. RUNCORN THEATRE RoYAL.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. F. Rigby and Mr. ;as. Handley, Miss James. daughter of the proprietress of the Theatre Royal, made an application for the renewal of the licence to that building.—Mr. Rigoy : On what ground do you make this fur- ther application. Has there been any provision against fire? —Miss James replied that the surveyor had inspected the building and all the necessary alterations were being made. —Mr. Rigby: But in case of fire how would you put it out: Is water laid on? Yes, I think so.—At every point? Yes, I think so.—ln ,eply to Mr. Rigby, Supt. Leah said he was not aware of ..nyth,ng being done.—Mr. Rigby said the Banco could not deal with the matter that day. Mrs. James mos exerei:e judgment in making every conceivable pro- tection as regarded the public, and then report to the Supt. Of Police, who would be in a position to enlighten the Bench as to whether the improvements had been made that ouz,ht to be wide. Until the public were thoroughly and entirely protected the application would be refused. It was there- fore idle to make a further application until everything had been done to protect the public against fire and accident.— We understand the building has been surveyed by Mr. Pier- point, of Warrington, and alterations he has suggested are being carried out at a cost of .£6O. BULL'S HEAD SUBSCRIPTION BOWLING GREEN.— This green was again occupied on Saturday after- noon with a handicap main of bowls, the proprietor (Mr. J. Evans) giving 10s, to which the competitors subscribed Is each. The green was in exeellent condition, and the bowling was of a first-class char- acter. The handicappers were Messrs. J. Shaw, W. Gleave, and T. Hackett, who fulfilled their duties satisfactorily, as was proved by the closeness of the games throughout the main. Several games were of an exciting character, especially those between J. Shaw and J. Gleave, G. Ball and R. Fairbrother, and J. Bridge and R. Fairbrother, the latter even- tually winning the main by defeating W. Gleave by.. 3. The 'following were the principal prize winners :-1, R. Fairbrother, 255; _2, W. Glcave, _ .

12s; 3, J. bridge, 6s; 4, j. Heald,' 6s.—An open main of bowls took place on the above green yester- day, but owing to the inclemency of the weather the final games were postponed until Monday. There was a good number of competitors from Widnes, Runcorn, and Earlestown, the majority of whom remain in.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was hell at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Wednesday. Mr. R. Shaw presided, and there were present Messrs. S. Taylor, H. White, T. Norman, J. Williams, J. Meadowcroft, H. Grice, W. Whittaker, W. Fisher, F. A. Lake, James Pritchard, J. W. Lightburn, T. Harris, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), and 31. Barker (surveyor.)

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICES.
div.p: THE APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICES.

Mr. Meadowcroft drew attention to the appointment of Dr. McDougall as medical officer at the last meeting of the Board, and contended that the suspension of Standing Order 17 was irregular and illegal.—The Chairman agreed that it was well to canduct the business of the Board upon ordinary and well-defined rules, but it was urgent and im- portant that the medical officer should be appointed at the last meeting.—Mr. Meadowcroft did not question the wis- dom of the action of the Board, but ho bad been throughout a sticker for legal methods being employed, and be was satisfied with the remarks of the chairman.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.-IMPORTANT REPORT.
div.p: THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.-IMPORTANT REPORT.

- -- Dr. McDougall, the medical officer of health, reported that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 21. Of these deaths two were due to violent causes, viz., one to drowning, and one to falling eft a ladder. Of the remaining nineteen death,' three were due to wasting, two to consumption, two to convulsions, two heart disease, three to diarrhcea and disease of glands, congestion of the lungs, cancer of the stomach. inflamma- tion of the lining of the membrane of the braio, chest affec- tion, dry nursing and natural decay accounted for one each. Ten deaths occurred amongst infants under one year. The 119 deaths chew a death-rate for the month of 13 per 1,000 lof the population. Ile had during the month made a house Ito house visitation of some of the more populous streets in the town. He had also inspected the common lodgingrhouses, the marine stores, and certain other localities that required immediate and spe- cial attention. The marine store dealers in the 1 course of business received consignments of green bones, and some of them had been in the habit of all-owing large heaps of these putrid matters to accumulate before dispos- ing of them. He had cautioned all of them against con- tinning the practice; but most probably some would require special treatment, lie had also daring his inspection come across sink stones in living rooms, and in the yards of some houses that were in direct communication with the sewers without the intervention of a trap. It would be apparent to the Authority that this was a great and dangerous evil that required immediate satisfaction. He would venture to sug- gest to every householder to examine their sink stones (elop stones), waste water and soil pipes, and see that they were thoroughly well trapped. In the case of sink stones the most effectual way et trapping where practicable would be to get the waste pipe' to discharge over a trapped grid in the yard. He hoped within a short time to present a special report on the sanitary condition of certain localities that would require some attention from the Authority. He had received during these visits every aesistance from the nuisance inspector. The report was stated to be a very important one, and was referred to the Health Committee.

div.head: COMMITTEES.
div.p: THE COMMITTEES.

The minutes of the various committees were passed. Mr. Meadowcroft had resigned his position as a member of the Health Committee and as chairman of the Highway and Sanitary Committee. The secretary was instructed by the Highway and Sanitary Committee to urge the Runcorn Gas Company to submit plans of their extensions. The clerk of works to the proposed new Salvation Army barracks ap- peared before the committee, and was informed that the building line adopted by the Board would be adhered to. The market superintendent reported to the General Purposes Committee that the receipts for the past month amounted to £2l 180 Bd, being an increase of £4 12s 4d on the corre- sponding period of last year. The Finance Committee re- ported that during the past month the treasurer had received £348 68 9d, and accounts amounting to £333 Is 7d were passed for payment.

div.head: TER RETIREMENT or )IR. BRISCOE.
div.p: TER RETIREMENT or )IR. BRISCOE.

Upon the report of the committee appointed to arrange for the annual election being presented, the Chairman said he thought this a proper time to refer to the retirement of a gentleman who had served the town for a period of about 30 years. Ile referred to Mr. Briscoe. who found that he was not strong enough to attend to the duties of the Board. It was a source of regret to him (the chairman) that Mr. Briscoe had decided to sever his connection with the Board, because be knew his value. The Board had been
greatly indebted to Mr Briscoe for the advice he had gi on numtrous important and trying occasions, and in retirement they lost a gentleman who had at all times
taken

a broad visw of every matter coming before the Board, and who without swerving to the right or to the left bad done his work manfully. Lie hoped that in his retirement Mr Briscoe would have that comfort and felicity which be deserved, and he was sure that he had the good wishes of every member of the Board, and also of those that he bad served so faithfully and well during the last 30 years.—Mr Norman and Mr Meadowcroft also bore testimony to the amianle and sterling qualities of Mr Briscoe, and his services to the town.

div.head: FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
On the motion of Mr F A Lake, it was unanimously de- cided that the members of the Free Library Committee should be increaatd from seven to eleven, including the Chairman of the Board.
THE CHARGES AGAINST THE SHIP CANAL DEPUTATION.

div.head: REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE.
div.p: REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE.

The committee appeinted to inquire into the allegation that Messrs. Shaw, Pritchard, and Speakman, members of a deputation to London respecting the Ship Cana Bill, had received £l2 from the Law Clerk in addition to their proper charges, reported "that they have made a minute and care- ful examination of the various minutes of the Committee and Board, and the vouchers, bills, and chequ.s relating to this matter, and have consid,red the statements both writ- teii and verbal of Messrs. Shaw, Pritchard, Speakman, and Linaker, and the evidence they have respectively preduced, and your committee finds as follows :—(1) That Mr. Lina- ker agreed to deduct from the balanee due to him the sum of £l2 (2) That such £l2 was deducted prior to the cheque for £144 Os 4d paid by this Board being issued, and that such cmque was consequently lees by £l2 than it would have been had not the balance due ta Mr. Linaker been reduced as aforesaid. (3) That Messrs. Shaw Prit- chard, and Speakman did not receive from Mr. Linaker, either directly or indirectly the sum of £l2, or any part thereof, and they were in no way benefited by such reduc- tion. (4) That the ratepayers, and not the deputation, received the benefit of the £l2.—(Signed) Wm. Fisher, John Meadowcroft, Fred. A. Lake, John W. Lightbarn, Thomas Harris."—The Chairman said at the last meeting it was understood what the issue was to be, and now that the committee had found the same verdict that one of Her Majesty's judges had come to—that the charge was a false hood from beginning to end—it was for the Board to deal with the matter.—The Law , Clerk read a letter he had addressed to the secretary (Mr. Marshall) to which he had received no ' reply, expressing his surprise at the scope of the inquiry, and declining to comply with the request of the committee I acting under instructions so limited. The committee was , asked for by himself on the chairman stating that he had been trying to obtain the payment of his hotel expenses , twice over, and if the committee would take evidence ac to the truth or otherwise of this statement of the chairman's he had no objection to the committee further inquiring into the correctness or otherwise of the statement made by him (Mr. Linaker) to Dr. McDougall in the summer of last I year, which was to the effect that at the request of Mr. ' Shim, who was accompanied by Mr. Pritchard, he agreed to allow to the deputation the. sum of £l2 out of his charges towards re-iinbursing them in the elifference of their inci- denial expenses while in London, between the 5s they had decided they ought to charge to the ratepayers, and the lOs , which in the first instance the deputation had agreed to , charge. The committee must remember that be had no knowledge of how Messrs. Shaw and Pritchard made out the totals of the expenses they claimed, and be never had I any information from which he could judge what might be I fairly considered their proper charges. Mr. Linaker said he could only state again that when he agreed to allow the £l2 from his law bill of costs it was not for the purpose alleged by Messrs. Shaw and Pritchard, and he was stating that the chairman had charged him with trying to obtain his hotel expenses twice over, when the Chairman interrupted him by;saying : Mr. Linaker is elating what is not true again.- , Mr. Linaker entered into the figures of the transaction. At this point Messrs. Whittaker, Norman, Grice and Williams rose for the purpose of leaving the room.—Mr. Lightbuaae^ said he should not like the responsibility left to a few mOnuers. —Mr. (Mee said he had no intention of shirking his respon- sibility, and it then transpired that tbe gentlemen were about I to attend the funeral of Mr. Jno. liazlehurst.—Mr. Linaker weret on to contend that Mr. Shaw had made four separate I and distinct assertions with regard to the £l2, and said his ' position was in the hands of the Board, who could deal with him as they thought fit.—The Chairman declared Mr. I Linker's assertion that he (the speaker) had stated that Mr. Linaker tried to obtain his hotel bill twice over, to be false.—Mr. Lightburn referred to the painful nature of the Comtnittee's investigations. Whatever Mr. Linaker's feel- ings might have been it was not a fact tbat the deputation I received £l2, and he thought he ought to apologise to the deputation, and let the matter end there.---Mr. Fisher moved that the Committee's report be adopted.—Mr. Lake seconded the motion. He was glad to say that the deputation were puite clear from the slightest suspicion of having received the £l2. The decision of the Committee was Quite mini- Moos, and he only hoped that Mr. Linaker would see that 1 an apology was due.—Mr. Linaker said the Committee did not state any reasons for their facts.—Mr. Fisher: We take the facts as we find them : we cannot eeasen on facts.—Mr. Linaker: Of the figures I know nothing. All I know is the reason that induced me Co take £l2 off my bill was to give the deputation something they did not like to ask the rate- payers to pay.—ln answer to Mr. Pritchard, Mr. Fisher said Mr. Linaker was giveu every opportunity to prove his came —Mr. Meadowcroft said the committee had conducted their labours with a desire to do strict justice to both sides, and there was not a single peint neglected on either aide. They felt it their daty to confine themselves strictly to the resolu- tion of the Board. He could not understand how the Law Clerk had got it into his bead that the deputation benefited in any way by the £l2 he took off his bill. For some time past it had been evident that there was not that cordial working on the part of the Law Clerk with the Chairman that there ought to be, and this was proved by the corres- pondence that has recently taken place in the public Press. It was clear there was a feeling of antagonism that ought not to exist, and which would reflect upon the Board if per- mitted to continue. There must be an end to it. His ex- perience as the previous chairman was that his views were misrepresented by someone. His predemosor retired front the chair with mingled feelings of regret that he had ever Occupied it. The former chairman retired from the chair with similar feelings, and he felt that they had arrived at a serious crisis. If they meant to loot upon the chair as a position if dignity and honour and pleasure they must stand by it, otherwise instead of being a position to be sought by men of influence and abil- ity, it would become an object of abhorrence.— The Chairman said he considered that the reasons that led to the attack upon the deputation, and perhaps the only satisfaction they could draw from it, was that they had been interested in economy—in seeing that the money of the ratepayers was properly spent, and spent as if it were their own.—Mr. Pritchard said the charge against the depu- tation was a very serious one, and when it was made by Mr. Linaker, a gentleman who occupied the position of law clerk to the Board, and Dr. McDougall, men who knew what they were saying and were capable of weighing the effect of their words, it became a question of very grave im- portance: The accusation was as dastardly as it was untrue, and it was a cruel and unjust thing that a deputation should be at the trouble and inconvenience of proving their honesty, to say nothing of the painful position in which they had heen placed for so long a time. The position Mr. Linker occupied was supposed to be one of trust and con- fidence, and he ought of all MeR to be the first to defend and guard, and not unjustly to assail the reputation of members of the Board. The legal adviser to the Board ought to be a man in whom they had perfect confidence, and in whom they could place implicit reliance, but instead of this he had brought unsubstantiated charges against some members, and the others were just as liable to misrepre- sentation as they had been. It was for the Board to see that the deputation was dealt with in as proper a manner as the circumstances warranted.—Mr. Lake was glad to say there was not the slightest ground for the charge; and he called upon the law clerk to make the amende honorable and apologise.—Mr. Tay:or also called upon Mr. Linaker to apologise.—Mr. Lisaker said when a man in his own in- ward conviction was satisfied that for a certain purpose he did a certain act, whatever might be the result of an in- quiry into figures which proved money which was al- lowed by his law bill did not go into the pockets of the de- putation, he could not possibly take the line suggested, and make an absolute apology for what had passed. Why should he give the ratepayers £l2 ? Ha was satisfied that the £l2 was never allowed with respect to the hotel bill.—Some further conversation took place, during which Mr. Meadow- croft said he could not join the other members in asking Mr. Linaker to apologise, because he thought it would be infra dig to do so ; and the report was then passed. The Board immediately dissolved.

div.head: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. JOHN HAZLEHURST OF RUNCORN. .. .
div.p: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. JOHN HAZLE- HURST OF RUNCORN. .. .

Mr. John Hazlehurst, of Roche House, Runcorn, died at his residence on Saturday morning last, at the advanced age of 82 years. The deceased gentleman was the second son of Mr. Thomas Haxlehurst, of Camden House, and was born on the 12ili March, 1503. At the time of his death he was the oldest surviving member of the Hazlehurst family, who have occupied a prominent position in the his- tory and progress of the town for the oast century. He was a member of the firm of Messrs. Hazlehnrst aud Sons. the establishment of 'whose works was coeval with the com- mencement of the industrial prosperity of the town. Mr. Hazlehurst bad taken little or no part in the public affairs of the town, preferring to live a quiet unostentatious life, but in religious matters, as a follower of John Wesley, he took a very active part. At 30 years of age he was appoin- ted leader of a society class at the old Brunswick Chapel, and this position he held to the time of his decease. The members, when he was unable to visit them at the chapel, met at his house, and the last occasion was about three weeks ago, when Mr. Hazlehurst offered up a heartfelt prayer. For a number of years the deceased was circuit steward of the Wesleyan Society in Runcorn, and also filled the position of treasurer to the Runcorn Auxiliary of the British and Foreign:Bible Society. One of Mr. Hazlehurst's greatest pleasures was to visit and console the sick and dying, however lowly their station, and by no class of per- sons will be be more regretted than the poor. He married on the 7th January, 1830, Sarah, the second daughter of Mr. Francis Salkeld, of Pool Dale, Heath-road, who remains to mourn his loss. The funeral took place on Wednesday; and although rain was descending heavily as the cortege passed along the route to the Cemetery the streets were crowded with persons who exhibited many tokens of mourning. The windows of the shops and houses in the neighbeurhood'were datkened Out of respect to the deceased, and there was a
Louse.'

general feeling of gloom. Walking at the bead of the pro. cession were Messrs. T. Norman, J. Simpson, R. Norman, T. Simister, Wm. Whittaker, R. Lea, Wm. Key, Joseph Williams, H. J. Grine. W. Hankinson, A. Unsworth, S. Horton, S. Ravenscroft. Wm. Blake, R. Morris, Dr. Robinson, B. Knlveton, R. Rawlinson, T. Boote, J. Timperley, John Suminerfield, James Gregory, J. Lunt, J. Unsworth, G. Yarwood, Mr. Quinn, and J. W. Wood- land. The aged members of the deceased's society clam followed. viz, Mrs. A. Johnson, Mrs. F. Sharpies, Mrs. E. Raven.croft, Mrs. E Williamson, Mrs. E. Hancock, Mrs. Ann Cox, Mrs. C. Holford, Mrs. E. Cooper, and Miss E. Boyers. Then came the private carriage of Mrs. Charles Hazlehturst, it which were the Revs. T. M. Armson, S. H. Pink, and R. Edwards; and the carriage of Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.P., occupied by the Revs. W. Preston, T. Hackett, and Dr. McDougall. The hearse drawn by four horses occupied the next position, on each side being the bearers—Messrs. Thomas Tomlinson, Darlington, Caldi- cost, S. Taylor, Keogh, and Is 4ac J.hnson. The first mourning coach contained Mrs. Hazlehurst (widow), Cap- tain T. F. Hazlehurst (son), the Hon. Mrs. liazlehurst (daughter-in-law), and Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst (nephew) ; second, Mrs. Hall, Mr. W. F. Salkeld, Mrs. Pink, and Captain C. W. Hazlehurst ; third, Mr. and Mrs. W. E. Lea, Mr. and Mrs. A. Salkeld; fourth. Mrs. J. H. Sal- keld, Mrs. Dakin, Mr. J. L. Wigg, and Mr. A. F. Brundrit ; fifth. Messrs. Goodwin, J. Brundrit, J.P., J. Ashton, and W. D. Jolliffe. Two closed carriages, one of which had belonged to the deceased, brought up the rear of a long procession. At the church beautiful wreaths were placed upon the coffin by mourners, and floral offerings had been sent from Mrs. M. Mathiesou, Mrs. G. S. Hazlehurst, Mrs. C. and Miss Hazleburst, Mrs. Thomas Hazlehurst, Mrs. A. Salkeld, and Messrs. W. F. Salkeld, J. H. Salkeld, A. F. Brundrit, Mrs. Hall and the servants at " Beaconsfield '' The burial service was taken part in by the Rev. T. M. Armson, Rev. S. H. Pink, and the Rev. R. Ed- wards. The body was placed in a shell, which was enclosed in a lead coffin, with a beautiful oak exterior with brass fittings, and was lowered into the family vault in the pre- eence of a large concourse of people. Mr. Randle had en- tire charge of the funeral arrangement., and the hearse and coaches were supplied by Mr. S. Yarwood.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday, under the presidency of Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton. Present :—Revs J. W. N. Tanner, J. J. Bryant, J. Lockwood, Messrs. Aaron, Lewis, Wallington, Smith, J. Arrowsrnith, J. Farr, J. G. Hamilton, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk.)

, FRODSHAM PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES—ne minutes of these committees stated that the Clerk had received an an- onymous communication stating that milk from cows suffer- ing from foot and mouth disease was betng sold in Frod- sham from a Helsby farm. The Clerk and Inspector had investigated the matter, and found there was not the slightest ground for the allegation.—The Inspector reported he bad examined the pump and ontfall works, and be sug- gested that the best and most economical plan of emptying tte tanks was to wheel out the solid matter, and he had arranged for such to be done.—The committees decided. however, to confer with the engineer as to the best mode of working the tanks.—ln reply to Mr. Hadfield, it was stated that a building in course of erection at Fredsham Bridge by a member of the committee did not come within tbe bye- laws.—Mr. F. F. Edmonds appeared before the committee and stated that the cutting for the new sewer at Overton had been followed by the loss of the water from two springs on his property to disappear. The Vicarage water supply had also gone.—lt was resolved to acquaint the Engineer with the matter.—The minutes were adopted. ALLEGED POLLUTION OF IRON DISH BROOK, BELsgy,— The committee appointed by the Parochial Committees to inspect this brook reported that on the 19th August there was nothing whatever of an offensive nature, but suggested certain small alterations.—The report was adopted on the motion of Mr. Arrowsmith.

HE-APPOINTMENT OF MR. FARRINGTON.-Mr. Walling- ton moved. and Mr. Aaron seconded, that Mr. James Far- • rington be re-appointed inspector of nusances for two years at a salary of £l4O per annum, and also inspector of canal boats for the same period at an annual salary of £lo.—The motion was carried unanimously, and Mr. Farrington re- turned thanks. There was no other business of public interest.

RECHABITE DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN. The Union (adult) and the Excelsior (juvenile) lents of the Independent Order of Rechabites celebrated their twelfth anniversary on Monfiay by a successful demonstra- tion. A procession of 50 adult members and 80 juveniles started from the Duke of Westminster Cocoa Rooms, the , head quarters of the Order, at half-past one. and headed by the Millbrow Brass Band and their ranks gay with flags and bannerettes, marched through the principal thorough- fares of the town. The streets were lined by hundreds of spectators. A stoppage was made at the residence of Dr. Robinson and at Lea's Temperance Hotel. The procession was marshalled by Bros. T. Lea, P.C.R., and Wilson, P.G.VV.C.R., and tne juvenile members were in charge of Bros. R. Harrop and It. Evans (superintendents). After- wards the members proceeded to the football field, kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. Joseph Ashley, and a variety of games and amusements were engaged in. On returning from the field about 300 persons sat down to tea in Bethesda Schoolroom, the tables being presided over by Mrs. Cart- wright, Mrs. Peters, Mrs. H. Gleave, Mrs. Evans, Miss Evans, Miss Richardson, Mrs. Cross, Mrs. G. Thomas, Mrs. Thompson, MTN. T. Lea, Miss Jones, and Miss Lea. Subse- quently a public meeting and entertainment took place. The Rev. Edward Jones occupied the chair, and on the platform were Messrs. Thomas Cunliffe, P.H.C.R., editor of the "Rechabite Magazine " and the Bolton Guardian, W. Dutton, D.T., of Norley, R. Wilson, P.D.O R., Robert Evans, P.C.R , Thomas Lea. P.C.R , J. E. Warburton (secretary), anti Richard Evans (superintendent of juvenile I tent). _

Tile Secretary (Mr. J. E. Warburtcn) stated that the number of members of the adult section on the Ist January, 1854, was 109. Thirty-two had been admitted during the year, making a total of 141. One member had died during the year, and nine had left for various causes, leaving a memberslip of 131, showing a net increase of 22, 11 being transferred from the juvenile ten.. During the present year 23 members had berm initiated, five being lost, giving 149 as the present ordinary membership, with two honorary members in addition. The nett increase from the beginning of 1884 to the present was 40, the average age being 27i years, which PAS considered very low indeed. The funds at the beginning of last year amounted to £255 14s 64d. At the end of the year they had increased to £290 173 ltd. being a gain of £35 2s 6d. Up to the end of June quarter that sum bad been increased to £303 16s 7d. The tent had sent a donation to the Caton Hall Colliery Relief Fund of £s—(applause)—which would bring up the total to £3OB. The average sick pay per member had been 10s SI This I was rather higher than they had bees accustomed to. The average, however, for the last nine years had been Gs 63, which was about the average for the whole of the Order. I The worth per member was £2 4s 41d. He would like to mention that out of the £3OO they had to pay no funeral money. All funeral expenses were paid Oct of the district I fund, en that the £3OO was for sick avd incidental expenses. With regard to the entire Order, there had been an increase in two years of 13,000 adults and about 10,000 juveniles. The total membership was now 53,597 financial members, 5,000 honorary members, and 30,000 juveniles, giving a total of nearly 100,000 members in 70 districts, and 1,127 tents. (Applause.) In conclusion, he announced that the official valuer had declared the Union tent to be solvent. (Applause.) Bro. Dutton, in a short speech, mentioned the fact that 21 years had elapsed since the Winsford and Norley district was formed. He was one of the 14 who commenced a tent in Norlev at that time, and when be told them that that 14 had grown into 1,503 men, 153 women, 693 boys, and 142 girls, making a total of 2,497, he thought they had something to congratulate themselves upon. (Applause.) He described the good results following from the establishment of the Order in the district, and congratulated the Runcorn tents upon their success. The juvenile tent, he said, was now at the bead of the district as regarded members.

Mr. R. Evans. superintendent of the juvenile tent, pre- sented the annual report, which showed that they had now a total of 124 members, which was an increase since June, 1834, of 37. The amount of cash they had in hand was now £2l is 6id, being an increase of £4 9s 3,11. Four members had been transferred to the adult tent. The sub- scription to the juvenile tent was sevenpence per month, for which the members received three shillings during sickness besides medical attendance, their parents being paid at death £3. They had further succeeded during the year in liquidating the debt on the banner, the entire cost of which was £l3 9a. (Applause.) The Chairman then addressed the meeting. Intemper- ance, he said, was the national curse. It was the obstrue- lion at civilization, education, religion, and everything that tended to elevate and ennoble Ina,,kind, and it was the duty. of every christian, and especially every chriatian minister, to do all in their power to stem the tide of intemperance. After giving some facts with regard to the Rechtbite Order, he wished them God speed in their work, and trusted they woulri, in conjunction with other societies, be able. to over- throw the enormous traffic in intoxicating drink. Mr. Tromas Cunlifl compared the Rechabite tents with other friendly societies whose members were permitted to drink intoxicating liquor, showing that members of the for- mer had less sickness, and lived to a greater age. brought tl the whom hadtin g es tist Votes of thanks to the speakers, to the chairman, the meeting a eod lo :en. the band and the afternoon'sproceedings glee party, and

Toe neighbours noticed a strong smelt of ga", and finding that Mr. and Mrs. Horton did not come down to open their shop they communicated with the police. On an entrance being effected, both of them were found dead in bod,haring been suffouted by gas. How the gas escaped is not known.

James Daniels, and John 13anner were each fined for I being drunk in Widnes.
