div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Aid. Davies, Conn. Preening, and Mr. John Fairclough. MISCELLANEOVS.—The following cases of drunkenness were beard :—Alice Haydock, in Bottermarktt-street, on the previous evening, discharged on promising to leave the town; John Titchett, in Winwick-street, on the 22nd ult., fined 7s 63 including costs; William Bennett, in Bank Talk, on the 26th nit, fined 5s and costs: Winifred Con- way, in Winwick-road, on the 21st ult., sent to prison for a month, and Mary Baldwin, ditto, fined 103 and costs; Mary Rabbit, in Robinson's-yard, on the 23rd ult., dis- missed, and Mary McLoughlin, ditto, fined 5s including costs.—William Darbyshire, Margaret Smith, and-Mary Broderick, were ordered to be bound over to be of good be- haviour, they having been guilty of disturbing the peace. —James Sumner was fined the costs, 7s, for allowing a horse and cart to cause an obstruction in Market-street, and for allowing horses to stray in Lovely-lane on the 23rd ult., James Monks and John Owen were each fined 2s 6d and the costs.—Edward Burke and Susannah Dale were ordered to pay 63 costs each, for stone throwing in Silver-street.—John Jordan, for playing pitch and toss in Cloth Hall-yard, off Bank.stmet, was fined 5s and

costs. LARCENY.—James McGuiness. a loafer, ARS sent to prison tor two months' with hard labour for stealing a horse's collar and a strap, value ss, from the stable of Mr. Henry Barber, contractor, on Saturday evening. A person in Mr. Barber's employment met prisoner coming from the direc- tion of the stable of his master. Prisoner, on seeing him, dropped the articles and decamped, but was subsequently apprehended. A DarNKEtt PASSENGER.—A young man named John Hopkins, who said that he lived at Liverpool, was charged with riding from Manchester to Warrington en the Ches- hire Lines Railway without having paid his fare. He ex- plained that a friend of his had his ticket, but he was too drunk at the time to give an intelligible account of him- self. The charge was reduced to one of being drunk on the premises of the Committee, and for that offence prisoner was fined ss, including costs. CAVELTT TO A Honss.—Walter Langdon and William Philips were charged, the former with working a cab-horse that was suffering from a painful wound, and the latter with causing it to be worked. Inspector Nicholls, of the R. S. P. C. A., prosecuted. Langdon was fined 5s and costs, and Philips lOs and costs. Scaoor, CASES.—The following parents were summoned by Mr. Riley for not sending their children regularly to school : Ambrose Foden, wire weaver, Hind-street, adjourned until Monday next; Arthur Willets, railway foreman, Beacher-street, warrant ordered; Michael Scully, tanner, Jockey-street, fifth offence, fined ss; James Savage. labogrer, Princess-street, ss; John Hughes, labourer, Dial- street (two cases), lOs ; Matthew Carley, forgeman, Kerfeot street Mb time), ss. In the case of Thomas McDermott, labourer, Dolman'a lane the summons was adjourned for four weeks tp give the child an .opportunity of attending school. TIISSDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- men Davies and Pickmere, Councillor Greening, Dr. Gornall, and Mr, E. J, Guest. r MISCELLANEOO9.—John Garland was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Market-Place on the pre- vious evenirg ; and Thomas Timothy, for drunkennese in Bridge-street, was fined ss, including costs. Hen#Y Griffiths, also charged with drunkenness, was dismissed. WEDNESDAT.—Before Mr. John Faircloggh.

DOCNEENNESS.—MichaeI Murphy, a young man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket- street, on the previous evening.—lnspector James told the magistrate that prisoner had been recently married.—Mr. Fairclough You are making a very bad beginning.— Prisoner was fined 5s and costs, which was at once paid by the wife. TRCSISDAY.—Before Majer Litton and Alderman Webster. AN ABSENTER.—John Kelly, charged with being an t-beentee from the training of the 4th Battalion (Kings) Liverpool Regiment Militia, at Altcar, this year; was fined 40s or 14 days' imprisonment without bard labour. His excuse was that he had been to sea. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White and Captain Reynolds. Misnmeamons.—Mary Malone was fined 5s Mad costs for drunkenness in Manchester-road. and William Marfield, a deserter from M Battery 2nd Brigade Royal Artillery, stationed at Woolwich, in July last, was committed' to Wal- ton to await escort —Peter Clough was summoned by his wife for the sum of £l2 178 6d, alleged to be due under a maintenance order; it was stated that defendant had not paid his wife, who s ipported herself, anything for 26 weeks. The case was adjourned for a fortnight on defendant's pro- mise to pay a certain amount within that time. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—Henry Caldwell, who did not ap- Dear, was summoned for assaulting William Bostock. in Battersby-lane, on Wednesday.—Defendant was engaged as a bricksater by complainant, and on the day in question demanded some money. Complainant refused, and defen- nt then, it was alleged, threatened and assaulted him.—lt apearing that the alleged assault occurred outside the jurisdiction of the borough magistrates, the case was dis- missed. MASTER AND SERVANT.—Mary Elizabeth Gregg, a young girl, summoned William Gallop, fustian cutter, to whom she is apprenticed, on a elaim for £2 compensation by reaeon of non-fulfilment of contract. Mr. Browne defended. Complainant said that she was kept at housework instead of being taught fustian cutting, and was sent away at a week's notice.—The defence was that the girl had heen kindly treated, but had been neglectful of her work. It was also contended that the girl and her friends consented that she should act as a domestic servant.—The Bench de- cided to cancel the indenturee, but disallowed the compen- s3tion claimed.--William Henry Gregg was summoned by Mr. Gallop for absenting himeelf from employment as apprentice to the latter, the sum of a 17s 6d being claimed as compensation.—Gregg told the magistrates that he was unable to support himself when .working for Mr. Gallop.—An order was made that defendant return to work, and pay the costs only. THEFT OF TlMBER.—Thonias Flynn, labourer, was charged with stealing a piece of timber, value 6d, the pro- perty of Mr. J. E. Wright, from the old buildings in course of demolition in Bridgrestreet. He appeared to have been in drink at the time, and the Bench dismissed him with a caution.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Sleekly and Tinsley. MisCEttaNEOns.—For being drunk at Hixton, on the 16th nit., Thomas Austall was fined 53 and costs.—Thomas Robinson, James Ratcliffe, and John Yates, charged with trespassing on land in the occupation of James Leather, and doing damage to hay grass to the amount of is, were ordered to pay 2s 61 each.—William Henry Wadsworth, Matthew Henry Beddard, and Matthew Warburton, boys, were each ordered to pay 2s 6d and costs for doing damage to growing turnips in a field at Sankey, belonging to Hannah Parsonage.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONThar.—Before Mr. F. Rigby, and Mr. James Handley. Pool: BATE DEFAULTERS.—Mr. W. Sutton, assistant overseer, summoned 60 persons for non-payment of poor rates. Forty persons settlid the claims out of court, and the Bench made the usu,ll order in the other cases. A VIOLENT PRISONER.— fhemas Flannigan, a young man, was charged with 'being drunk and disurderly, and also with assaulting P.C. Fryer. About balf•paat eight on Saturday night the prisoner was drunk and creating a dis, turbance in Regent-street, and P.C. Frye: took him into custody. On the way to the police station the prisoner at- tempted to trip up the constaWe, struck him on the jaw with his fist, and kicked him on the hip.—Police Clerk Wallace said be never saw a more violent man in the police office —The prisoner was ordered to pay a total sum of £1 lie 4d, or go to gaol for a month. THEFT or Ducks.—Abraham Hough and Joseph Cawley, young men, living at Frodsham Bridge, were charged with baring, on the 25,h August, stolen eight ducks, worth Li, the property of Mr Joseph Acton, Lower House-Farm, Sut- ton., One of five ducks produced was identified as the pro- eecutor's by his son Dennis and his servant, Ellen Miller. On Saturday night Mrs. Elizabeth Harding bought a couple of ducks 'for 6s from the prisoner Cawley. Hough was Present at the time. On Sunday morning constables Egerton and Povey entered the house of the prisoner Caw- ley, and there fouud three ducks and a bag of feathers upon the Premises. The prisoners, who made no defence, were committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

LORD HARTINGTON AT WATERFOOT: The Marquis of Hartington paid a Visit on Settle.. day to Waterfoot, a portion bf the Rossendale Divi- sion of North-East Lancashire, for which he will be a candidate at the next election, and delivered an im- portant address on current political affairs. He arrived at Rewtenstall in the afternoon, and was met by Mr. Thomas Brooks, of Crawahaw Hall, whose guest he was to be during, his stay in the locality. About six o'clock his lordship proceeded to Water. foot, calling in the first place at the Liberal Club and making a brief inspection of the altered and im- proved premises which have been provided for :the [ social and political well-beilig of Om Liberals of that 4istriet r. Edward Ashworth, Stag Hills, presi- dent of the club, ana other prominent members, were present and gave a cordial welcome to the noble Mar- quis Meanwhile a large company had assembled in the Bethesda Chapel, Newchurch, tea having been previously served in the schoolroohn, and to this place Lord Hartington, accompanied by Me. Ashworth, Mr. T. Brooks, Mr. Henry Maden, Mr. T. HaWhite- head, ard others, at once proceeded on leaving the club.—Mr. Ashworth, who presided, briefly explained the object of the meeting. Lord Hartington began by explaining that he did not wish to make what might be calla an election- eering speech before the issue that would be placed before the country at the coming election had been more clearly defined. He then proceeded to speak of the recent change in the Government of the country, and eontended that the late Government in resigning office had followed the only statesmanlike and hon- ourable course that was open to them. They could only have continued to hold office on condition that they did the bidding of others in matters as to which they entertained a different opinion. If they had not resigned they would have done the very thing which they complained of the late Opposition doing. They had always complained that the Conservative min- ority in the present Parliament had never accepted the decisions of Parliament, however clearly, however plainly, however often they had been expressed. There were, he confessed, reasons other than the re. jection of their financial proposals which made the fall of the late Government more or less probable, either at the time it took place or within some short subsequent period. From the very commence- ment of their tenure of office the late Gov- ernment had been exposed to the most per- sistent and the most bitter opposition from the Conservative party and Mr Parnell's followers. The work of obstruction was only too easy of accomplish- ment. "A certain amount of inquisitiveness not much tempered by discretion, a great deal of ignorance accompanied by unlimited aesurance, a good deal of fluency, some obstinacy, a total disregard of the wishes and the will of the majority, coupled with an equal disregard of the true interests of the nation," formed a sufficient stock in trade for an Opposition which was determined at all hazards, even at the cost of the interest of the nation, to thwart and embarass the Government to which it was opposed. In respect of questions of foreign policy, he defended the con- duct of the late Government, and declared that if we were now in a more satisfactory position in respect of foreign affairs than when the late Goverment left office it was because the present Government were pursuing precisely the same policy as their predeces- sors in office—a policy which they lost no opportunity to denounce when they were in Opposition. Going on to deal with home affairs, Lord Hartington ridi- culed the Conservative policy as set forth by Lord Randolph Churchill. , In his statement of policy, Lord R. Churchill had given no indication of how the Con- servatives were r:lisposed to act in respect of the great reforms on which the country has set its heart. One question of the immediate future was that of land law reform, and with regard to it Lord Hartington ex • pressed disbelief in the efficacy or advantage of the proposals that were being made for arbitrarily or forcibly redistributing the land of this country, and he protested against those proposals being considered part of the Liberal creed until they lied been more fully and freely discussed than they had hitherto been. In the meantime he recommended the adop- tion of those remedies which have long been advoca- ted by land reformers, but have been up till now only partially applied. After an allusion. ,to the question of local government, the urgency of which, he said, was increasing every day, the noble lord dealt briefly but somewhat empbatically with Irish affairs. He characterised the change of front of the present Go. ye-a nent as a blow at political morality and at the cause of lorder in Ireland. While grateful t 6 Mr. Parnell for the clear manner' in which be had defined his demands, he believed that Mr. Parnell had by that declaration 'insured his own defeat. Ve belleated that no partyln this country would concede the terms on which Mr. Parnell said his alliance could be pur- ceased. Mr. Parnell's action might result in a series of short Governments, it might result in some uncer- tainty and change of policy, but after such inconve- niences had been endured for a. while the time would inevitably come wawa a practically united country would impose a firm and decided veto upon proposals PA fatal and so mischievous to the integrity of the Empire and the prosperity of the people. (Ap- plawe.)

SCOTCH MINERS.—A conference of delegates representing all the mining districts of Scotland was held in Glasgoir cr Thursday. It was decided to recommend the Ayrshire and Lanarkshire miners to adopt a uniform working da3i of eight hours, as bad been done in Fifesbire. A resolution to the effect that the Scotch miners.generallv should only work five days a wear until further notice was aclop'e(l, and it was further agreed that after the restriction of the AM- pat had commenced, a general request for an advance of Oti per clay in wages should be made. WARRINGTON BREWSTER SESSIONS. The. annual Brewster Sessions for the Borough of War- rington were commenced at the Sessions Room in Irlam- street, on Tuesday, when the following magistrates were on the bench: The Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Aldermen Davies and Pickmere, Councillor Greening, Dr. Gornall, and Mr. E. J. Guest, B.A. The business was the renewal of the licenses for fully-licensed houses only. There were a con- siderable number of people in court, and amongst those present interested in the temperance cause were the Revs. J. Yonge, J. McTurk, J. H. Jones, G. E. Cutting, Calvert, Father Scannell, Mr. William Roberts, and a deputation of ladies. The Rev. J. Yonge, addressing the Bench, said that he had the honour of introducing to their worships several ladies who were present that morning and who were deeply interested in the promotion of temperance, and who desired to dO all that they could to cause the magistrates to do what was in their power to promote that cause. If they would allow him to introduce the ladies to their notice, one of them was prepared to state the reasons why they were there. The Mayor thought that the Bench would be perhaps deficient in chivalry if they refused to hear the ladies, but it might be well for him to state that, strictly speaking, no representatives of any society or institution had any locus standi in that court. It was purely a question for , the inhabitants and occupiers. If they had any objections, and urged them,- the Bench were hound to listen. He thought, however, that every • gentleman on the Bench would be chivalrous enough to give the ladies a patient hearing. Mr. White (magistrates' clerk) : To-day is only for the renewing of the existing licenses, and not for the granting of new ones. Mr. Yonge replied that they were aware of that. They knew they had no locus stancli, except by the courteous permission of the Bench. They had understood that that was the best day to make their representations to the Beech, and that was the reason why the ladies and several minis- ters were present. The Mayor r I presume the question has simply reference to the new licenses. ' Mr. Yonge replied that the ladies wished to refer to the question of refusing new licenses, and, if it could be so, of refusing the renewal of licenses where there bad been convictions. . Mr. White said that there had been five convictions daring the year, but they were only in respect to three houses. Mr. Percy Davies, who represented one of the applicants for renewals, said that under the Licensing Act notice should have been given of any objection that would be taken. Mr. White: It is not alleged tat they have a, right. They only ask. ~ The Mayor: Ido not think any unfairness will accrue. You may depend upon it that what the ladies will say wili induce us to do no injustice either on one side or the other.

.Mr, White: They would. not wish it. The remarks, presume, would be of a general character, and this can hardly be called an opposition. • Mrs. Garnett said that she had been told that a magis- trate on the bench on a former occasion bad asked Where are our temperance women ?" They were there that morn- ing. They had only come te ask the magistrates not to grant any new licenses, and to withhold licenses from any houses against which there had been convictions during the past year. Miss Parker said that, in supplementing what Mrs. Gar- nett had said, she should like to draw attention to the fact that Warrington bad obtained an unenviable notoriety be- cause of the drinking habits of the women of th§ commu- nity. His werahip bad just said that nothing ,foal they should say would affect the justice of the decision of the Bench. It was on behalf of justice that they appealed—on I behalf of the homes inWarrington that were blighted by the drinking habits of the women. She thought it was about two years ago when it was recorded in a local paper that there were some hundreds of women found on Sunday after• noon drinking in public houses. They appealed to them to lessen the temptations to drink. She trusted that in view of the great eternity that was coming, they would endeav- our to shield the hox.es of the town by reducing the number of temptations which assailed the women. She saw in the Chief Constable's report that there had been 257 convictions of women for drunkenness, and that they were generally girls or young women. If the women drank, what was to become of the children of the future generation? Mr. White: The number on Mr. Hunt's list is 174 con- victions, and there were 5341ummoned but not convicted. - The Mayor: The, numbers are precisely the same as last year. Mr. Hunt (Chief Constable): The convPctions of females are just the same as last year, but the dismissals are a few more.

The Rev. J. H. Jones': May I inquire as to the nature of the convictions against these publicans? Mr. White said that James Welsby was convicted in Cltober of two offences, one selling during prohibited hours anll the other permitting drunkenness for which he was fined 20s and 50s and costs; John Wood, November, 1884, selling during prohibited hours, and December, fined 20s, and December 15th, permitting drunkenness, a and costs. A new tenant had been put in that place. arah Bell had paid 3s 6d costs for an oversight in selling during pro- hibited hours, and James Kennion was fined 20s and costs for permitting drunkenness. Mr. Hunt said that there had been no off-license holders brought before the magistrates. The Mayor said that as compared with the total cases of drunkenness ten years age, there was a diminution. It wee 1,033 ten years ago aud for the year ending Auguet, 1885, there were 718, so that there was more than 300 less, with an increased population. They would admit that as a very favourable circumstance. There was a difference of opinien as to the course to pursue with a view of checking the evil. People might entertain widely different opinions, and yet be quite conscientious in this matter. He was, he must confess, rather afraid that if public-houses were done away with it would' only afford facilities for private drink- ing in private house*, where much more vice and drunken- ness would be laid bare to the wives and children living in those houses, than would be the case where people went to a well-regulated public-house. That was only his opinion' but if he had an opinion he thought it right that he should fairly express it. He did not differ with the ladies at all in the desirability of dithinishingdrunkenness in every possible legitimate way, and the only question was how best could it he combated? It was a vexedtquestion, and had engaged the consideration both of legislators and of patriots of every kind, and a great diversity of opinion existed upon that question. However, it was Very good of the ladies to take the interest in it that they did. No one could possibly misconstrue their good intentions, and he should be very pleased himself if he could see their wishes fully rea- lised. The Bev. G. E. Cutting said that it was not on behalf of any organization, or any particular shibbeloth, but on be- , half of public decency, that he, as a Christian minister, felt bound to ask that his Sabbath might be made as peaceable' as possible. He bad resided a few months in Warrington, and his Sabbaths had on three occasions been disturbed by drunken brawls. As a ratepayer and a citzen he appeeled to them to use their valuable influence to put dawn by the stern hand of justice, as far as possible, those houses against which convictions had been made. Mr. Guest said that he should not like It to go forth that the °ninon expressed by the Mayor was his opinion on this subject. The facilities for private drinking were great now, and he did not think it would be any disadvantage to this country if the number of public-houses was reduced. He thought that the facilities for drinking in public-heusee were too numerous at the present time, and, as far as he had any power he should do what he could to diminish that number. The Mayor said that of course there was a principle of justice that mast be observed in dealing with this question. They must-not forget that if they gave way to anything like fanaticism they were much more likely to stern the flowing tide of temperance than to, promote it. But per- haps that was hardly the place to discuss it. Dr. Gomel' remarked that he should not be honest to his canvictions if he did not express his utter dissent with what the Mayor had that morning said. As tong as he was on the bench, knowing the difficulties that the police had to get A. conviction against a publican, he should never sanc- tion the renewal of any license where one had been obtained. Mr. Hunt said that it was Row turned 21 years since he came amofigst them as a public officer, and 19 years since he became Chief Constable. He must say that there had been Ft great improvement indeed in the morals of the people, ' and also in the way in which landlords and licensed victual- lers conducted their business. He said, after considera- lien, that he did not. think there was anywhere a more law- abiding people as publicans than there was in Warrington, With regard to girl drinking, there was a great deal of it. There was more of it in public-houses and beer-houses than be liked to see, but it more particularly occurred in private , houses: There was no doubt that off licenses formed greater facilities for beer drinking. After detailing the particulars of the convictions that' bad been obtained, Mr. Hunt said that since it had gone abroad that the magistrates showed a disposition to lessen the number of off licenses there had been a decided improvement. He did not think so many loaves had been put down as being supplied, in- stead of beer being put down. On the whole he thought that the license holders of Warrington, of any class, were as well conducted as it was possible. The Mayor said that Mr. Hunt quite confirmed the opinien he had ventured to express, that 9upoosing, public-houses weee closed or done away with, it would only give greater facilities for private drinking. It had come under his per- sonal knowledge that ehopleeepers holding off-licenses had lent themselves to a system of putting down bread and other articles in their customers' books, when" beer had been supplUd. Therefore he was afraid that he could not alter his °Pinion. The case of James Kennion, of the Black Horse, rumor- street, was adjourned Mr. Hunt informed the magistrates that he had reason to believe that drinking had been carried on on the premises of Elijah Lawton, who held an e4f-license in the neighbour. hood of Bewsev-road, and Mr. Percy Davies, who appeared for Lawton, protested against these remarks being made, no notice of objection 'eaving been given. He thought it very unfair of Mr. Hunt to make these remarks. This case was also referred to • the adjourned lie utsing sessions, when new aPplications will be heard. This was all the businessi ' '
In his annual report to the magistrates the Chief Con- stable ststed that during 'the year there were 87 licensed victuallers, five of whom had been convicted; 48 beerhouse

keepers, one being convicted of an offence against his licence ;71 shopkeepers, but none summoned. During the year 417 males and 174 females had been convicted of drunkenness, and 74 males and 53 females dismissed, mak- , ba,g a total of 718, as compared with 651 last year, and I 1,033 in 1876. The trahsfers for the year had been :-- Licensed victuallers 18, beerhonse keepers, 37. Referring to the cases of drunkenness during the year, the magistra- tes would observe that there were 67 more cases that 1884, viz., 49 males and 18 females. The 227 females preceeeded against were principally girls and young women who drank in private houses, the beer, Etc., being mostly supp ied by off-licence holders. .

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The Old Trafford season was brought te a close with the Colts' match of last weak. The idea of the committee in arranging the match was to find a good fast bowler to take Crossland's place, but in this they were disappointed. Judging from the fact that none of the opponents of the Lancashire team were drawn from such clubs as Preston, East Lancashire, Burnley, Broughton, Longsight, and a few others, there mut be a screw loose somewhere, and if

we are to have a thoroughly representative County Eleven matters such as these must be seen to. In the Yorkshire and Sussex match, 26 wickets fell for 1,039 runs, almost entire best batsmen coming to the fore, and in the latter half Of the week against Burro? the Tykes proved themselves' the stronger eleven, winning.by three wickets. Gloucester dismissed Middlesex in a very decided manner. To this success Dr. Grace was the main contribu- tor, not only with his magnificent innings, but also with the ball. In the list of averages for his county beheads the list in both batting and bowling, a remarkable performance for one who has been playing in first-class county matches for 20 years. After this performance they met Somerset. shire, and beat them nine wickets. This WAS no surprise, looking at the position the vanquished hold, but rather to the contrary. Their improved show was in consequence of having got together a better team than on most occasions this season. Kent, after gaining an easy victory over Hampshire, closed their season on Saturday by lowering the colours of Middlesex. The victers, when stumps were draws, had four wickets to Sparc. In a match between a IVI.C.C, and ground team and an eleven of Ealing, concluded at Lords on Saturday, Seaton, a Notts professional, scored 248 not out With the end of the present week the cricket season ctf 1885 will practically close. Already most of the county averages have been published, and the remainder will go forth to the public within the next few days. Notts will again carry off the championship, closely followed by York- shire, in turn well backed up by Lancashire and Kent. Up to the present the record is as follows:

- Won. Lost. Drawn. Notts Yorkshire Lancashire Kent surrey— Derbyshire 1 Gloucestershire . 4 Middiessex 5114!-13X In the Yorkshire season the form shown has been of a very off and on nature, some of the best teams met having been beaten easily, while some of the weakest have managed to defeat them. _ _

Surrey have this year shown up well, and many of their wins have undoubtedly resultad from the magnificent scor- ing by W. W. Read. Thls batsman for 26 completed innings has secured an average of 48-2. His total runs were L 250. Middlessex hhve been unlucky, but as they have seemed some fresh talent likely to do them good service, there is hope for them showing up mixt year. Kent has bad variable swans hi-playing off her fixtures. Towards the conclusion, however, she has palled up a • little.

Hard frost prevailed in Scotland on Tuesday morning. Potatoes were much damaged. Tne Prince of Wales arrived on Thursday at Stockholm, where he was received by King Oscar, the Princes, and State Officials, and was enthusiastically cheered by a large concourse of people on departing from the Royal Castle at Drottingholen. . .

THE POSTMASTER GENERAL has issued a circular enjoin- ing upoa servants of the Department, especially postmasters, to avoid doing anything at the approaching general election that may lend colour to the soggestion that in the discharge of their official duties they are influenced by political or party motives. . Tartan LIVES LOST—AS a rowing galley was crossing Harwich Harbour on Wednesday morning, to attend the Pin Mill regatta, it was capsized by a sea, and of the five occupants three were drowned, namely, Elliott, Antliff, and Seager, all belonging to Harwich; The two others Were saved by watermen. LORD R. CHURCHILL AT Siay.rvartma.—Lord Randolph Churchill was present on Thursdarnight at the Sheffield Cutlers' Feast and responded to the toast of Her Majesty's Ministers. He said the only merit he would claim for the Government was that they had not been idle. The most serious difficulty they had had to encounter was In the po- sition of affairs in Central ASig., The Government took office with a firm determination to arrive, if humanly pos- sible, at an amicable understanding with Russia, nd as the result of protracted negotiations he ' was able with some amount of confidence to sty that the differences with regard to the Pass of Zullicar had been arranged. The Russian Government, having -More exactly surveyed the ground in dispute, bad found it within their power largely to modify the proposals idregard to the frontier which they made Oo the late Government. He believed that an arrangement would be accomplished with Russia which would give to the present state of affairs in Central Asia some degreevof per- manence. Provisions for strengthening the Indian frontier and the increase ad recrgantsition of our forces in 'lndia would be actively pursued, and he believed there was no fitter nian for hie work' than the Present Viceroy. Num] BUSINESS AT Nnwrox.--There was an extraor- dinary amount of business for transaction by the magistra- tes at the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last. In ad- dition to being the annual licensing day, there were more summonses and charges of a miscellaneous character for hearing than there has been for some years past. Though two " courts " were held at the same time in different parts of the building, the whole of the business was not con- cluded until a late hour in the afternoon. THE EABLESTOWN FOOTBALL CLUB. -- The list of

matches for the ensuing season arranged for the Earles- town Football Club has just been issued. The first team fixtures includes matches with Chester, Blackburn Rovers, Turton, Black:urn Park-road, Havenham, Crewe Alexandra, Oswestry, Hurst (whiners of Manchester and District Chal- lenge Cup), Chester College, Bootle _Everton, Southport, Stanley, and Withnell. The second team will sneet Sr. Helens Amateurs let team, Gorton (Manchester) lat. Hung 2nd, Liverpool North End Ist, Bootle 24d, Oakfield Rovers Ist, Crewe Alexandra 2nd, Everton 2nd, and New Springs , . let:

Comm GREEN Comma FINED.—At the Newton Town Hall on Saturday, David Hobson, a collier employed in Number 2 pit at the Collins Green Colliery, was sum- moned for an offence against the Coal Mines Regulation Act, by unramming a Charge of powder; described as a "shot" which had misfired, on the Slst July. Mr. James Newton, the certificated manager, proved the case. In reply to the Bench, he said if the shot had exploded when it was on- rammed the elefendant would have been killed. They were not allowed in any case to withdraw " shots " which had I misfired. The defendant, who pleaded guilty, was fined 10s and costs.—William Chadwick, a collier at the same mine was alga fined 10s and costs for a like offence: IMPROVEMENTS AT THE NEWTON TOW HALL.—The interior of the Newton Town Hall has lately been under- going a complete renovation, repainting and decorating, at the hands of Mr. Winstanley, painter, Newton. ANTI-VACCINATION.—In reference to the discussion (re- ported in another column) on anti-vaccination at the,War- rington Board of Guardians meeting on Wednesday, the following comment appeared in a Liverpool contemporary on Thursday :—" Anti-vaccinationists have discovered another method of retaliating on their poor-law persecutors, and this is to invite their assistance in beatihg the drums, blowing the trumpets, and waving the banners of indigna- tion. At the meeting of the Warrington Guardians on Wednesday a letter was read from the Earlestown and Dis- taict Anti-Vaccination Society, asking on what terms they could obtain the services of the workhouse band to assist in giving animation to the prospective martyrdom of cer- tain persons who preferred to endure the seizure of their goods rather than pay small penalties for disobedience to thew. The anti-vaccinationists desired the guardians to assist them in vindicating the liberty of. the subject to spread a loathsome disease, and the guardians avere disposed to view the application' as an insult, though it might be more properly described as a coarse joke. But as Dr. John- son says— ;
Fate never wounds more deep the generous heart Than when the to.oekhead's insult points the dart.

The source of the insult made it all the more dietasteful, aad it was agreed to ' treat the letter with the contempt it deserved," its deserts being that it was allowed to 'lie on the table." It is true that there was one guardian (Mr. Rate cliffe) who seemed to be in sympathy with the anti vaeci- nationists, though hadisavowed their want of faith in Dr. Jenner ; but this gentleman was ordered to "sit down," which he did upon making a protest ag.iinst the caprice which ruled from the chair." HOT POTATOW—Mary Ellen Cross, of Wigan, was summoned, at Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday fore- noon, for obstructing High-street, Newton, on the 12th ult. ENTERTAINMENT.—Brother George Clarke, P.W.C.T., pre- sided at the session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tempters on Monday evening. One member was initiated, after which the programme of the evening," Open meeting in lodge form" was proceeded with. A good num- ber of friends and members were present. The Chairman (Brother Clarke) spoke of the work of the order and the position of the lodge. Songs and recitations were given, and the proceedings concluded with a coffee supper, about ten teclock.

FIRIL—Some alarm and excitement were occasioned in many parts of Earlestown and the surrounding district on Saturday night by what appeared to be the reflection from some extensive coullagation in the neightourhocal of the old Sankey Mills. A good number of persons proceeded thereto, when it, was discovered that a large quantity of old baskets and other rubbish were being destroyed by fire on the Vitriol Mountains. The same thing was repeated on Monday evening. The flames shot up to a considerable 'height, and their reflection was visible a great distance way.

TRIPS FROM TER VuLceic—There were two picnics of the workmen employed at the Vulcan Foundry on Saturday last. About, half-past seven o'clock the employes in the " boiler shop" started from Eartestown station for Chester, where they pleasantly spent the day. About eight o'clock. over 30 of the " erectors " assembled at the Wargrave Inn (Mr. Peter White's), and half an hour later commenced a ride to Hale, in a large omnibus /supplied by Mr. Connor, of Warrington. The "Out" was a most enjoyable one, and the pleasure-seekers—both at Chester and Hale—were highly delighted.

_ Ti ROBBERY OP A WATCH AT BUATONWOOD.— John Thornton and Charlet Clubb were charged on remand at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, with stealing a watch, the property of John Dodd, at Burtonwood, on the previous Saturday. THE Vuecare hem FOUNDRy.—The. slackness of trade at the Vulcan Iron Foundry has caused some uneasiness among the workpeople during the past week or two. Following so closely upon the virtual stoppage of the Sankey Sugar Works, the present prospects of the district during the en- suing winter months are not bright or encouraging. In the last fortnight several men have been discharge& from the Vulcan Works, and it ie expected that more will follow un- less there is shortle an :mprovement. The men are being discharged. as the jobs "on hand are finished, and 'up to Thursday night about half a dozen men had left. Wright was awarded the third prize for the best basket of butter, .not lees than six half-pounds. - CAPTURE OP RUNAWAY INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL LADS.— On Tuesclarmorning P.C. Parker, stationed at VVinwick, effected a capture of runaway boys. About ten o'clock he was walking along the road when he saw two lads whom he suspected had' escaped from some reformatory or other institution. ' When :they had got near him he asked where they had come from, whereupon they imme- diately ran. away. He followed them, and after a pretty long chaid he succeeded in capturing them. It subse- quently transpired that both lads had absconded on the pre- vious day' from the Boys' Refuge Industrial School, St. Anne-street, Liverpool, and they were accordingly locked up. Their names were Penis O'Brien, aged 13, and Henry Hutchineon; 12, and in order to expedite their flight they bad thrown their, shoes over a hedge. div.head: WIT AND HUMOUR.
div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

"Did not the eight of the boundless blue sea, bearing on Its bosom the white-winged fleets of commerce, fill you with emotion V" "Yes," replied the tourist, "for a while it did; but after a while it didn't fill me with anything—it sorter emptied me." . , • • The landlord of a hotel at a quiet but rising watering- place makes the startling announcement in his-advertise- ments that "Nobody dresses here, and health and happiness are most sought for. Seven-year-old frcm the North, who is on a visit to friends in town, seeing the father of the family, on the first meeting of the visit, brushing his teeth: "Div ye aye ehairp yer teeth afore ye tak' yer braikfast ?" Tenant: I've jiat been thinkin', landlord, that I wid like my lease o' ninety-nine years changed tae yin o' as lang as weds grow an' watters rin.—Landlord : Toots, man! Whit's a' the hurry? Whin yer present lease is oot, jist come back tae me an' I'll renew It fur ye! [Exit tenant.] An Englishman who was travelling in America was struck by the universal application of the term "gentle- man" in that country, and inquired of an Americin friend who really were "gentlemen" in the States. " Wal, I guess every one who isn't a lady !" was the reply. A-Washington lads' was much surprised recently upon receiving notice from her, dusky cook that she was about to leave her service in order to enter into the holy state of matrimony. "Why," said she, "I did not even know that you had an admirer!" 014 yes'os, fur some time!" "Who is it, Mary ? " "Don't you 'member, Miss Lizzie, that I 'tended a inne'l 'bout two weeks ago? It's the corpse's husband!"

SEEKING KNOWLEDGE.—Western Congressman: "Say, Jim, have you a dictionary?" Eastern Congressman: "No, Bill. What do you want of a dictionary?" "You know I have received a lot of letters from my constituents lately." "Yea ; I have noticed that you had a big mail." "Well, nearly all of them were urgent requests that I should make a big speech—the greatest effort of my life." "A speech, but what on?" "On the tariff." "Well ?" • " Well, I haven't any dictionary." "But why do you need a dictionary?" "I want to find out what the word means." AN OLD LADY'S PERPLEXITY.—A Devonshire woman of mature age went into a chemist's shop and said to the assis- tant—" I've got a cruel bad cough, surely. I've heard that they Brown's bronchial troches are the things. Have 'ee got any?" The assistant pointed to a small box on the counter, and said: "Yes, there they are." "How much is it ?" was the inquiry. The price was paid, and the old woman took her departure. At night, the assistant missed a box of glycerine soap (three cakes). A couple of days after she returned to the shop, and said—"l want 'cc to take back two of they things I had Vother day. I took one of 'em. It was ghastly hard to chew and awful to swallow, but it cured the cough." "My dear," said a wife to her husband, "I know that I am dreadfully cross with you at times, that I am not patient as I should be; and I think the same can be said of you." "Yes, certainly," he frankly acknowledged; "I am almost as bad as you are." "What's that ?" say that lam just as much to blame as you are" "I think," went on the lady; "that we ought to cultivate a mutual toleration of each other's faults ;" and she bent over him and fondly kissed him. "You are not looking well to-night, dear," he said, stroking her hair. "No," she replied; my feet pain me dreadfully." " That's because you wear shoes two sizes too small for you." Than the trouble began once more. An Englishman had taken a shooting in Scotland, and, he being an unpractised sportsman, the situation was rather novel to him. after the first day's shooting, when, with the assistance of the keeper, a bag of about fifty brace of grouse had been got, the Englishman was asked what he wished to be done with the birds. "What is usually done with them ?" he inquired; and it was explained to him that, after enough had be n laid aside for larder requirements, the remainder were generally distributed among friends. The custom was observed, the shooting tenant sending grouse to his yirious friends. At the close of the second' day the keeper inquired what was to be done with the fresh supply of birds, wben the innocent sportsman looted at the heavy bag of grouse. "Oh, bury them !" he exclaimed, "I'll be shot if I'll write out more addresses!"

Wily SHE APPLAUDED.—"Seated to the right of me at a place of amusement," writes a Transatlantic musical critic, "we a lady whose interest was not aroused till a thin dis- consolate-looking girl made her appearance. Then she began to applaud furiously. As I could discern no possible occasion for such a manifestation. I felt surprised; but, as she kept it up all the evening and seemed to have no assist- ance from any of the audience, I took a hand, as they say, and also began applauding the thin disconsolate-looking girl. My good nature, however, bore, as good nature often does, bitter fruit. The lady turned and said, "What are are applauding for ?" I stammered an insufficient answer. You don't think she does well, do you?' 'No, madam.' She's awkward, and she can't sing,' said she contemptu- ously. I had time to recover myself. Might I ask,' I said, with conscious dignity.' why, madam, if such is the case, you are so enthusiastic ?"She owes me nine dollars and thirty-five cents," said my neighbour, with scorn and asperity, 'and if this here show don't succeed I'll be that much out I' " GOVISSNMENT 1317SINESS.—Mr. Hyde's Royal Mail con- tains many instances of the impression that appears to pre- vail in some parts of England and the United States that the post-office is a sort of fountain for every kind of in- formatilm and a universal provider into the bargain. Thus, a farmer writes to the postmaster of a country town to say he has a thirty-stone pig "now quite ready for killing," and will be glad if the postmaster w;11 find him a customer; another correspondent offers the Postmas er•General some patridges in exchange for a parcel of mithridate mukard ; Frenchman inquires if the Postmaster-General will inform him whether the lady to whom the writer is about to make an offer of marriage is de id or alive; a young lady from the U.S A. writes a chatty letter to the English Postmaster- General, in the course of which she remarks. " We are quite well off in worldly goods, but should be better off if you would inform me about that fortune I expect from a great- uncle, great•aunt, or somebody. It is about half a million, either on my father's or mother's side. If you would be so kind as to write and inform me, I would be a thousand times obliged." A gentleman from Tennessee also has his eye on the main chance; but his inquiry is for an instrument that will "attrack" gold. His style is lees mellifluous than that of the lady. He wants a good watchmaker to tell him if there is at instrument "maid to find mettel—g old or silver —that are in the ground. If it will attrack it. A instru- ment for that perpos. I understand there are sutch a thing made. If so, be pleas tell me where I can by one and what It will cost me. I send you a stamp."

div.head: DEMONSTRATION OF _THE_ PRESCOT
div.p: DEMONSTRATION OF _THE_ PRESCOT
AND ,WHISTON MINERS.

The unfortunate dispute' at the Carr% Colliery shows no prospect of settlement. On Friday afternoon a large gather- ing of those on strike and their sympathisers took place at Whiston. Nearly a hundred persons formed in precession at the Crown Hotel, Prescot, at five o'clock. They marched four abreast, and preceded by the Fairclough Braes Band, two men in front bearing a Union Jack on cross . poles. They were accompanied by the check-weighman, -John Fegan, and the route taken was through Present, Whiston by Dragon-lane, to -11nyton Quarry, and back to the/ Pot- teries, where between 300 and 400 assembled. A cart was utilised as a platform, and Mr. Josiah Haye Was called to Ithe chair. lie briefly introduced Mr. Samuel Woods, miners' agent, who said that they were all aware that they in Whistoa were in the midst of a straggle that had been going on for four or five weeks, and one that was likely to continue for a considerable time I longer unless the masters showed more consideration to the men. On Monday a deputation from the Miners' Federation, consisting of Messrs. Pickard, Aspinwall, Fegan, and him- self, had waited on the managers of Care's Colliery, Knowles and Barton. The first ttro named were admitted to the office. Their humble servants, himself and Mr. Fegan, he supposed were not considered worthy of such a distin- guished audience. (Laughter.) A test was suggest,d with the hand riddle for three days by three men, in order to fix the prices on an equitable basis, but having in mind from Painful experience the expedient of the employers of West Lancashire of having. 130 work for certain picked men who have nobly stood up for their fellow-men, and who when they have sought work elsewhere have found a red letter had gone before—(shatne)--they returned, and asked if the test proved satisfactory that the men, including the check- weighman, should start work again without prejudice. Mr. Barton, who was alone, could not give them an answer, but promised that Mr. Knowles should send to Mr. Pickard. No reply was received, and the committee of the Federation at Manchester decided therefore to leave the Matter in the hands of their local representative, and on Wednesday it was resolved that no test be made, representative,, the strike must go on until they were met in a fair and satisfactory manner. There would be no trial, no resumption of work, until they received that promised letter. There was no doubt but that it was inspired by their em- ployers. It favoured tberb, and it was time they had a local paper of their own. Speaking to the resolution in band, he said the committee did nbt want them to go about begging, but they required that all should de their share to support those on strike. Ths Federation had paid since the commencement of this struggle, £223 He begged to move the following resolutions:—" That this meeting of the Pres- cot and NiThiaton miners is of opinion that a strong union in their ranks is a pressing necessity, and pledges itself to use all leeitimate means to bring such a union into existence." "That the introduction of the hand-riddle at the Cates Colliery, being an attempt to force on the ellen an old ob- solete custom, which is entirely unnecessary and uncalled for, as well as a great reduction in wages, this meeting de- sires to urge on the men to still resist by all legal means, and stand by their chechweighmen • and hereby promises them all the available assistance in their power, pecuniary and otherwise."—They were seconded by Mr. Thomas Smith, and carried unanimously...—The usual votes of thanks closed the proceedings.

The Home Secretary has appointed a working collier as mining inspector for the county of Durham, the person selected being Mr. John Plummer, under-viewer at Hetton Colliery. PROGRESS AND EXPENDITIMI IN EDUCATION.—A return showing the educational progress and expenditure of Scot- land in 1884, compared, with that of England and Wales, was issued on Monday morning. In England and Wales there was last year accommodation for 4,826,000 scholars, an increase of 156,000, or 3.3 per cent. In Scotland there was accommodation for 656,000, an increase of 35 per cent. The 'scholars on registers had increased in England and Wales 1.5 per—cent. and in Scotland 3 3 per cent. The percentage of passes in standard examinations, in England and Wales showed an increase of 07, in Scotland 04. In England and Wales the increase in the number of children examined in Standard IV. and upwards was 108, in Scot- land 49. The number of certificated and assistant teachers in England and Wales showed an increase of 9.6, in Scot- land 4.5. In the cost of maintenance per scholar, the board schools show an increase from £2 is 3id in 1883 to £2 Is 81d last year in England and Wales, an from £2 21 lid in 1883 for Scotland to £2 2s 8d in 1884. Voluntary schools showed an increase in England and Wales from £1 148 10-kcl in 1883 to 15s 31 last year, and in Scotland from Li 165 10 in 1883 to £1 Ids lid last year. LORD RIPON AT RIPON.—The Marquis of Ripon, whe presided on Monday over a crowded meeting at Ripon, tinder the auspices of the Liberal Association, said we were on the eve of the most important General Elcction which had taken place in this country for the last balf century. Some of their opponents went about trying to persuade the Eng- lish people that they owed this great extension of the fran- chise to the Consetvatives—(langhter)—but to put forth such a contention at a public meeting was an insult to the audience. With reference te the recent nomination of the Royal Commission on Trade, all of them, of course, lamen- ted the depression of trade and agriculture ; but were these evils likely to be removed by the inquiries of tins Commis. ron ? The Commission was so constituted at the very commencement that the Government found it impossible to obtain the euPport of any Free Traders, and it was now re,. duced to a condition in which he ventured to say that its recommendations were not likely to command the confidence of the country. (Hear, hear.) Could it be supposed that the English people were so silly as to believe for a moment it would be possible to put a protective duty upon manu- factures, and not extend it to agricultural produce ? (Hear, hear.) The farmers would have something to say to any proposal of that description. In some parts of the country many farmers still maintained a lingering belief in protec- tion. He thought they were entirely wrong, for it could be demonstrated that the only result of patting, a duty on agricultural produce would be that the whole of it would go into the pockets of the landlords, to increase or to main- tain their rents. (Applause.) div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. Sir ilenry 'Wolff's mission has so far not been vanelt of a success. He has been vaunted as an ideal diplomatist who only wanted a career—but his career has yet to be made. In Constantinople he was poorly received, and yet the Minister under whose auspices he went was a good friend to Turkey cluring the events of '7B. What may be Sir Henry Wolff's programme, what proposals he is authorised to offer, and what terms he will be allowed to take, is, of course, yet to be divulged. It is a question how far the Turkish Government will consent to I allow the occupation of stations on the Nile by I Ottoman troops on the terms which the Govern- ment might be willing to concede. Long habit has induced the Sultan to regard Egypt as a great finan- cial opportunity for his country, or rather for him- self. English offers are not likely to come up to his idea of liberality, and perhaps Sir Henry Wolff's mission in the end may hold the position it did at the commencement. A few English regiments would be sure to find headquarters at Cairo and Alexandria. It may be that the Sultan feels the disadvantage of concluding a negotiation with a provisional envoy. Hitherto things have advanced very slowly indeed. I notice that accounts have been very silent as to Mr. Gladstone's enjoyment of his tour. The barbs and arrows of the Tones weather report show that the wind was strong over those Norwegan waters. ' That he has derived benefit from his cruise there can, happily, be no doubt, and as the announcements that have been made on this score come With the authority of Sir Andrew Clarke's assent, they may .be regarded as entirely trustworthy. Coming, too, from more:northern latitudes and keener airs, Mr. Gladstone will not feel the Scotch air cold, unless indeed we have to atone for an old-fashioned sum- mer by an unusually stern autumn. In politics it is just now the season of the little masters. With the Sunbeam at anchor and the ex-Premier at home, . . .

interest awakens and big subjects arise. A most ingenious doctrine has been put forward to explain Prince Bismarck's blunder about the Caroline isles. The Chancellor's well remembered motto of Beati Possidentes might suffice as a cause why he should wish to add to German possessions. But it does not. Germany desires to colonise, just as England desires to colonise—in order to increase the market for her manufactures. England had, of course, the other motive of finding a career for her surplus population. The Chancellor is very anxious to keep such population as he has—and there is no surplus—at home. How is the army to be kept up if the soldiers escape conscription by a patriotic flight to the colonies? On the other hand, Ger- many must have colonies to absorb her manufac- tures. At present her manufactures are largely " placed " in Britain, where by reason of their cheapness they are able to supplant the native articles. But German goods may be driven out of the British market, and so the Chancellor has seized the Caroline isles to supply the loss of the British isles. It is a pity that arguments so ingenious should be founded on facts so gratuitously as- sumed. ' America is going to borrow an idea from us, and perhaps we in turn might take a hint from her. Across the Atlantic a murderer as a rule finds one of two des- tinies reserved for him, to be lynched before trial or publicly executed after it. He is still liable to be lynched, but public executions will be less frequent. One ,State has already done away with them, sub- stituting a procedure which we might well adopt. The Americans are a very sensible people, and have the great advantage of not being hampered by pre- cedents. When they introduce a novelty they have no old vested interests to consider and to con- ciliate. They do the best they can from the first. Now we have an old law that a man must be tried in the district in which he committed his crime and must be hanged, or, as the judge of assize eupho- niously puts it," be left for execution," in the dis- trict in which he is tried. One sees the reason plainly enough. In those old days it was vely de- sirable that the locality should be impressed by the fate of the murderer. Now that we have the press and the telegraph wire the need is at an end. We read of executions instead of seeing them. The hanging is all done privately and intending mur- derers are dissuaded by their penny papers. And yet we have the old stupid rule which necessitates a gallows in every county gaol, with all the horrible results of bungling and miscarriage. Now in America they adopt a very simple and a very sensible rule. Each State will now have its own prison, within the walls of which the executions shall take place. The fatal drama will soon have been too often rehearsed not to be quite safe to be perfectly performed. Then another rule has reference to the body of the murderer. The French plan is to deliver it over to be dealt with "for the benefit of science." Science plays ghastly tricks with the headless trunk, but has never been, so far as I have heard, much benefitted. We make burial within the walls of the gaol part of the sentence. The Yankees are more tender-hearted. If the relatives 'wish the body of the murderer they can write to the governor of the gaol, and he must give it up. These are two very simple hints which it would be no derogation to our insular pride to adopt, as, in having the executions private America is following our lead. I hear there are a great many Americans this season at Hamburg. They leave the tennis ground to their English cousins, but muster very strong at the bi- weekly dances. A rather well-known periodical is going to change hands. Lord Ripon and Charles Russell a-e going to run it. The idea is to make it the organ of the Roman Catholics, who have plenty of weekly papers, but are not represented by a monthly issue. It has hitherto been edited by Mr. Maynell, Limself, a Roman Catholic and well-known contributor to London journals. His wife is a sister of Mrs. But- ler, the painter of the Roll Call, and one of the best art-critics we have. Mr. Maynell will retain his post as ;editor. When Parliament meets again some changes will be found that have long been needed. •The division lobbies have been made less gaunt, and the library has got a thorough overhauling. The workmen are at present busy reducing Westminster Hall to a con- dition of cleanliness and repair, though the great stained glass window opposite the door will still bear evidence to the dynamite explosion. Now that ;the courts are removed, Westminster Hall is almost unvisited by the ordinary Londoner. Once Parlia- ment is up it seems almost as if no one would be 'allowed in who could not produce his Baedeker as ,evidence that he was a bona-fide traveller. Since the explosion, indeed, the public have been entirely /kept out, so that perhaps its proximate opening may be rather an occasion. Mary Anderson's Rosalind is admitted to have been one of the manliest performances of the many which have lately been seen. She looked very 'handsome, her tall figure and her slightness of pro- portion enabling her to take the part with some show of the probable. Her audience was very friendly, but necessarily rather critical, and the Actress was perhaps a little timid, and certainly moved on a stage to the proportions of which she was not accustomed. Youth and beauty go for -much, and most of the other etceteras Miss Ander- son possesses too; but she has not genius, and she has not abandon. The stereotyped criticism comes back with renewed force, the criticism that applies -to all her ambitious parts. Painstaking, and con- scientious to a fault, she remembers her part, but .she cannot forget herself. You are always at the rehearsal, so to speak, and never at the play. Very little has been heard of late of the Claimant. His projected series of lectures and public demon- strations was nipped in the bud by a hint from the Home Office that as he was on ticket-of-leave it be- loved him to be circumspect in his procedure. 'Another project of taking a public-house to be "The Tichborne Head" was resisted by the Claimant himself, who did not think it consonant with his dignity. NQW he chiefly—exclusively as 'far as I know—confines his public appearances to the yard in which trapped pigeons are shot. He was at Ashford the other day, shooting off a pigeon match in a field adjoining a little public-house, "entrance one shilling, reserved seats half a crown." The Claimant, it will be remembered, is a capital shot. It looks as if Sarah Bernhardt was in difficulties. There is nothing she dislikes now so much as sign- ing an engagement It used to be her delight to enter into almost contradictory contracts and under- take to pay penalties that would almost take your breath away. She had a'fine scorn for lawyers and a contempt for law. But she has had her experi- ences and has now passed to the other extreme. She likes long runs and hates distant contracts. Now, however, she has signed for America and has under- taken to spend a year in the new world, for which she is to be paid a minimum of £lB,OOO. A new play of Sardou's isyet in store for her winter sea- son in Paris, but the first of May must see her on the boards of New York.
The first sitting of the conference on the crofter question, called by the Highland Law Reform Association of London rind Edinburgh, wae held on Wednesday at Portree.

div.head: etteto to the editor.
div.p: etteto to the editor.

MR. W. CROSFIELD'S CANDIDATURE. Sir,-1 beg to inform the electors of our borough, through the medium of your paper, that the reports which have been circulated, during the past few days, to the effect that !Qr. William Cresfield has withdrawn from his position as Liberal candidate for Warrington at the next general elec- tion, are absolutely false. Mr. William Crcafield has not now, aad never has had, the slightest intention of acting in the manner stated, and I can only look upon the circulation of this report by the Tory party as another evidence of their acknowledged weakness.—I am, your obedient servant, . H. ROBERTS, Liberal Agent. Warrington Liberal Association, Sept. 3, 1885. • THE DRUNKENNESS OF YOUNG FEMALES IN WARRINGTON. i .

Sir,—May Ihe ail-Owed to use the columns of your paper to ask any persons who are willing—by suggestion or per- sonal work—to assist in the organising of some plan to benefit the poor young girls of our town, who, as a class, are becoming notorious for their profligate habits. Our Chief Constable reports that "The 227 females proceeded against during the past year are principally girls and young women," and he says "The drunkenness amongst girls is increasing." Are we to stand idle on one side and do nothing to shield them We are our sister's keeper, and sin will lie at scme of our doors if a hand is not held out to save them from perishing. A meeting is shortly to be held to consider the matter, and the co-operation of all who feel the burthen of the responsibility of caring for these girls is earnestly requested. Something must be done to supply them with at least one pleasant evening in the week, and to show them that there are better ways of spending their time than wandering dangerously about our streets, or loitering on the slippery threshold of our publichouses. We do earnestly trust that not a few hearts may he touched, so that some plan may be devised either for individual or collective effort, and that a pally good work may be done this winter amongst these poor girls.—l enclose my card and beg to remain. yours , truly, SYMPATICA. September 3rd, 1885.

"LIVE AND LET LIVE." Sir,—l don't always agree with our worthy Mayor's notions of law, but I do cordially endorse his opinion les- pectmg the interference of women at a Brewster Sessions, and thank him for (figuratively of course) " sitting on " them. And it surprised one to see that a strong-minded minister introduced them. A very eminent man placed on record this dictum : —" Women who have habitually drunken husbands are within their right when they appeal to a magistrate for assistance ; but a woman who appears in court, for the pur- pose of airing her vanity by making speeches against drink, when her husband or near relatives are sober men, only makes it appear that she has her doubts about their con- duct ; and so does no good, bat harm." I hops the picture is relished by those who allowed their " home-neglecters " to figure where they did this week. It is evident that these lady meddlers could not, or would not," look at home," for thsy only interfered to harass a trade as lawful and as right as any other, even as those in which their own rela- tives are employed. They won't leave any small " footsteps on the sands of time "-by their procedure, and will only bring on them- selves the contempt that both they and their instigators de- serve. At any rate their mock-philanthrophy is easily seen through, and, if nothing else, is sufficiently!absurd to raise a hearty laugh, and to call to mind the old proverb about "The water on the duck's back."—Yours, in disgust, ROB ROY.

Mu. CHAMBERLAIN'S VISIT TO WARRINGTON. Sir,—The above event is disturbing the minds of local Tortes to an alarming extent. The old women of the party are shaking their heads, while from the young bloods " curses not loud but deep " are heard on every side. The whole vocabulary of Tory abuse and slander is being heaped upon him, by men who have not brains to understand either the right honourable gentleman or his policy. They are at least conscious of the fact that the member for Birming- ham is a power in the land, and we shall show them, on Tues- day next, that the Liberals of Warrington are not behind- hand in their enthusiasm for oae of the greatest leaders of political thought in England. I doubt not that every Liberal will work to make the demonstration a great success. Coming, as it does, at this time, Mr. Chamberlain's visit is one of national importance, and it is a matter of gratification to the Warrington Liberals that the right hon. gentleman has found time in the midst of multifarious engagements to come amongst us. It will do our party in this borough an immense amount of good. No doubt the coming struggle will be the most severe ever known. For the first time in the history of the country the real voice of the nation will be heard, demanding wider and more extended liberties. The great and important work which must come before the next Parliament will call forth all the energies of the most active minds. There will be no room for respectable mediocrities. Let the Liberal party in this town work as they worked in 1880. and we shall re- turn our candidate by a much larger majority, and thus relegate the Baronet of Walton to that private life be so much adorns, and enable him to spend the rest of his days in pursuits much more congenial to his nature than the heated arena of party strife.—Yours. Sep. 2, 1885. A LATCHFORD VOTER.

div.head: " CODLIN 'S YOUR FRIEND, NOT SHORT."
div.p: " CODLIN 'S YOUR FRIEND, NOT SHORT."

Sir,—Let me beg that for the future you will try to tone down a little your political articles, and shenld any of your correspondents dare to utter their thoughts, over a nom d• plume. kindly warn the mediocrities of the Tory world as to the identity of the presumptuous individuals. I ask you to do this as a favour, not to myself, but to the party over the way, who have had such large and wide experience in literary work. It is said drowning men clutch at straws, but our home•cared Tories try to grasp at shadows. Laws! how that Morley Common business has startled them. Another such an affair as that and it wi be dangerous for a Rad to appear in the streets. Talk about the Liberals wanting "a cry," why, scarce a Radical walks but could supply a dozen "cries," and then have a few odds and ends to supply the Tories with. Talking of "cries," it is rather curious that my friend Sir Gilbert should be trotted out at Ship Canal meetings, and the people should be asked to remember in November who supported that great movement, What a pity Mr. Adamson is not a Tory ; it would have made a splendid " cry " for Lancashire Toryism. I understood this question was to be kept outside of party politics, and here we have the Tories making all the capital, their poor wits will enable them, out of it. They must be senseless, er else they would have kept the kind and benevoleat Walton squire's name out of this question as much as possible. When all Warringtonians were working with might and main to raise funds to get the Bill passed, how much did Sir Gilbert contribute? When the vote was taken Sir Gilbert let it be known that the canal would go "into his vitals," and his servile admirers withheld their votes; yet now becomes to the front, and makes himself ridiculous by shaking his head and waving his hands, and telling the people it has his " cordial and hearty support." The question is asked—" Where were the Liberals at the recent ship canal meeting ;" why, where they always are; having done the work, they turn their attention to some- thing else, and leave the Tories, as usual, to do the shout- ing. It was always so ; Liberals do the work and the Tory Minks behind muttering " Codlin 's your friend not Short." It seems to cause quite a flutter when Sir Gilbert appears in public. Each time he stands up on a public platform, a demonstration must be made, in season and eut of season, and yet he is, Not a bad man; not a goad man; • Scarce a man at all, one fears. , It is surprising what a number of people express astonish. , meat at the Tory party bringing out Sir Gilbert again ; "4 throwing a chance away, besides deriding the intelligence of the party." These are the remarks one constantly ' bears. _ . .

I suppose, Mr. Editor, that Mr. Chamberlain is about the best abused public man that we have. There cannot be any doubt about him " fetching " the people next Tuesday evening. Already I see the Tories are crying out to Mr. Hampson to arrange far a Tory meeting. Well, imitation is the sincerest flattery, and there is nothing I should like better than to see one or two Tory big guns brought to Warrington. Suppose they bring Mr. Wharton, chief ob- structionist and general bill-blocker, or Lord Randolph, who, to his other accomplishments, may add one more;

'Tie slender, Whose edge Is sharper than the sword, whose tongue Outvenoms all the worms of Nile. But political discourses, or the lecture room, and political literature are not in the way of Tory working-men. I can make a much more suitable and, I are sure, welcome sugges- tion, to which Mr. Hampson is quite welcome; that is, get rip a series of pic-nics at Walton Hall, with steam round- a-bouts and a tolerable tap. A most enthusiastic and suc- cessful meeting can at any time be held. An invitation is all I expect for this advice. I see other steps are being taken to educate working-men in Tory principles, whatever they are. I refer to the es- tablishment of Primrose Leagues, or Habitations, through the country. These seem to be chiefly under the control of ladies ; " dames " is the word. Bless us all ! who could resist a "dame of the Primrose League ?" Why, in one of these "habitations "a man must completely lose his senses; and think of the amount of " political lying " that will have to be done afterwards.

_ I am afraid, sir, that Warrington is going to have a very had attack of politics. Already the Tory conscience is making cowards of them all, and you know cowards are they who chiefly delight in sending forth lying spirits. Mr. W. Crosfield is, I see, attacked for being a member of the Liverpool Dock Board. Well, this is no great fault surely. Had he .nade a speech against the Canal, or voted against it, no doubt both would have been pounced npon. The enemy appears to be baffled on this point; none the less plenty or mud must be thrown, so that some of it may stick. The Tories are in dismay ; nothing they do seems to prosper. The Liberals may with " Grizzle " say:— Thisa far our arms with victory are cruwn'd, For, though we have not fought, yet we have found No enemy to fight withal.

div.head: CLIFFORD DIX.
div.p: CLIFFORD DIX.
Major General Babington, late of the, Madras Staff Corps, was found shot dead in a wood near Dumfries on Thursday.

FAIN WORTH AGRICULTURAL SHOW. The 21st annual show of the Farnworth Agricultural Society took place on Thursday, and it is gratifying to re- cord that the event was attended with an encouraging measure of success. In its career the society has had many difficulties to overcome, and about three years ago its financial condition was of such a character that the com- mittee seriously contemplated terminating the existence of ' the institution. It was decided, however, that a further effort should be made to wipe off the burdensome debt of £3OO. and last year a highly successful chew enabled them Ito reduce the amount by £2OO. Thursday's show will, it Is anticipated, enable the management to clear off the debt entirely. Although the weather was showery the visitors were very nuneerous, several thousands passiag through the turnstile. The Widnes Soap Works Band was on the ground the whole of the day, and played selections of music. The arrangement of the show ground was similar to that adopted in former years, and there was every ac- commodation for exhibitors and spectators. Prizes were offered for competition to the value of about £OOO, includ- I ing 12 silver cups. The entries in the various classes com- pare very favourably with those of the past five years, as will be seen from the annexed table :- 1880. 1831. 1882. 1883. 1884. 1885 Cattle 4B 39 35 36 38 55 Horses and Donkeys 157 153 138 123 182 20i Pigs 2l 16 20 17 26 Butter.. Roots Potatoes 3B 24 13 20 19 23 Seed. Corn, &c 23 14 27 7 14 8 Poultry. &c 229 163 184 107 139 268 Pigeons Dogs Implements Extra. Stock Bread lO Farm and Gardea Produce In the aggregate the entires were about 100 in excess of 1884. During the past year the poultry classes had been revised. Formerly it was necessary to enter the birds in pairs, but on the present occasion single birds could be shown, with the satisfactory result that there were upwards of 100 mete entries. The show of implements was not very extensive, but the machinery and other appliances were such as the agriculturists of the neighlsourhood would be likely to be interested in. Mr J R Whalley, of Mill Green Farm, was the chief exhibitor, and he Fes awarded the silver medal of the society. A silver medal was also awarded to Messrs J H Peck and Co., of Liverpool and Wigan. for an ambulance of improved construction, and a similar success was secured by Messrs J A Lawton and Co., of Liverpool, for a new tandum dog cart. Silver medals were also won by Messrs J S Warburton and Co, Preston ; R Rushton, of Woolton ; J Blake, of Liverpool; R A Heap, and T Welsby. Mr J it Whalley secured two first prizes for his collection of agricultural implements. The judges were as follows :—Horned cattle: Mr Jame,: Dickenson, Upholland, Wigan ; Mr Joseph Cliff, Whitley Hall, near Northwich. Heavy horses, Mr G Hammer, Sea- combe, Cheshire ; Mr C W Brierley. Rosedale, Tenbnry, Worcester; Light horses : Mr Edward Humphreys, Car- narvon ; Mr J E Parsons, Charwelton, Daventry. Butter, bread, and seed corn : Mr ft A Lambert, Old Swan, Liver- pool ; Mr Frederick Chambers, Wavertree-road, Liverpool' Roots, farm and garden produce, and implements : Mr Joseph Knowles, Appleton, Cheshire ; Mr W Scotson, Moss- ley Hill, Aigburth, Liverpool. Poultry :, Mr H Beldon, Baildon, Yorkshire ;Mr P Lyon, Liverpool. Pigeons : Mr E C Stretch, Ormskirk. Dogs : Mr II C Joplin, Mr Frank Adcock, Mr James Mawdslev, Dr W A G James, Mr James Taylor.
