MR. CHAMBFALAIN'S VISIT TO WARRINGTON. The arrangements in connection with the visit of the Right Hon, J. Chamberlaiu to Warrington have now been completed. The proceedings will open with a Conference at half-past two o'clock in the Ca-operative Hall. Tickets of admission to the Conference have only been issued to the duly ap- pointed delegates from the various Liberal Associa- tions of South-west Lancashire and Cheshire, and the discussion will be confined to these gentlemen, but any local Liberals who may desire to be present will be admitted without tickets as visitors. More than 170 delegates have been appointed to attend the Conference, and the list of those who intend to be present includes nearly the whole of the Liberal candidates for the various divisions of Cheshire and South-west Lancet, shire. The programme of the business of the Con- ference includes several important resolutions. After the Conference the delegates will partake of tea at the Lion Hotel, to which they have been invited by the officers of the Warrington Liberal Association. The evening meeting in the Public Hall will be attended by the delegates, the candidates for the various divisions referred to above, and the mem- bers ot Parliament whose names appear in the ad- vertisement. Mr. S. Rigby will occupy the chair, and the first resolution, which welcomes Mr. Cham- berlain and expresses gratification at the measures passed by the late Liberal administration and confi- dence In the leaders of the Liberal party, will be moved by Mr.McMinnies, M.P., seconded by Mr. W. Crosfield, the Liberal candidate for Warrington, and supported by Col. McCorquodale. Mr. Chamberlain will respond to this resolution, and after his speech he will proceed to address the overflow meeting that will be held in the Co-operative Hall. The second resolution, which deals chiefly with future legislation, especially in reference to land law and local goyernment reform, will be moved by. Mr. I. S. Leadam, Liberal candidate for the Altnncham division, seconded by Colonel Gamble, Liberal can- didate for St. Helens and supported by Mr. G. W. Latham, Liberal candidate for Crewe division. The speakers at the Overflow Meeting will in- clude the chairman (Mr. P. Rylands, M.P.), Mr. C. M. Percy, the miners' candidate for the Ince Divi- sion; the Right Hon. J. Chamberlain, M.P. • Mr. J. E. Barlow, Liberal candidate for the Snutsford Division; Mr. M. Guthrie, Liberal candidate for one of the divisions of Liverpool; Mr. W. P. Sinclair, M.P. ; Mr. J. T. Brunner, Liberal candidate for the Northwich Division; Mr. E. K. Muspratt, Liberal candidate for Widnes Division; and Dr. Pilkington, Southport. Resolutions similar to those submitted to the main meeting will be proposed at the over- flow meeting. The demand for tickets has been unprecedentedly large, and had it been possible to obtain a meeting place of three or four times the size of the Public Hall it would have easily been filled. Locally, tickets have only been sent to the various members of the ward 'committees in the borough, and consequently it is necessaiy that all other Liberals who desire to be present should apply at the Liberal Club as directed in advertise- ments. It has been possible to comply with but a very small proportion of the applications for tickets which have come in from Earlestown, Widnes, Run- corn, and the various other neighbouring towns. Some incidents have occurred which prove unmis- takeably the great popularity of Mr. Chamberlain, and the strong desire there exists to see and hear him. Working-men, too poor to pay train fare, have walked into Warrington from distant places in order to secure tickets of admission; and letters have been received from others which attest the exceed- ingly high esteem in which the right honourable gentleman is held. Some idea may be had from these letters of the enthusiasm that has been kindled by the announcement of the visit of Mr. Chamber- lain to this locality. During his stay the right hon. gentleman will be the guest of Mr. W. Long, J.P., of Thelwall Heys.

div.head: LUNCHEON.
div.p: THE LUNCHEON.

The luncheon to-ole---pl;c-e-ir; a Cent upon the ground at half-past one, and there was a good attendance. Mr. Smith, of the Griffin Inn, was the caterer. In the abeence of the Hon. Leopold W. H. Powys, the president, Captain D'a Willis, occupied the chair, and he was supported by the Rev. T. Chambers (rector of Halewood), Rev. Geo. Band (vicar of Farnworth), Mr. Longton (chairman of the Show Committee), Mr. Hall (agent to Lord Derby), Dr. Booth, Mr. Warburton, and the judges. The visual loyal toasts were proposed by the chairman and honoured. "The Bishop and Clergy of all denominations" was given by the Chairman, and responded to by the Rev. Geo. Bond. The Chairman, in proposing "Success to the Farnworth Agricultural Society," said it was gratifying that the year 1885, as regarded agriculture, could compare very favour- ably with many of its predecessors. (Applause.) They had had a healthy year, and he believed it had been a good year for cattla; sheep, and other live stock. Cattle, it was reported. had increased five per cent., and sheep one per cent. He thought many farmers would agree with him that if they would only bring plenty of manure and put it in the land they would he successful. They must be very proud to see that at the Royal Agricultural Society that year a farmer under Colonel Blackburne had taken a prize for an agricultural horse. Mr. Ashton, of Roby, had also taken a prize for the beat arable farm of upwards of 100 acres. That reflected great credit on that part of the county. Then, again, Mr. Ward's daughter took the first prize at the Royal show for butter. an honour which that lady and her fatner were very proud of. When they saw at the Royal Agricul- tural Show, which was the first society in England, that people from that district were taking prizes, they wouli naturally be very proud of it. The Farnworth Society, they found, had passed through great difficulties. Three years ago the society was £3OO in debt, but he heard it had been reduced by over £2OO, and that satisfactory result was no doubt owiag to the able management of Mr. Wm. Longton and Mr. James Warburton, the chairman and vice-chairman of the committee, and other members of the committee, whose services were highly appreciated by all in that neigh- borahood. He was glad to tell them that the results of the show that day exceeded what they expected. He hoped the committee would be well rewarded for their efforts. He had great pleasure in coupling with the toast the names of Mr. Longton and Mr. Warburton. (Applause.) Mr. Longton and Mr. Warburton suitably responded.— The health of the Chairman was then drunk, and Mr. Hale proposed the health of the judges.—ln responding, Mr. Scotson referred to the depression in agriculture, and said he could only see two things to mend it. The landlord should drop the rent, the labourer should be content with less wages. He alleged that the tenant farmers suffered far more than the landlord by the depressien.—Mr. Hamer also re- sponded.
A fire broke out on Thursday morning in the Islington Industrial Home for Boys, Caledonian-road. The inmates were safely removed. The hulloing was gutted. The loss is partly covered by insurance.

Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting held on Tuesday, at Dutton Workhouse. Present— The Revs. J. W. N. Tauner, J. Lockwood, J. J. Bryant, Messrs. T. Norman. E. Aaron, W. Fisher, W. Whittaker, J. Arroweinith, E. A. Wallington, Lewis, W. Handley, J. Parr, J. G. Semilos, J. Smith, P. Speakman' Campkiu, T. Hewitt, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy Clerk). TIM ASYLUM QUESTION Aomx.—The Rev. J. W.N. Tanner moved that the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. 'T. Norman, W. Fisher, P. Speakman, R. Ashton, J Weir, E. A. Wallington, and H. Linaker (clerk) be appointed a commit- tee to visit the Chester County Asylum —The motion was seconded by Mr. W. Whittaker.—Mr. Aaron remarked that three members from Runcorn appeared to be a large num- ber to have on the committee.—Mr. Norman : You must bear in mind that almost three-fourths of the inmates of that asylum are from Runcorn. (Loud laughter.)—Mr. Parr: It's an insane place is that. (Renewed laughter.)— Mr. Speakman said he should not like the insinuation t 3 go forth that three-fourths of the inhabitants of the asylum were from Runcorn. Mr. Norman must mean three-fourths of the persons sent there by the Union were from Runcorn. —Mr. Norman said that was his meaning.—Mr. Hamilton moved that Mr. Norman's name be struck off the committee, and that only third-class railway fares be allowed, but he received no seconder.—After some further discussion it was resolved, on the 'nation of tha Rev. J. Lockwood, seconded by Mr. B. Aaron, that the committee consist of the Rey. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Norman, Wallington, Weir, and the clerk (Mr. H. Linaker), and that the clerk pay all expanses and present the aceount at the next Board meeting. SORCHanGES.—A letter was rent from the Local Govern- ment Board inquiring whether the surcharge of £3 is against J. Whitfield, assistant overseer, Walton Inferior ; of £67 Ws 5d against R. Andrews, assistant overseer, Fred- sham; and of Os against the clerk to the Board had been paid to the treasurer of the Union.—The Clerk stated that the two first-named sums had been paid, but he was appeal- ing against the surcharge upon him.

ST. HELENS NATIONAL REFORM UNION.—A meeting of the members of the St. Helens branch of the National Reform Union was held on Tuesday evening in the rooms of the Union, Naylor-street. There was a fair attendance. Mr. H. 4. Riley had been announced to deliver a lecture on "Taxation," but a letter from that gentleman was read expressing his regret at his inability to attend, and promising to give the lecture in a fortnight.—Mr. J. A Maonabb ob- served that, as the Marquis of Ripon would be in St. Helens on the night named by Mr. Riley, they might ex- pect that gentleman's lecture in three weeks. Mr. Sandford was then voted to the chair, and he said the general elec- tion was getting nearer, and it would lee well to ask what they, as the Reform Union of St. Helens, Were doing. He thought it behoved every one of them to be up and doing—to be as men of one mind, or, rather, to be a great many minds uni- ted in one—and make themselves felt in tbetown. (Applause.)— Mr. Harwood said be thought the Irish question was likely to occupy the coming Parliament as much as any question, and he suggested that it should occupy their attention that evening. (Hear, ar.)—Mr. Macnabb, Mr. J. Scott, Mr. 1 Thomas Glover, and Mr. Brockbank expressed themsalves in favour of equal local government for Ireland, but con- sidered it best fur both countries that in Itripeiiel matters she should remain under the British flag, and have such questions settled at Westminster.—Mr. James Hart saw no reason why Ireland should not have her Parliament re- stored, and all matters settled by Irishmen.—The Chairman said his firm conviction was that it would not do to separate Ireland from England as an independent nation. He be- lieved Ireland would never lose anything by being governed by England. Mr. Gladstone and his Government had done more to redress the wronide of Ireland than any Parliament that ever existed, and if it had not been for the Parnell ob- structionists and the Opposition, he (the chairman) believed that the Irish people to-day would have been in a position to have said that Mr. Gladstone had passed measures that they were quite able to live under, and also to live to ad- vantage. (Applause.)—A vote of thanks to the chairman closed the proceedings.

The moonlight outrages in Kerry continue. The police on Wednesday morning received information of two housms baying been fired into. SUDDEN DEATN.—Thomas Rigby, 74 years of age, of 2, Randon-street, St. Helens, was found dead in bed at three o'clock on Tuesday afternoou. Deceased had gme back to bed after having had his dinner. GREAT FIRE AT BARROW.—About forty thousand poncins damage has been caused by a great fire at the works ot the Barrow Shipbuilding Company. The fire broke out about ten o'clock on Tuesday night. It originated in the engi- neering department, and destroyed planing machines, lathes, models, and other plant. The fire raged with owe:- sive fary during the greater part of the night.

LATEST NE W Alderman Sir Charles Wheltham, who was Lord Mayor of London in 1878, died at his residence in London on Friday morning A thunderstorm passed over Lincolnshire on Thursday evening. At Billinghay, one man was killed and another injured by the lightning. Two boys. named. Curry and Pownall, were committed for trial at Birmingham, on Friday, charged with setting fire to the Penn-street Industrial School. The Kilmarnock Burns' Museum Committee, on Friday, puechased from Mr. Richardson, of Glasgow, the original manuscript of Burns' "Pain o' fihanter " for the sum of £235. The eleventh annual conference for the North-Western Poor Law District (Lancashire and Cheshire) was opened at Blackpoel on Friday morning, Mr. J. T. Hibbert, M.P., presiding. An inquest was held at Studley, Dorset, on Faiday, on the bodies of two young ladies, Dora Burgess and Miss Trimmell, who were drowned en Thursday while bathing in Studland bay. PROPOSED Tax ON CORN.—Lord Bateman, speaking at the annual dinner of the Leominster Agricultural Society on Friday, advocated the imposition of a tax on wheat and corn when the prize reached a point at which it was un- profitable to the British farmers. In his opinion, the recent- ly appointed Royal Commission would end in nothing. Tan COTTON TRADE.—Our Accrington correspondent telegraphs that the depression in the cotton trade is being seriously felt in East Lancashire. In almost every town there are a number of looms idle. In Darwen alone there are five mills stopped, representing 2,580 looms. In the Rosendale Valley trade was never so bad as at present. TES OLDHAM STRIKE.—The seventh week's strike pay was ()Aid on Friday, the number on the association's funds, Including children, being nearly eleven thousand. There are fifteen thousand unemployed operatives receiving no strike pay, and a number of these have others dependent on them. No serious suggestion has as yet been made for the settlement of the dispute, but there is a growing opinion that it might be arranged by a lye per cent, reduction and fall time. • THE SOLIETILL MURDER.—At the Solihull Police *Court, en Friday, John Duff was charged with the murder of John Gateley, at the Gardeners' Arms, Solihull, on December sth, 1880. Evidence was advanced with the object of iden- tifying the prisoner with a man in a long ulster, who was seen in the yard where the deceased's body was found. Superintendent Yardley said Ire examined the deceased's clothes, and found several books containing names and money entries, headed "Irish Defence Fund." Prisoner was committed for trial. THE CHOLERA. MADRID, FRIDAT.—Tbe official cholera bulletin issued this morning reports 2,500 cases and 788 deaths in Spain yesterday. FIGHTING NEAR CADIZ. It is reported from‘Madrid that a body of gendarmerie have encountered and defeated an armed band of Socialists in the neighbourhood of Grazalema, situated to the north- east of Cadiz. SPAIN AND GERMANY.—IMPORTANP COM- MUNICATION. A Central News telegram states that King Alfonso has written to the Emperor of Austria, requesting him to inform the Emperor of Germany that the safety of the Spanish dynasty is endangered by the action of the German Gov- ernment in the Caroline Islands. THE EVACUATION OF EGYPT. It is stated in diplomatic circles in Paris that the Porte, following the' advice of France, insists on a precise date being settled for the English evacuation of Egypt. It is furthermore understood that the French Government have intimated to the Sultan that no arrangement without this will be either durable or binding.
